chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Retrieval Agents and Lakebase Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This lecture introduces retrieval agents and AI engineering on Databricks. We begin with why prompting alone isn't enough and how Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) fills the gap. We then trace the evolution from prompt engineering to context engineering to harness engineering, and survey Databricks' retrieval approaches — from managed Genie Agents (recommended) and Knowledge Assistants (legacy), to fully custom code-first agents. Finally, we introduce Lakebase, Databricks' managed Postgres database, and Lakebase Search, which brings hybrid vector and keyword search directly into your operational database for co-located retrieval.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Retrieval Agents and Lakebase Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
1. Explain what retrieval agents are and why they are needed
2. Distinguish prompt engineering, context engineering, and harness engineering
3. Describe Genie Agents as the simplest managed retrieval solution on Databricks
4. Identify the knowledge source types available to a Knowledge Assistant
5. Compare declarative vs. code-first approaches to building retrieval agents
6. Explain what Lakebase is and its key capabilities for AI applications
7. Describe Lakebase Search and when to use it vs. AI Search

chunks.heading: A2. The Common Retrieval Pipeline
chunks.text:
Regardless of the framework or product you choose, every RAG system follows the same four-stage workflow. 

Understanding these stages helps you evaluate managed solutions and know what you're building when you go code-first.

 

 
 
 Indexing 
 
 Ingest & Parse 
 Documents → chunks + metadata 
 
 
 Embed & Index 
 Embedding model → vector search index 
 
 

 
 
 ➔ 
 

 
 
 Retrieval 
 
 Receive Query 
 User question hits the system 
 
 
 Plan & Route 
 Select sources → tailored sub-queries 
 
 
 Search & Rank 
 Vector search → rerank → evidence set 
 
 

 
 
 ➔ 
 

 
 
 Generation 
 
 Generate Answer 
 LLM grounds on retrieved chunks → cited answer 
 with source citations 
 
 

 
 
 ➔ 
 

 
 
 Feedback Loop 
 
 Observe & Improve 
 Traces + human feedback → refine retrieval & generation 
 continuous quality loop 
 
 
 

 
 
What are the four stages of a retrieval pipeline?
 
 

 Every RAG system — whether managed or custom — flows through four stages: two offline (preparing the index) and two online (handling the request), with a feedback loop that improves quality over time. 

 
 Indexing : Ingest source documents, parse, chunk, embed, and index them into a searchable store (plus normalize metadata). 
 Retrieval : Receive the user query, plan retrieval by selecting sources and crafting sub-queries, then search and rank results from one or more indexes. 
 Generation : Use an LLM to generate a grounded answer from the retrieved context, including source citations back to the original documents. 
 Feedback loop : Use tracing, evaluation (LLM judges, human review), and user feedback to continuously refine both retrieval behavior and answer quality. 
 

 In Section C, you'll see how Genie Agents and Knowledge Assistants handle these stages for you, and how custom agents let you own each stage directly.

What's the difference between prompt, context, and harness engineering?
 
 

 Prompt engineering focuses on crafting the instruction text sent to a model. It involves choosing the right words, formatting, and examples. It's tactical and operates at the level of a single query. 

 Context engineering is broader. It's the art and science of designing the entire information environment a model receives at inference time: not just the question, but all the supporting data, instructions, history, and constraints that shape the model's decision. It answers one question: "What does the model see?" 

 Harness engineering is broader still. It's the entire scaffolding around the model — the runtime loop that executes each conversation turn, the source of truth codified in-repo, the deterministic guardrails, and the workflow automation that make an agent reliable in production. It answers a different question: "How does the system around the model operate?" Context engineering is one component of it — the Foundry framing calls this

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Retrieval Agents and Lakebase Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: C. Retrieval Approaches on Databricks
chunks.text:
Databricks offers a spectrum of retrieval approaches — from fully managed to fully custom. **Genie Agents are the recommended managed path for RAG**; Knowledge Assistants remain available but are a legacy option. The code-first path gives you complete control.

 

 
 LEGACY 
 Managed RAG 
 Knowledge Assistant 
 Bring your own AI Search index, choose your chunking strategy, and attach multiple source types (up to 10). Full control over the retrieval pipeline. 
 

 
 RECOMMENDED 
 Managed RAG 
 Genie Agent 
 Attach a Unity Catalog volume. Databricks handles parsing, chunking, indexing, and search via Lakebase — you write zero pipeline code. 
 

 
 RECOMMENDED 
 Full Control 
 Custom Agent 
 Write your own retrieval logic, prompts, tools, and orchestration. Use LangGraph, custom Python, or any framework — essentially unlimited flexibility. 
 

 

**Genie Agents** are the go-forward declarative option: you declare *what* you want retrieved, and the system optimizes *how*. 

**Knowledge Assistants** offer additional customization (bring your own AI Search index) but are a **legacy path** — Genie Agents are recommended for new projects. 

**Custom agents** are code-first: you own the retrieval logic end to end.

chunks.heading: C2. Knowledge Source Types
chunks.text:
Agents can draw from multiple governed UC knowledge sources:

| Source Type | Description | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| **Files in UC Volume** | Point to a Unity Catalog Volume containing files like `txt`, `pdf`, `md`, `ppt/pptx`, or `doc/docx` files. KA parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes them for you. Files >50 MB are automatically skipped. | Document collections that change over time (policies, manuals, specs) |
| **AI Search Index** | Attach a pre-built AI Search index (using embedding models like `databricks-gte-large-en`). You own the parsing/chunking/indexing pipeline. | Custom RAG pipelines where you already manage the index and schema |
| **Files in UC Table / File Table** | Use a UC table (e.g. **streaming table** or have **Change Data Feed enabled**) with a `content` column (BINARY/STRING) storing file contents plus a `_metadata`/`metadata` struct with file path/name/size/mod time.| Documents ingested via connectors (SharePoint, Google Drive, Jira, Confluence) that land as file tables |

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Retrieval Agents and Lakebase Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: C3. Declarative vs. Code-First
chunks.text:
Databricks offers two approaches to building retrieval agents:

| | Declarative (Genie Agent) | Code-First (Custom Agents) |
|---|---|---|
| **Approach** | Declare what you want; the system learns and optimizes how | Write retrieval logic, prompts, tools, and orchestration yourself |
| **Setup time** | Minutes | Hours to days |
| **Customizability** | Configuration- and feedback-driven | Essentially unlimited |
| **Optimization** | Automatic via feedback loops and platform research upgrades | Manual tuning and experimentation |
| **Best for** | High-quality Q&A over docs, fast prototyping | Novel architectures, complex multi-step / tool-heavy workflows |

This course focuses on the **declarative** path. We’ll explore the components that understand the retrieval building blocks (document parsing, chunking, and AI Search), then bring them together using Genie Agents as the recommended managed approach.

What is Lakebase and what are its key capabilities?
 
 

 Lakebase is Databricks' fully managed, serverless Postgres database — built directly into the Databricks platform. It separates stateless Postgres compute from a durable cloud storage layer, enabling autoscaling , scale-to-zero , instant branching , and fast failover . 

 
 Transactional workloads — Build low-latency OLTP applications alongside your lakehouse data, connected via Databricks Apps or any standard Postgres driver. 
 Lakehouse sync — Sync Unity Catalog Delta tables into Lakebase so applications can query them at sub-millisecond latency. 
 AI & agent state — Use Lakebase as an online feature store for ML models or as a state and memory store for AI agents. 
 Native Unity Catalog integration — Governance, permissions, and identity flow seamlessly across the platform. 
 

 With that foundation in place, the next question is: how do we search this data efficiently? That's where Lakebase Search comes in.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Retrieval Agents and Lakebase Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: E. Lakebase Search for Retrieval
chunks.text:
Managed retrieval products like Genie Agents handle document-based RAG end to end. But when your data already lives in an operational database — customer reviews, product records, support tickets — you may want search **inside** that database so a single query can retrieve, JOIN, and enforce permissions in one transaction.

**Lakebase Search** (GA) adds hybrid vector and keyword search directly to Lakebase Postgres projects through two managed extensions:

 

 
 
 Extension 
 lakebase_vector 
 Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search via the lakebase_ann index type. pgvector-compatible syntax. Uses IVF + RaBitQ quantization — supports 1B+ vectors per index, builds 50–100× faster than HNSW, and indexes survive scale-to-zero. 
 

 
 + 

 
 
 Extension 
 lakebase_text 
 BM25 full-text keyword search via the lakebase_bm25 index type. Compatible with PostgreSQL's tsvector types and operators. Top-K pushdown (Block-Max WAND) retrieves only the K most relevant results instead of scoring every match. 
 

 
 = 

 
 
 Combined 
 Hybrid Search 
 Run both searches and fuse results with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). Reviews ranked well by either signal surface, and those ranked well by both rise to the top — the best of exact-term and semantic retrieval. 
 

 

 
 Learn More 
 
See the Databricks documentation on Lakebase Search ( AWS | Azure ) for setup instructions and query examples.

Instead of querying rows and columns, we'll point Genie at a Unity Catalog **volume** of Airbnb PDFs, enable **content search** so Genie can index the files, and then ask natural-language questions in **Agent mode** that are answered with **citations** back to the source documents.

2. **Created** a Genie Agent and attached the volume as a document source
3. **Enabled content search** so Genie could index and retrieve from the files
4. **Queried** the documents in Agent mode and validated cited, grounded responses

This shows how Genie can serve as a natural-language interface over **unstructured documents**, not just SQL tables.

chunks.heading: B2. Save the Embedding
chunks.text:
Next, we're going to save this embedding locally for demonstration purposes. 

Of course, you would probably save your embeddings in a table in Unity Catalog or have them computed on-the-fly and stored in ephemeral memory in your app. 

Running the next code will create a file called `embedding.txt` in your Workspace folder. After running the next cell, go to the Workspace folder to the left and inspect the file.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Information Retrieval with Lakebase Search
chunks.heading: NOTE: Run the query in Lakebase
chunks.text:
Now let's perform a vector similarity search using the embedding you just saved. 

There are a few operator classes to be familiar with, whose definitions can be found in the docs ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/projects/lakebase-vector#operator-classes) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/oltp/projects/lakebase-vector)). We will be using the `vector_cosine_ops` class, which computes the cosine similarity between embeddings. Its query operator is denoted by ` ` and returns a **cosine distance** — lower values mean higher similarity. We alias this as `distance` so you can see the score alongside each result, just like the `score` column in the BM25 query later.

Fill in the three `FILL_IN` placeholders below:
1. The **embedding column** (`embedding`) on the left side of ` `

2. The **1024-dimensional embedding** from `embedding.txt` — paste it on the right side of ` `

3. The **table name** (`doc_chunks`)

4. The output should return a chunk of text along with a distance score of ~ 0.501

 
 
 
 
 SQL Query 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 SELECT chunk_text, <FILL_IN> <=> '<FILL_IN>' AS distance
FROM <FILL_IN>
ORDER BY distance; 
 

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```sql
SELECT chunk_text, embedding 'paste your 1024-dim embedding from embedding.txt' AS distance
FROM doc_chunks
ORDER BY distance;
```

**Note:** Paste the full 1024-dimensional embedding vector from your `embedding.txt` file in place of the placeholder above. The `distance` column shows cosine distance — chunks with the **lowest** values are the most semantically similar to your query.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Information Retrieval with Lakebase Search
chunks.heading: NOTE: Run the query in Lakebase
chunks.text:
Now let's perform a keyword search using the `lakebase_bm25` index. 

The key operator here is ` `, whose definition can be found in the docs ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/projects/lakebase-text#operators) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/oltp/projects/lakebase-text)). Its signature is `tsvector bm25query_tsvector` and it returns a `double precision` value representing a **negative BM25 score** — order **ascending** to get the most relevant results first.

Fill in the four `<FILL_IN>` placeholders below:

1. All columns and the BM25 score (`*,`)

2. The **tsvector column** (`chunk_tsvector`) on the left side of ` `

3. The **search term** to match against (e.g. `'Victorian'`)

4. The **BM25 index name** (`doc_chunks_ts_idx`)

5. The output should return a chunk of text along with a distance score of ~ -0.556.

 
 
 
 
 SQL Query 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 SELECT <FILL_IN>,
 <FILL_IN> <@> to_bm25query(to_tsvector('english', '<FILL_IN>'), '<FILL_IN>') AS score
FROM doc_chunks
ORDER BY score; 
 

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```sql
SELECT *,
 chunk_tsvector to_bm25query(to_tsvector('english', 'Victorian'), 'doc_chunks_ts_idx') AS score
FROM doc_chunks
ORDER BY score;
```

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Information Retrieval with Lakebase Search
chunks.heading: NOTE: Run the query in Lakebase
chunks.text:
Finally, we will perform a hybrid search. 

It retrieves the top candidates from each search _independently_, then combines them into a single ranking using **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**. Results that rank well in either or both searches score higher. You can read more here ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/projects/lakebase-search#combine-results-with-hybrid-search) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/oltp/projects/lakebase-search)).

Using what you learned in B3 and B4, fill in the four `<FILL_IN>` placeholders below:
1. The **1024-dimensional embedding** from `embedding.txt` — paste it on the right side of ` `

2. The **tsvector column** (`chunk_tsvector`) on the left side of ` `

3. The **search term** (e.g. `'Victorian'`)

4. The **BM25 index name** (`doc_chunks_ts_idx`)

5. You will see the `rrf_score` column, ranked from best search results to least. 

 
 
 
 
 SQL Query 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 WITH vector_ranked AS (
 SELECT chunk_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY dist) AS rank
 FROM (
 SELECT chunk_id, embedding <=> '<FILL_IN>' AS dist
 FROM doc_chunks
 ORDER BY dist
 LIMIT 40
 ) v
),
keyword_ranked AS (
 SELECT chunk_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score) AS rank
 FROM (
 SELECT chunk_id,
 <FILL_IN> <@> to_bm25query(to_tsvector('english', '<FILL_IN>'), '<FILL_IN>') AS score
 FROM doc_chunks
 ORDER BY score
 LIMIT 40
 ) k
)
SELECT d.chunk_id, LEFT(d.chunk_text, 120) AS preview,
 COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + v.rank), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0) AS rrf_score
FROM doc_chunks d
LEFT JOIN vector_ranked v ON d.chunk_id = v.chunk_id
LEFT JOIN keyword_ranked k ON d.chunk_id = k.chunk_id
WHERE v.chunk_id IS NOT NULL OR k.chunk_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC, d.chunk_id
LIMIT 10; 
 

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```sql
WITH vector_ranked AS (
 SELECT chunk_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY dist) AS rank
 FROM (
 SELECT chunk_id, embedding ' ' AS dist
 FROM doc_chunks
 ORDER BY dist
 LIMIT 40
 ) v
),
keyword_ranked AS (
 SELECT chunk_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score) AS rank
 FROM (
 SELECT chunk_id,
 chunk_tsvector to_bm25query(to_tsvector('english', 'Victorian'), 'doc_chunks_ts_idx') AS score
 FROM doc_chunks
 ORDER BY score
 LIMIT 40
 ) k
)
SELECT d.chunk_id, LEFT(d.chunk_text, 120) AS preview,
 COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + v.rank), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0) AS rrf_score
FROM doc_chunks d
LEFT JOIN vector_ranked v ON d.chunk_id = v.chunk_id
LEFT JOIN keyword_ranked k ON d.chunk_id = k.chunk_id
WHE

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Before a retrieval agent can answer questions about your documents, those documents must be transformed from raw files into searchable, structured data. This lecture covers the key Databricks AI Functions that power this pipeline: `ai_parse_document` for extracting text from PDFs, `ai_classify` and `ai_extract` for structuring content, and `ai_prep_search` for chunking text for AI Search or leveraging reverse ETL for Lakebase Search integration. We'll also cover how chunks flow into an AI Search index: what happens when you create one, how it stays in sync, and why the text you embed differs from the text you retrieve.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
1. Describe how `ai_parse_document` extracts structured content from PDFs
2. Explain the role of `ai_classify` and `ai_extract` in document processing
3. Use `ai_prep_search` to chunk text for AI Search
4. Compare different chunking strategies and their trade-offs
5. Explain what happens when an AI Search index is created and how it stays in sync
6. Distinguish between `chunk_to_embed` and `chunk_to_retrieve` and why they differ

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: A1. From Raw Files to Searchable Data
chunks.text:
Document Processing Pipeline: parallel branches from parsed document 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Raw PDF 
 UC Volume 

 
 

 
 
 ai_parse_document 
 Extract text + layout 
 -> VARIANT output 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 ai_prep_search 
 Chunk for VS 

 
 
 ai_classify 
 Categorize content 

 
 
 ai_extract 
 Pull structured fields 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Enriched Chunks 
 chunks 
 + category labels 
 + extracted fields 
 -> AI Search 
 
 

 
 
How does the document processing pipeline work?
 
 

 RAG systems are only as good as the data they retrieve. Before documents can power a RAG agent, they must be processed through a pipeline that extracts, classifies, and chunks the content. Databricks Knowledge Assistant can ingest UC Volumes and tables directly. It runs its own parsing and chunking pipeline under the hood, so you don't need to wire these AI Functions yourself. 

 Databricks provides a set of AI Functions ( AWS | Azure | GCP ), SQL-callable functions powered by foundation models, that handle each stage. As an example workflow, we might have: 

 
 ai_parse_document produce a VARIANT output 
 ai_prep_search , ai_classify , and ai_extract run in parallel off that parsed document 
 Join the classifications and extracted fields onto the chunk table as extra metadata columns for filtering or ranking in AI Search

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: B1. How It Works
chunks.text:
`ai_parse_document` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_parse_document) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_parse_document) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_parse_document)) invokes state-of-the-art generative AI models to extract structured content from PDFs and images. It returns a structured JSON object (VARIANT type) with layout-aware text extraction.

 
 
 ai_parse_document: from raw PDF to structured output 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Raw PDF 
 
 
 
 table 
 
 img 
 
 
 
 
 
 ai_parse_document 
 OCR + layout analysis, 
 figure descriptions, 
 bounding boxes 
 
 
 
 
 Structured JSON 
 document: 
 elements: [...] 
 pages: [...] 
 error_status: [...] 
 metadata: {...} 
 
 

 
 
What are the four stages of a Knowledge Assistant pipeline?
 
 

 Databricks AI Functions transform raw PDFs into searchable data in three stages: Parse (ai_parse_document) extracts text and layout as structured JSON 
 Classify + Extract (ai_classify, ai_extract) categorize and pull structured fields 
 Chunk (ai_prep_search) splits text into semantic chunks for AI Search. 
 version is an option flag that tells ai_parse_document which schema/output version to use.
 v2 ('2.0') is the recommended version: it gives you the newer output format (HTML tables, improved layout, etc.) and is what v2 ai_extract / ai_classify examples are tuned for.
 

 SELECT
 path,
 ai_parse_document(content, MAP('version', '2.0')) AS parsed_content
FROM READ_FILES('/Volumes/...', format => 'binaryFile')
 
 The output includes document:elements (individual content blocks) and document:pages (page-level breakdown), giving you flexible access to the parsed content.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: C. Classifying and Extracting with AI Functions
chunks.text:
Next, we will look at some examples of how to use `ai_classify()` and `ai_extract()`. Parsing the raw PDF into a structured JSON is straightforward as indicated above. However, we now have to use the table-valude function `variant_explode` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode)) to un-nest our parsed document.

 
 
How does variant_explode work?
 
 

 The variant_explode table-valued function turns a VARIANT array or object into a set of rows with three columns: 

 
 pos INT — the position of the element within the array or object 
 key STRING — the field name (objects only; NULL for arrays) 
 value VARIANT — the field value or array element 
 

 Behavior depends on the input shape: 
 
 VARIANT object → key and value are the object's keys and values. 
 VARIANT array → key is always NULL ; value holds each element. 
 NULL or non-VARIANT-array/object input → no rows are produced . To preserve the row with NULL values instead, use variant_explode_outer ( AWS | Azure | GCP ). 
 

 SELECT pos, key, value
FROM variant_explode(parse_json('{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}'));

-- pos | key | value
-- ----+------+--------
-- 0 | name | "Ada"
-- 1 | age | 36
 

 Use variant_explode as a lateral source (e.g., in a LATERAL VIEW or comma join) to flatten semi-structured VARIANT columns into queryable rows.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: C1. Categorize Content: `ai_classify`
chunks.text:
`ai_classify` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_classify) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_classify) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_classify)) assigns a label to text from a set of categories you define. It's useful for routing documents through different processing paths.
- `ai_parsed_document` produces a `VARIANT` column called `parsed_content`. Passing `parsed_content` lets ai_classify see the full, parsed document instead of just a single text string.
- `["invoice", "receipt", "contract", "report"]` is the set of categories you want the model to choose from.

 
 
 ai_classify: assigns a category label to text 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Parsed Text 
 
 
 
 
 "Total due: $4,092..." 
 
 
 "Payment terms: Net 30" 
 
 
 
 
 
 ai_classify 
 parsed_content, 
 ["invoice",...] 
 
 
 
 invoice 
 Single label returned 
 
 
Sample Code:
 WITH elements AS (
 <read_file_logic> t,
 LATERAL variant_explode(parsed:document:elements) AS element
 <additional_WHERE_logic>
),
classified AS (
 SELECT
 content,
 ai_classify(
 content,
 '["property_description","pricing_information","location_details","amenities","host_information","other"]'
 ) AS cls
 FROM elements
)
SELECT
 content,
 cls:response[0] AS category -- Parse the results from ai_classify()
FROM classified

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: C2. Pull Structured Fields: `ai_extract`
chunks.text:
`ai_extract` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_extract) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_extract) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_extract)) extracts specific fields from unstructured text. You define what to extract, and the AI model finds the values.

 
 
 ai_extract: pulls structured fields from text 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Parsed Text 
 
 
 
 
 "From: Apex Roofing" 
 
 
 "Date: Jan 15, 2026" 
 
 
 "Total: $4,092.64" 
 
 
 
 
 
 ai_extract 
 parsed_content, 
 ["invoice_id",...] 
 
 
 
 Structured JSON 
 error_message: null 
 metadata: {...} 
 response: 
 invoice_id: "1234" 
 date: "Jan 15, 2026" 
 total: "$4,092.64" 
 
 

Sample Code:
 WITH elements AS (
 <read_file_logic> t,
 <variant_explode_logic>
),
extracted AS (
 SELECT
 content,
 ai_extract(
 content,
 '["invoice_id", "date", "total"]'
 ) AS ext
 FROM elements
)
SELECT
 content,
 ext:response.invoice_id AS invoice_id,
 ext:response.date AS date,
 ext:response.total AS total
FROM extracted
LIMIT 15

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: D1. What is `ai_prep_search`?
chunks.text:
`ai_prep_search` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search)) is a Databricks AI Function that **chunks text for AI Search**. Instead of manually splitting text by character count or using custom chunking logic, `ai_prep_search` uses AI models to split text into semantically meaningful chunks.

 
 
 ai_prep_search: chunks text at semantic boundaries for AI Search 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Parsed Text 
 
 
 
 
 "Property is located in..." 
 
 
 "House rules include..." 
 
 
 "Host info: Superhost..." 
 
 
 
 
 
 ai_prep_search 
 AI-powered semantic 
 boundary detection 
 
 
 
 Chunk Array 
 
 Chunk 1: "Property is..." 
 
 Chunk 2: "House rules..." 
 
 Chunk 3: "Host info..." 
 
 
 
 
Sample Code:
 SELECT ai_prep_search(parsed_text) AS chunks
FROM parsed_documents

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: D2. Chunking Strategy Considerations
chunks.text:
Regardless of the chunking method, keep these principles in mind:

- **Chunk size vs. embedding model limits** - chunks must fit within the embedding model's context window (e.g., 512 tokens for many models). Text beyond the limit is silently truncated.
- **Overlap** - including a small overlap between consecutive chunks (e.g. 10-20%) prevents information from being lost at chunk boundaries.
- **Granularity trade-off** - smaller chunks are more precise for retrieval but may lack surrounding context. Larger chunks capture more context but may dilute the signal.

 
 Lost in the middle 
 
The "Lost in the Middle" phenomenon means LLMs tend to overlook information buried deep in long contexts. Creating smaller, focused chunks ensures critical details aren't missed during retrieval.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: D3. Embed vs. Retrieve: Why They're Different Columns
chunks.text:
From `ai_prep_search` we can produce two distinct columns from the same parsed content. Understanding this separation is important before you create an AI Search Index.

 
 
 chunk_to_embed vs chunk_to_retrieve: different text for different purposes 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ai_prep_search 
 Example output per chunk: 
 chunk_to_embed 
 chunk_to_retrieve 
 chunk_id 
 chunk_position 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 chunk_to_embed 
 Context-enriched text: 
 "Title: House Rules 
 Section: Pets > The fee..." 

 

 
 
 Embedding Model 
 [0.23, -0.41, 0.08, ...] 

 
 
 chunk_to_retrieve 
 Raw original text: 
 "The fee is $50 per pet 
 per night. Max 2 pets." 

 

 
 
 LLM Context 
 Generates answer from 
 clean, original text 
 
 

 
 
Why not use the same text for both?
 
 

 Embedding and retrieval serve different goals: 

 
 Embedding needs to answer: "What is this chunk about?" Adding surrounding context (headers, section titles) helps the embedding model place the chunk in the right region of vector space, even if the chunk text alone is ambiguous. A chunk that says "The fee is $50" is meaningless without context — but prepending "Cleaning Policy > Late Checkout" makes it findable. 
 Retrieval needs to answer: "What should the LLM read?" The LLM needs the original text to generate accurate answers. Prepending metadata here would waste context window tokens and could confuse the model with formatting artifacts. 
 

 This separation is a key retrieval quality technique: optimize for findability when embedding, optimize for readability when retrieving.

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: E1. What Happens When You Create an Index
chunks.text:
Once your chunks are in a Delta table, you create an AI Search index to make them searchable. 

 
 
 Index creation lifecycle 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Step 1 
 Read Source Table 
 
 
 
 
 "Property is located..." 
 
 
 "House rules include..." 
 
 
 
 
 
 Step 2 
 Compute 
 Embeddings 
 Calls embedding model 
 on each chunk_text row 
 [0.23, -0.41, ...] 
 
 
 
 Step 3 
 AI Search (ANN) 
 Index 
 Organizes vectors for 
 fast nearest-neighbor 
 lookup 
 
 
 
 Step 4 
 Store Synced 
 Columns 
 chunk_id 
 chunk_text 
 source_path 
 
 

**Parameter to pay attention when creating a VS endpoint**

| Parameters | What It Does |
|---|---|
| `endpoint_name` | Which VS endpoint serves the index (shared compute in this course) |
| `source_table_name` | The Delta table containing your chunks |
| `index_name` | Fully-qualified name for your index in Unity Catalog |
| `pipeline_type` | `TRIGGERED` (sync on demand) or `CONTINUOUS` (sync automatically) |
| `primary_key` | Unique row identifier used to track which rows have been processed |
| `embedding_source_column` | Which column to send to the embedding model |
| `embedding_model_endpoint_name` | The model that converts text to vectors (e.g., `databricks-gte-large-en`) |
| `columns_to_sync` | Which columns to store alongside vectors so they can be returned in search results |

This initial sync can take several minutes depending on the number of rows and chunk sizes.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Document Parsing and Chunking Strategies
chunks.heading: E2. Keeping the Index in Sync with Change Data Feed
chunks.text:
When you write chunks to a Delta table for AI Search, you'll enable **Change Data Feed (CDF)**:

```sql
ALTER TABLE chunks_table SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true)
```

For Delta Sync indexes on standard endpoints, CDF is required and is what enables incremental sync behavior. With CDF enabled, AI Search processes only rows changed since the last sync, rather than rebuilding the index the way storage-optimized endpoints partially do on each sync.

 
 
 Change Data Feed: Delta table tracks changes, VS index reads only the diff 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Delta Table 
 (chunks) 

 
 
 existing row (unchanged) 
 
 + new row (INSERT) 
 
 ~ updated row (UPDATE) 
 
 - deleted row (DELETE) 

 
 
 CDF log 

 
 
 Change Data Feed 
 Records only the diff: 
 _change_type 
 _commit_version 
 _commit_timestamp 

 
 
 sync 

 
 
 AI Search 
 Index 
 Processes only changed 
 rows, not the full 
 table on every sync 
 Fast incremental updates 
 
 

**Sync modes** control *when* those changes flow to the index:

| Mode | Behavior | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **`TRIGGERED`** | Syncs only when you explicitly call `index.sync()` or through the UI | You control when updates happen, which is good for batch workflows where you update chunks periodically |
| **`CONTINUOUS`** | Syncs automatically as the source table changes | Near-real-time freshness, but uses more compute |

chunks.text: In this demo, we'll use Databricks AI Functions to transform raw PDFs into structured tabular data. We'll parse documents, classify their content, and extract specific fields, turning unstructured files into queryable tables.

chunks.heading: Learning Objectives

By the end of this demo, you will be able to:
1. Parse a PDF using `ai_parse_document`
2. Classify parsed content using `ai_classify`
3. Extract structured fields using `ai_extract`
4. Store the results in a Delta table

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: A. Classroom Setup
chunks.text: As a part of the workspace setup, certain assets have been managed for you (volumes, PDF, etc.). Here, we read in from the shared catalog `dbacademy`, schema `rag_all`, and volume `vol_all` the PDF `airbnb_listings.pdf`.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: B. Parsing Documents with `ai_parse_document`
chunks.text:
Let's start by parsing the Airbnb listings PDF. The `ai_parse_document` function reads the binary content and returns a machine-friendly format: a structured JSON representation of the document.
- We'll use the pre-defined variable from above `LISTINGS_PDF`
- We will also use `MAP('version', '2.0)`. This pins the parse output to the v2.0 schema (elements array, bbox, descriptions, etc.) instead of relying on whatever the current default version is.

1. After running the next cell, expand the **parsed** column to view the parsed PDF contents.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: B1. Exploring the Parsed Output
chunks.text:
The parsed output is a single `VARIANT` column containing a nested JSON structure. To work with individual content blocks, we need to flatten it. The query below uses two key SQL patterns:

- **`LATERAL variant_explode(parsed:document:elements)`**: The colon (`:`) operator navigates into the VARIANT to reach the `elements` array. `variant_explode` ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/variant_explode)) then converts each array element into its own row, giving us one row per content block. The `LATERAL` keyword lets it reference the `parsed` column from the same `FROM` clause.
- **`element.value:type::STRING`**: Each exploded row has a `value` column (the array element as VARIANT). The `:` operator drills into fields like `type` and `content`, and `::STRING` casts the result to a string.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: C. Classifying Content with `ai_classify`
chunks.text:
After parsing, we have a flat list of text blocks — but we don't yet know *what kind* of content each block contains. Is it a property description? Pricing info? House rules? **Classification** answers that question: it reads each text block and assigns it a category label from a list you define.

This is a separate step from **extraction**, which pulls out specific field values like property name or neighborhood. Think of it this way:
- **Classify** → *"What type of content is this?"* (e.g., `property_description`)
- **Extract** → *"What specific facts does this content contain?"* (e.g., `property_name: "Sunny Victorian"`)

Classification is useful on its own — for example, you could filter your table to only `pricing_information` rows — and it also helps downstream extraction by letting you target the right labels to the right content.

A few things to note in the query below:

- **`LENGTH(...) > 50`**: Filters out short elements (headers, page numbers, etc.) that don't carry enough text for meaningful classification.
- **`ai_classify(content, '["property_description", ...]')`**: The second argument is a JSON array of candidate labels. The AI model reads the text and picks the best match.
- **`cls:response[0]`**: `ai_classify` returns a VARIANT with a `response` array. The `[0]` index retrieves the top predicted label.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: D. Extracting Structured Fields with `ai_extract`
chunks.text:
In order to turn unstructured text into structured, queryable data, we need to pull out specific pieces of information — names, locations, categories, numbers — from free-form prose. This process is called **entity extraction**: the AI reads a block of text and identifies the concrete facts buried inside it.

For example, a paragraph like *"Sunny Victorian in Hayes Valley with WiFi and a garden"* contains several distinct facts: a property name (`Sunny Victorian`), a neighborhood (`Hayes Valley`), and amenities (`WiFi`, `garden`). Extraction locates and returns each of these as named fields, so you end up with clean columns you can filter, join, and aggregate — just like any other table.

`ai_extract` handles this for you: you tell it which fields to look for, and it returns a structured JSON object with those fields populated. Let's extract property name, neighborhood, property type, and key amenities from the parsed listing text.

A few things to note in the query below:

- **`LENGTH(...) > 100`**: Uses a higher threshold than `ai_classify` because extraction needs enough surrounding text to locate meaningful field values.
- **`ai_extract(content, '["property_name", "neighborhood", ...]')`**: The second argument lists the field names you want. The AI model scans the text and returns a JSON object with those keys populated.
- **`ext:response.property_name`**: The result VARIANT has a `response` object. Use dot notation to access each extracted field by name.

We can also explore the raw `ai_extract` VARIANT output directly, without unpacking individual fields. This lets you see the full JSON structure returned by the function, useful for understanding the schema before deciding which fields to extract.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: E. Storing Results in a Delta Table
chunks.text:
Let's combine parsing, classification, and extraction into a single pipeline and save the results. The query below chains everything into one `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` statement:

1. The `elements` CTE parses the PDF and flattens it (same as section B1)
2. The `classified_extracted` CTE runs both `ai_classify` and `ai_extract` on each element. Since they're in the same `SELECT`, Databricks can process them in parallel per row
3. The final `SELECT` unpacks both results and writes them as named columns

Run the cell below to create a structured table from the parsed PDF content.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Transforming PDFs to Structured Data
chunks.heading: F. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. **Parsed** PDFs using `ai_parse_document` to extract structured content
2. **Classified** parsed text into categories using `ai_classify`
3. **Extracted** structured fields using `ai_extract`
4. **Stored** the results in a Delta table for downstream analysis

This **Parse → Classify → Extract** pattern is ideal for turning unstructured documents into structured, queryable data.

chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This lecture covers the theory behind AI Search before you build one in the next demo. We'll explore how embeddings and similarity search power retrieval, how AI Search is organized into endpoints and indexes and the search modes it supports, how agents use AI Search under the hood, and when to choose managed RAG vs. building your own. We'll also cover how Unity Catalog governs the entire pipeline.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
1. Explain how embeddings transform text into searchable vectors
2. Describe how cosine similarity drives retrieval ranking
3. Describe the roles of AI Search endpoints and indexes
4. Compare the index types for providing embeddings (managed, self-managed, direct access)
5. Distinguish semantic, keyword, and hybrid search
6. Compare managed RAG (Knowledge Assistants) and custom RAG approaches
7. Explain how Unity Catalog governs AI Search indexes

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. What Are Embeddings?

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: A2. The Similarity Search Pipeline
chunks.text:
When you search a vector index, the system:
1. Converts your query text into an embedding vector
2. Finds the closest vectors in the index (using cosine similarity or other distance metrics)
3. Returns the corresponding text chunks, ranked by relevance

 
 
 Similarity Search Flow 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Query Text 
 "pet-friendly?" 

 

 
 
 Embed 
 [0.23, -0.41, ...] 

 

 
 
 Find Nearest 
 Cosine similarity 

 

 
 
 Top Results 
 
 Chunk 1 (0.94) 
 
 Chunk 2 (0.87) 
 
 
 

For fast retrieval at scale, Databricks uses **Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN)** algorithms, trading a small amount of precision for dramatic speed gains.

When you use `similarity_search` on an AI Search index, your query text is embedded, compared against all vectors in the index, and the top matches are returned with their similarity scores. You'll see this in action in the next demo.

 
 Learn More 
 
See the full AI Search documentation ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) for details on endpoints, indexes, and APIs.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: A3. What Is AI Search?
chunks.text:
**AI Search** is a retrieval solution built into the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform and integrated with Unity Catalog governance. Given a query, its core job is to find the stored embeddings that are **most semantically similar** (using vector similarity). It is the retrieval engine behind RAG systems, recommender systems, and image or video search.

To stay fast at scale, AI Search uses the **Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)** algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. This means lookups remain quick even across hundreds of millions of vectors.

Every deployment is built from two components: **endpoints** and **indexes**. We look at those next, then at how embeddings get into an index and the ways you can search it.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: A4. Providing Embeddings: Index Types
chunks.text:
How do vectors get into an index? There are three approaches. The first two keep the index automatically in sync with a Delta source; the third gives you manual control. In each diagram, the left side shows how the index is **created** and the right side shows the **query endpoint** at serving time — the numbered steps trace a single query.

**Databricks-managed embeddings (Delta Sync)** — you point at a text column and choose an embedding model; Databricks computes the embeddings, optionally saves them to a table, and keeps the index synced as the source changes. The simplest path, and the one used in this course. At query time, (1) the query is embedded with the same model, (2) compared against the vector index, and (3) the nearest results are returned to the app.

 
 
 Databricks-managed embeddings: source Delta table to embedding model to vector index, queried at serving time 
 
 
 
 
 
 Create vector index 
 (Databricks calculates and 
 optionally saves embeddings) 
 Query endpoint 
 
 
 
 Source Delta 
 table 
 
 
 
 Embedding model 
 
 
 
 Embeddings

 Vector index 
 
 
 
 
 
 Query 
 
 
 
 LLM 
 application 
 
 
 
 
 
 1 
 
 2 
 
 3 
 
 

**Self-managed embeddings (Delta Sync)** — you precompute embeddings and store them in the source table; the index still auto-syncs on changes, but there is no embedding model on the create side. You **cannot later convert** a self-managed index to managed — you would recreate it.

 
 
 Self-managed precalculated embeddings: source Delta table syncs to a vector index that is queried at serving time 
 
 
 
 
 
 Create vector index 
 (precalculated embeddings) 
 Query endpoint 
 
 
 
 Source Delta

**Direct Access** — you write vectors directly through the REST API or SDK, with no source table and no automatic sync. Best when an external pipeline computes embeddings or you need real-time upserts.

 
 
 Direct Access: a vector index with no source table and no automatic sync, queried at serving time 
 
 
 
 
 
 Create vector index 
 (precalculated embeddings, 
 no automatic sync)

Available on storage-optimized endpoints only, a full-text search index needs no embedding column : it searches text directly with BM25 keyword matching and uses triggered sync. Useful for pure key

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. Two Paths to RAG
chunks.text:
Now that you've built the full custom pipeline (parse, chunk, index, search), let's zoom out. Databricks provides two complementary approaches to building retrieval systems:

 
 
 Managed RAG vs Custom RAG: two paths from documents to answers 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Documents 
 PDFs, tables, 
 UC Volumes 

 
 
 

 
 
 Managed RAG 
 Genie Agent 
 Parsing, chunking, embedding, 
 indexing, serving are automatically implemented 

 
 
 Custom RAG 
 AI SQL Functions + Additional Logic 
 ai_parse_document → ai_prep_search 
 → Delta table → AI Search index 
 Full control over every component 

 
 
 

 
 
 Answers 
 LLM + retrieved 
 context 
 
 

**Managed RAG (Genie Agents):**
- You provide documents (in a UC Volume or AI Search Index)
- The system handles parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, and serving
- Optimized automatically via feedback loops
- Best for: standard RAG use cases where speed to production matters

**Custom RAG (Agent Framework + AI Search):**
- You build the pipeline yourself with full ownership of each step
- Full control over parsing strategy, chunking approach, embedding model, and retrieval logic
- Use AI Search indexes as retrieval tools in your custom agent
- Best for: unique requirements, complex multi-step reasoning, novel architectures

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2. Governance with Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
AI Search indexes are governed by Unity Catalog. Access to Unity Catalog objects in the retrieval pipeline is controlled with Unity Catalog privileges, while AI search endpoints are controlled with endpoint ACLs. Audit visibility is available through system tables, and lineage can be captured across Unity Catalog tables and paths used in the retrieval pipeline.

 
 
 Governance across the retrieval pipeline with Unity Catalog and AI search endpoint ACLs 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Governance across the retrieval pipeline 

 
 
 UC Volume 
 Source PDFs 

 

 
 
 Delta Table 
 Chunks + metadata 

 

 
 
 VS Index 
 Vectors + synced cols 

 

 
 
 VS Endpoint 
 Query interface 

 

 
 
 Agent 
 RAG 

 
 
 UC privileges 
 UC privileges 
 UC privileges 
 Endpoint ACLs 
 Queries via 
 endpoint

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 06 Lecture - AI Search on Databricks
chunks.heading: C. AI Search vs. Lakebase Search
chunks.text:
Databricks now offers two search options for retrieval. They complement each other and serve different architectures:

| | **AI Search** | **Lakebase Search** |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Managed search service over Unity Catalog tables and volumes — handles embedding, indexing, and retrieval as a fully managed stack | Postgres extensions adding vector + keyword search inside a Lakebase project |
| **Primary use case** | Production search — search bars, recommendation systems, and document RAG for unstructured content (PDFs, docs, slides) | Operational search — query structured and semi-structured data already in Postgres |
| **Used by** | Search bars, recommender systems, Genie Agents, custom RAG agents, any application calling the AI Search API | Applications backed by Lakebase — customer-facing apps, internal tools, agent memory |
| **Search modes** | Vector (ANN), keyword (BM25), hybrid (RRF), and hybrid + reranker | Vector (ANN), keyword (BM25), and hybrid (RRF fusion) |
| **JOINs with operational data** | No — results come back as a separate retrieval call | Yes — search, JOIN, and filter in one SQL query, one transaction |
| **Permissions model** | Unity Catalog ACLs on the index | Postgres row-level GRANTs on the same tables |
| **Index management** | Fully managed by Databricks | You create indexes with `CREATE INDEX ... USING lakebase_ann / lakebase_bm25` |
| **Lakehouse integration** | Native — indexes sync from UC tables/volumes via Delta Sync | Via synced tables — sync a UC table into Lakebase with type mapping for search columns |

 
 When to choose which 
 
Use AI Search when you want a fully managed search engine — search bars, recommendations, or document RAG — with built-in hybrid retrieval, reranking, and quality evaluation out of the box. Use Lakebase Search when your data already lives in Lakebase and you want low-latency search co-located with your operational tables — for example, searching customer reviews, product catalogs, or support tickets alongside structured metadata in a single SQL query.

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 07 Lab - Chunking PDFs and AI Search
chunks.heading: B1. Extract Elements with `ai_parse_document`
chunks.text:
The `ai_parse_document` function returns a `VARIANT` value describing the layout of a document: its pages, elements, and the text content of each element. To work with individual elements as rows, you explode the `elements` array out of the returned `VARIANT`.

Complete the following in the TODO cell below:

1. Call `ai_parse_document()` on the `content` column, passing `MAP('version', '2.0')` as the options argument.

2. Read the source PDF using `READ_FILES()` with the `binaryFile` format.

3. Use `variant_explode()` on the `elements` array to produce one row per document element.

4. Save the resulting DataFrame as a table named `parsed_house_rules`.

**NOTE:** This will parse ~300 PDF elements and may take a minute or two to complete.

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
parsed_df = spark.sql(f"""
 WITH parsed AS (
 SELECT
 path,
 ai_parse_document(content, MAP('version', '2.0')) AS parsed
 FROM READ_FILES('{HOUSE_RULES_PDF}', format => 'binaryFile')
 )
 SELECT
 path,
 element.value:type::STRING AS element_type,
 element.value:content::STRING AS content
 FROM parsed,
 LATERAL variant_explode(parsed.parsed:document:elements) AS element
 WHERE element.value:content IS NOT NULL
""")

parsed_df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("parsed_house_rules")
```

chunks.heading: C1. Generate Chunks
chunks.text:
The `ai_prep_search` function intelligently chunks parsed text. It uses AI models to split text at semantically meaningful boundaries, which produces higher-quality retrieval units than simple fixed-size splitting.

**IMPORTANT:** `ai_prep_search()` needs the full `ai_parse_document` `VARIANT` per document — not the flattened elements stored in `parsed_house_rules`. This means you must run it against the original parsed output rather than the table you created in Section B.

Complete the following in the TODO cell below:

1. Pass the full `parsed` `VARIANT` column into `ai_prep_search()`.

2. Explode `prepped:document:contents` to produce one row per chunk.

3. Extract the `chunk_id`, `chunk_position`, `chunk_to_retrieve`, and `chunk_to_embed` fields from each chunk.

4. Save the results to a table named `house_rules_chunks`, enabling `mergeSchema`.

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
chunks_df = spark.sql(f"""
 WITH parsed AS (
 SELECT
 path,
 ai_parse_document(content, MAP('version', '2.0')) AS parsed
 FROM READ_FILES('{HOUSE_RULES_PDF}', format => 'binaryFile')
 ),
 prepped AS (
 SELECT
 path,
 ai_prep_search(parsed) AS prepped
 FROM parsed
 )
 SELECT
 p.path,
 chunk.value:chunk_id::STRING AS chunk_id,
 chunk.value:chunk_position::INT AS chunk_position,
 chunk.value:chunk_to_retrieve::STRING AS chunk_to_retrieve,
 chunk.value:chunk_to_embed::STRING AS chunk_to_embed
 FROM prepped p,
 LATERAL variant_explode(p.prepped:document:contents) AS chunk
""")

chunks_df.write.mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("house_rules_chunks")
```

chunks.heading: C2. Understanding the Output
chunks.text:
The chunks table contains two columns of particular interest as you build an AI Search index:

| Column | Purpose | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `chunk_to_retrieve` | Shown to the LLM after retrieval | The raw (or near-raw) chunk text, preserving full content and structure so the model has everything it needs to answer questions. |
| `chunk_to_embed` | Sent to the embedding model | A cleaned, context-enriched string that prepends document-level metadata (title, section headers, page number, captions, etc.) to the chunk text, optimized purely for retrieval quality. |

Complete the following:

1. Fill in the query below to select all rows from `house_rules_chunks`.

2. In the first row of the produced table, click the dropdown to expand the `chunk_to_retrieve` and `chunk_to_embed` columns.

3. Inspect the results and confirm that the raw text is stored in `chunk_to_retrieve` while `chunk_to_embed` holds the context-enriched text prepared for embeddings. To see the format of `chunk_to_embed`, review the documentation ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search#chunk_to_embed-format) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search#chunk_to_embed-format) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/sql/language-manual/functions/ai_prep_search#chunk_to_embed-format)).

chunks.heading: D. Write Chunks to Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
You need to persist the chunks in a Delta table with Change Data Feed (CDF) enabled — this is **required** for AI Search to sync automatically. CDF tracks and records all changes (inserts, updates, deletes) to the table, allowing downstream systems to efficiently detect and process data modifications.

Complete the following in the TODO cell below:

1. Add a `chunk_id` column generated with the `uuid()` expression to serve as the primary key for the table and index.

2. Alias `chunk_to_embed` as `chunk_text` (the column AI Search will embed) and `chunk_to_retrieve` as `retrieval_text`.

3. Write the DataFrame to `CHUNKS_TABLE` in `delta` format using `overwrite` mode with `overwriteSchema` enabled.

4. Set the `delta.enableChangeDataFeed` table property to `true`.

 
 Learn more about CDF 
 
See the Databricks documentation on Change Data Feed ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) for a deeper dive.
 
 

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import expr, lit, col

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 07 Lab - Chunking PDFs and AI Search
chunks.heading: Map ai_prep_search outputs into your chunks table schema
chunks.text:
chunks_with_id = (
 chunks_df
 .withColumn("chunk_id", expr("uuid()")) # PK for the table / index
 .withColumn("source_path", col("path"))
 .select(
 "chunk_id",
 col("chunk_to_embed").alias("chunk_text"), # for embeddings
 col("chunk_to_retrieve").alias("retrieval_text"),
 "source_path"
 )
)

chunks_with_id.write.format("delta") \
 .mode("overwrite") \
 .option("overwriteSchema", "true") \
 .option("delta.enableChangeDataFeed", "true") \
 .saveAsTable(CHUNKS_TABLE)

spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE {CHUNKS_TABLE} SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true)")

print(f"Chunks table written: {CHUNKS_TABLE}")
display(spark.table(CHUNKS_TABLE))
```

chunks.heading: E2. Create the Delta Sync Index
chunks.text:
Create a **Delta Sync Index** with **managed embeddings**, meaning Databricks automatically computes embeddings from the source column you designate.

Complete the following in the TODO cell below:

1. Call `create_delta_sync_index()` on the `AISearchClient` object `client`.

2. Set `source_table_name` to `CHUNKS_TABLE` and `index_name` to `VS_INDEX`.

3. Set `primary_key` to the column that uniquely identifies each chunk.

4. Set `embedding_source_column` to the column holding the context-enriched text and `embedding_model_endpoint_name` to `EMBEDDING_MODEL`.

5. Use `pipeline_type="TRIGGERED"` so the index syncs on demand rather than continuously.

**NOTE:** Index creation and the initial sync can take several minutes. The `except` block re-syncs the index if it already exists, so re-running the cell is safe.

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python

chunks.module: Building RAG Agents with Agent Bricks
chunks.lecture: 07 Lab - Chunking PDFs and AI Search
chunks.heading: Create the index if it doesn't already exist
chunks.text:
try:
 index = client.create_delta_sync_index(
 endpoint_name=VS_ENDPOINT,
 source_table_name=CHUNKS_TABLE,
 index_name=VS_INDEX,
 pipeline_type="TRIGGERED",
 primary_key="chunk_id",
 embedding_source_column="chunk_text",
 embedding_model_endpoint_name=EMBEDDING_MODEL,
 columns_to_sync=["chunk_id", "chunk_text", "source_path"],
 )
 print(f"Index '{VS_INDEX}' created and syncing.")
except Exception as e:
 if "already exists" in str(e):
 index = client.get_index(endpoint_name=VS_ENDPOINT, index_name=VS_INDEX)
 print(f"Index '{VS_INDEX}' already exists. Syncing latest data.")
 index.sync()
 else:
 raise

print(index.describe())
```

chunks.heading: F. Test the Index
chunks.text:
Now that the index is online, test it with three different search modes:

| Subsection | Search Mode | `query_type` | How It Works |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Similarity Search (Vector ANN) | *default* | Semantic vector similarity using Approximate Nearest Neighbor |
| F2 | Hybrid Search | `hybrid` | Combines vector and BM25 keyword matching via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) |
| F3 | Full-Text Keyword Search (Beta) | `FULL_TEXT` | BM25 keyword-only matching, no embeddings |

chunks.lecture: 07 Lab - Chunking PDFs and AI Search
chunks.heading: F1. Similarity Search (Vector ANN)
chunks.text:
The default search mode uses Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) vector similarity. The index converts your query text into an embedding and finds the most semantically similar chunks.

Complete the following in the TODO cell below:

1. Retrieve the index with `client.get_index()` using `VS_ENDPOINT` and `VS_INDEX`, then print its detailed state.

2. Call `similarity_search()` with the query text *"What are the house rules about pets?"*.

3. Return the `chunk_id` and `chunk_text` columns, limited to 3 results.

**NOTE:** If the index is still syncing, wait a few minutes and re-run the cell.

 
 
Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
index = client.get_index(endpoint_name=VS_ENDPOINT, index_name=VS_INDEX)
status = index.describe().get("status", {}).get("detailed_state")
print(f"Index status: {status}")

results = index.similarity_search(
 query_text="What are the house rules about pets?",
 columns=["chunk_id", "chunk_text"],
 num_results=3,
)
print(f"\n--- F1: Similarity Search (Vector ANN) ---")
for row in results.get("result", {}).get("data_array", []):
 print(f"\n--- Chunk ---")
 print(row[1])
```

chunks.text:
Hybrid search combines vector similarity (ANN) with BM25 full-text keyword matching, merging results via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). This mode is useful when queries contain exact terms that must match — such as specific names, error codes, or technical terminology — where pure semantic search might miss keyword-specific results.

1. Complete the TODO cell below by setting the `query_type` argument to perform a hybrid search.

2. Use the same query text and result count as F1 so you can compare the returned chunks directly.

 columns=["chunk_id", "chunk_text"],
 num_results=3,
 query_type="hybrid",
)
print(f"\n--- F2: Hybrid Search (ANN + Keyword, RRF) ---")
for row in results_hybrid.get("result", {}).get("data_array", []):
 print(f"\n--- Chunk ---")
 print(row[1])
```

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This lecture establishes the foundations for building AI agents on Databricks. We cover what agents are, how they use tools registered in Unity Catalog, how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables tool discovery and execution, and how Unity Gateway provides governance across the stack.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
1. Define what AI agents are and identify their core components
2. Explain how Unity Catalog functions serve as governed agent tools
3. Describe how MCP enables agents to discover and call tools at runtime
4. Identify common tool patterns: structured retrieval, unstructured retrieval, code interpreter, and external connections
5. Understand the role of Unity Gateway for governance and access control

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. Single Agents
chunks.text:
An **AI agent** is an intelligent software system that can perceive its environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve specific goals. Unlike traditional AI systems that require continuous inputs from users, AI agents are autonomous systems that can:

- **Reason** about complex problems and situations
- **Plan** sequences of actions to achieve objectives
- **Adapt** their behavior based on new information
- **Interact** with external systems and data sources
- **Learn** from experience to improve future performance

A very simple example of agent framework is shown below. Here, a system prompt and the user's prompt are passed to the agent, where it then uses tools to help plan and process information to return back to the user.

 
 
 Agent Framework 
 Agent Framework containing Generative AI models, Tools, and Sequence of decisions, taking System Prompt and User Prompt as input and producing Response and Output. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 System Prompt 
 + User Prompt 
 
 Response/Output 
 
 
 
 Agent Framework 
 
 
 Generative AI 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 fx 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Tools 
 Image 
 Generation 
 Language 
 Model 
 (GenAI Examples) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Sequence of decisions 
 
 

 
 
What makes a software system an AI agent?
 
 

 A plain LLM call maps one prompt to one response. An agent wraps that model in a loop that can take actions and react to their results: 
 
 Reason & plan — break a goal into steps instead of answering in one shot. 
 Use tools — call functions, query data, or reach external systems to get real information. 
 Observe & adapt — read each tool result and decide the next action, looping until the goal is met. 
 Stay grounded — rely on retrieved, governed data rather than only the model's frozen training knowledge. 
 
 On Databricks, the tools an agent calls are Unity Catalog functions — governed, discoverable, and permission-checked — which is what makes agent actions auditable and safe in production.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: A2. Multi-Agent Supervisors
chunks.text:
An example of a common multi-agent architecture is the **supervisor-worker** (also called router-delegate) pattern:

 
 
 Supervisor-Worker Multi-Agent Architecture 
 A Supervisor Agent receives user requests and delegates to specialized worker agents: Data Agent, Research Agent, and General Agent. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Multi-Agent System 
 
 Supervisor Agent 
 Routes and synthesizes 
 
 
 
 Delegates to 
 
 
 Workers 
 
 Data Agent 
 UC functions, SQL 
 
 Research Agent 
 AI Search, docs 
 
 General Agent 
 Knowledge, reasoning 
 
 

**How it works:**
1. The **supervisor** receives the user's request and analyzes intent
2. It **delegates** to the appropriate worker agent (or handles simple requests itself)
3. The worker executes with its specialized tools and returns a result
4. The supervisor **synthesizes** the response and returns it to the user

For example, in the OpenAI Agents SDK, this delegation is implemented using **handoffs**:

```python
from agents import Agent

supervisor = Agent(
 name="Supervisor",
 instructions="Route requests to the appropriate specialist.",
 handoffs=[data_agent, business_agent],
)
```

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: A3. Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent
chunks.text:
Factor | Single Agent | Multi-Agent
---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -----------------------------------------------
Number of tools | Works best when total tools is modest (≈ up to 8–10); beyond that, tool selection and prompt management start to degrade (heuristic, not a hard limit). | Better when you have many tools spanning distinct capabilities (often >10) and need clear separation between them.
Domain complexity | One focused or tightly related domain. | Multiple distinct domains or verticals.
Instruction length | Shorter, coherent system prompt that a single agent can reliably follow. | Would require a very long, fragmented, or conflicting prompt if kept in one agent.
Failure isolation | Failures are acceptable as one unit; easier to reason about as a whole. | Need to isolate, debug, and replace individual agent capabilities without changing the whole system.
Team ownership | Single team owns most or all behaviors. | Different teams own different domains, tools, or behaviors and need independent evolution.
Latency | Minimal overhead; typically fewer model calls and simpler orchestration. | Extra routing/orchestration calls add latency and token cost.
Scalability / parallelism | Scales fine while domain and tools remain bounded; limited parallelism within one agent’s context window. | Better for parallelizing work across domains, distributing context, and scaling capabilities, at the cost of more coordination complexity.

 
 Note 
 
Start with a single agent. Only decompose into multiple agents when you observe tool selection errors, instruction conflicts, or when different teams need to own different agent capabilities independently.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: A4. Agents on Databricks
chunks.text:
Now that we understand single and multi-agent architectures, let's look at how to build agents on Databricks. The platform offers a spectrum of approaches — from fully managed, no-code options to fully custom, code-first development.

 

 
 
 LEGACY 
 Knowledge Assistant 
 Bring your own AI Search index, choose your chunking strategy, and attach multiple source types (up to 10). Full control over the retrieval pipeline. 
 

 
 
 MANAGED 
 Genie Agent 
 Declarative agents that understand your data. Attach tables for structured queries or UC volumes for document search — Databricks handles tool orchestration and query generation. 
 

 
 
 CODE-FIRST 
 Custom Agent 
 Write your own agent logic, tools, and orchestration. Use the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or any Python framework, then deploy it as a Databricks App, the recommended way to host agents. 
 

 

**Knowledge Assistants** offer customization (bring your own AI Search index) but are a legacy path. **Genie Agents** are the recommended declarative option for data-aware agents: you declare *what* data or documents your agent should work with, and the platform optimizes *how*. **Custom agents** are code-first: you own the agent logic, tools, and orchestration end to end, and Databricks Apps is the recommended way to host them.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: The Frontier: Platform Capabilities for Custom Agents
chunks.text:
Custom agents don't have to be built from scratch. Databricks is adding platform capabilities that take care of common agent infrastructure for you. Here's what the frontier currently looks like:

 

 
 
 NEW · BETA 
 Agent developer CLI 
 Create a “hello world” custom agent in under 10 minutes with a handful of commands, pre-configured with the capabilities below. 
 AWS | Azure | GCP 
 
 
 
 NEW · BETA 
 Managed memory and sessions 
 Help agents get the right context at the right time, within a conversation and across sessions. 
 AWS | Azure | GCP 
 
 
 
 NEW · BETA 
 Agentic sandboxes 
 Let agents access data and run code in an isolated, secure environment. 
 AWS | Azure 
 
 
 
 GA 
 Agent hosting 
 Host your agent on Databricks serverless infrastructure. 
 AWS | Azure | GCP 
 
 
 
 GA 
 Tracing and evaluation 
 End-to-end tracing and evaluation for agents with MLflow. You will use MLflow tracing throughout this course. 
 AWS | Azure | GCP 
 
 
 
 GA 
 Out of the box tools and MCPs 
 Pre-built first- and third-party MCP servers, plus pre-built tools for web search, code execution, and more. 
 AWS | Azure | GCP 
 

 

 
 Note 
 
Beta features can change and may need to be enabled in your workspace before you can use them. Availability can also differ by cloud: Databricks Sandbox documentation is currently available for AWS and Azure only.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. Model Context Protocol (MCP)
chunks.text:
On Databricks, [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) is an open standard for connecting AI agents to tools and context such as data, functions, and external services. Databricks managed MCP servers ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/mcp/managed-mcp/) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/generative-ai/mcp/managed-mcp) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/generative-ai/mcp/managed-mcp)) are Databricks-hosted, ready-to-use MCP endpoints for AI Search, Genie Agents, Databricks SQL, and Unity Catalog functions. They let agents connect to these tools through a standard interface while Unity Catalog permissions remain enforced and usage can be monitored and managed through Unity Gateway.

 
 
 MCP on Databricks 
 User query flows into an agent on Databricks that acts as an MCP client. The agent discovers and calls tools from managed MCP servers (Genie for structured data, AI Search for unstructured data, UC Functions for custom logic) and returns a response to the user. All traffic governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 User Query 

 
 Response 

 
 

 
 Databricks 

 
 Agent 
 
 
 
 
 
 MCP Client 
 Discovers and calls tools 

 
 
 MCP Servers 

 
 Genie 
 Structured 
 data 

 
 AI Search 
 Unstructured 
 data 

 
 UC Functions 
 Custom 
 logic 

 
 
 
 

The main benefit of MCP is standardization. You can create a tool once and use it with different agent frameworks or clients that support MCP.

 
 Learn More 
 
Read more in the Databricks docs for MCP on Databricks ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) and managed MCP servers ( AWS | Azure | GCP ). For the broader protocol, see the official MCP documentation .
 
 

 
 
Why does MCP matter for agents?
 
 

 Standardization. Without a shared protocol, every agent framework needs bespoke glue to reach each tool and data source — an N-frameworks × M-tools integration problem. 
 
 Define once, reuse anywhere — expose a tool through MCP and any MCP-aware client or framework can discover and call it. 
 Runtime discovery — agents list the available tools and their schemas at runtime instead of hard-coding them. 
 Governed by default — Databricks managed MCP servers surface Genie, AI Search, Databricks SQL, and Unity Catalog functions behind one interface, with UC permissions enforced and usage tracked through Unity Gateway.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2. Genie Agents
chunks.text:
The diagram below frames a Genie Agent as a single agent whose main tool is text-to-SQL (optionally augmented with the trusted UC functions you registered) — and, just as important for the enterprise, the **governance model** around it. The user authenticates as themselves; the agent's **ACL** decides whether they can run it; and every query executes **on behalf of that user**, so the warehouse borrows the *author's* compute delegation while data access is enforced against the *end user's own* Unity Catalog permissions and audited back to them.

 
 
 Genie Agent: single agent with tool calling and on-behalf-of governance 
 Left to right: a user authenticates as themselves; their identity is checked against the Genie Agent ACL (CAN VIEW / CAN RUN); the single managed agent plans and calls its built-in text-to-SQL tool or attached UC functions; SQL runs on a SQL warehouse under on-behalf-of execution, where compute comes from the author's delegation embedded at config time, data access uses the end user's own identity and Unity Catalog permissions, and every query is audited to the user. Unity Catalog beneath the warehouse enforces row filters, column masks, and per-user permissions. A grounded answer with sources returns along the bottom to the user. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 User 
 authenticates 
 as themselves 

 ACL -->
 
 identity 

 
 
 Genie Agent ACL check 
 CAN VIEW / CAN RUN? 

 Agent -->
 

 
 
 Genie Agent (single managed agent) 

 
 
 Plan & decide which tool to call 
 natural language → action 

 
 
 Tools 

 
 Text-to-SQL 
 generates & runs SQL (built-in tool) 

 
 UC Functions 
 attached trusted tools · e.g. avg_neigh_price 

 Warehouse -->
 

 
 
 SQL Warehouse 
 on-behalf-of execution 

 
 COMPUTE — author's delegation 
 embedded at config time 

 
 DATA — end user's identity 
 user's own UC permissions 

 
 AUDIT — attributed to the user 
 every query is traceable 

 Unity Catalog (down) -->
 

 
 
 Unity Catalog 
 row filters · column masks · per-user enforcement 

 
 
 grounded answer + sources 
 
 

 
 
Why is a Genie Agent considered a single agent with tool calling?
 
 

 A Genie Agent is a managed single agent . You do not write its orchestration loop, its prompt, or its retrieval code — Databricks does. But conceptually it behaves exactly like the single agents you already know: 
 
 It calls a tool. Its primary tool is text-to-SQL : it turns a natural-language question into a SQL query and runs it on a SQL warehouse. You can also attac

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: B3. Other Tools
chunks.text: While we will focus on agent tools in UC, it's important to point out that there are other tools that exist outside those discussed in this course.

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks

chunks.heading: C. Governance and AI Management with Unity Gateway
chunks.text:
Engineering Budget 
 $50,000 per month

 Budget policies

 Rate limits 
 
 Chargeback 
 
 Usage attribution

 Omnigent 
 $22k of $25k used 
 
 Customer support 
 $15k of $15k used 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Blocked! 

 
 

 
 
What does Unity Gateway provide?
 
 

 Unity Gateway is the Databricks central AI governance layer for LLM endpoints ( AWS | Azure | GCP ), MCP servers ( AWS | Azure | GCP ), and coding agents. Use Unity Gateway to analyze usage, configure permissions, enforce guardrails, and manage capacity across providers. 

 
 Governance : Track which users, agents, and applications are making LLM calls, how agents use MCP servers and APIs, and applies consistent policies across models and tools
 MCP Governance : On-behalf-of execution so agents act with the request user's exact permissions instead of a shared service account. 
 Rate limiting : Protect endpoints from overload with per-endpoint and per-identity (user or group) QPM/TPM limits ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) 
 Guardrails : Apply input/output safety filters and data-protection policies to block or mask harmful or sensitive content 
 Usage tracking : Monitor token consumption and costs across Unity Gateway endpoints and coding agents using system tables 
 Payload logging : Log request/response payloads to Unity Catalog Delta tables via inference tables for audit, debugging, and model improvement

chunks.lecture: 01 Lecture - Agents, MCP, and AI Governance on Databricks
chunks.heading: C1. Fallback Example
chunks.text:
Without Unity Gateway, each agent or application would have to implement its own access control, guardrails, and logging, making safety, compliance, debugging, and cost control much harder to do reliably at scale (especially across multiple models and providers). The diagram below illustrates how Unity Gateway handles endpoint fallback routing. 

 
 
 Unity Gateway Endpoint fallback routing 
 Requests route from a client to Model 1, falling back to Model 2 or Model 3 on 429/5xx errors, with all outcomes logged to inference and usage tracking tables.
