 Learn More 
 
Databricks Foundation Model APIs integrate with Unity Gateway, but you enable Unity Gateway features (like usage tracking and inference tables) per endpoint. In the new Unity Gateway (Beta), usage tracking is on by default for Gateway endpoints, once the feature is enabled and the endpoint is created.
See: Unity Gateway documentation ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.heading: C2. Workspace-Scoped Endpoints and UC-Native Services for LLM Use-Cases
chunks.text:
Legacy Model Serving Endpoints 
 Workspace-scoped AI Gateway 
 Endpoint in Workspace A 
 Duplicate in Workspace B 
 Per-workspace permissions 
 
 
 Define once, govern centrally 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Model Services 
 Unity Catalog securable object 
 Defined once in catalog.schema 
 Shared across the metastore 
 Discoverable in Catalog Explorer 
 Unity Gateway controls 
 Centralized UC privileges 
 
 

 
 
When and why model services are recommended
 
 

 Model serving endpoints are not legacy for all AI workloads. However, for most governed LLM use cases, Databricks recommends moving to model services because model services shift LLM access from workspace-scoped endpoints into Unity Catalog, where the service can be defined once, shared across workspaces, permissioned centrally, and managed through Unity Gateway controls. 

 
 Standardize approved models across multiple workspaces 
 Centralize access control instead of managing permissions workspace by workspace 
 Apply governance controls such as rate limits, service policies, and guardrails consistently 
 Track usage, token consumption, and costs in a system-level way

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: This demonstration focuses on how to create Unity Catalog (UC) functions using both SQL and Python for AI agent use cases, expose them via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and test how a model chooses between them. You will combine concepts from both SQL and Python function creation, demonstrating how to build a comprehensive toolkit that leverages the strengths of each approach within a single agent workflow.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this demo, you will be able to:
- Create and register both SQL and Python functions in Unity Catalog for Agent use cases
- Perform initial testing of your UC functions using multiple approaches
- Understand how to equip functions with proper context for AI Agent use cases
- Discover and call UC functions as agent tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
- Test how a model selects and calls your UC functions as tools
- Identify when different tools have been used and understand how the agent utilized each tool type
- Compare the strengths of SQL vs Python tools in agent workflows

chunks.heading: A. Classroom Setup
chunks.text: Run the next cell to install the libraries for this demo and set up your catalog, schema, and data.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. Inspect the Airbnb Dataset
chunks.text: As a part of the classroom setup, the Airbnb dataset has been processed and stored as a Delta table within Unity Catalog. Run the next cell to query the first few rows of the dataset.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: A2. Initialize the Databricks Function Client
chunks.text:
Initialize the [Databricks Function Client](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/tree/b2d072e56661aedb84cce9be60292b2c54e12224/ai/core#databricks-managed-uc), which is a specialized interface for creating, managing, and running UC functions in Databricks. 

For building agent tools with the open source UC library, please see [this documentation](https://docs.unitycatalog.io/ai/client/#databricks-function-client). This demonstration will focus on leveraging Databricks-managed UC for building both SQL and Python agent tools.
- Supported [execution modes](https://github.com/unitycatalog/unitycatalog/blob/main/ai/core/src/unitycatalog/ai/core/utils/execution_utils.py#L25) include **Serverless** (default) and **Local**. We will use **serverless** in this notebook.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: B. Define and Register UC SQL Functions
chunks.text:
Before digging into the code, it's important to understand some terminology. 
- Built-in functions like `SUM` and `AVG` are SQL functions, but these are specifically called **system functions**. However, a **SQL function** is any reusable computation that can be called in a SQL statement, even ones defined by users.
- Any function registered via Unity Catalog, regardless of being written in SQL or Python, is considered a **user-defined function (UDF)**.

In this notebook we will use the term **SQL function** or **function** to mean a function that is or will be registered to UC, hence a SQL UDF. 

 
 
 
 Note 
 
 For more information on UDFs in Unity Catalog, please see
 this documentation ( AWS | Azure | GCP ).

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. SQL Tool: Airbnb Data Analysis
chunks.text: We start by creating SQL functions that will serve as our agent tools for analyzing the San Francisco Airbnb listings data. These functions include proper documentation that will help the agent understand how to use them. This tool will be created with **SQL only**.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: Recommendations for SQL Functions
chunks.text:
The following SQL functions follow recommended practices:
1. **Clear parameter names and types**: Use descriptive parameter names with appropriate SQL data types
2. **Comprehensive comments**: Use `COMMENT` clauses for both the function and each parameter to provide clear descriptions
3. **Deterministic behavior**: Mark functions as `DETERMINISTIC` when they always return the same result for the same inputs
4. **Proper return type**: Explicitly specify the return data type
5. **Error handling**: Consider edge cases like NULL values in the function logic

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2. Test SQL Tool Using SQL Syntax
chunks.text: Let's verify that our SQL function works correctly by testing it with various inputs directly in SQL. This helps ensure our function behaves as expected before an agent uses it.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: C. Define and Register UC Python Functions
chunks.text: Now we'll create Python functions that complement our SQL tools by providing capabilities that would be difficult or impossible with SQL alone. Python functions enable advanced data processing, external API integration, and complex business logic. Note we can choose to wrap the Python logic in SQL syntax or use the `DatabricksFunctionClient()`. We will choose to leverage the latter since we already demonstrated how to use SQL to create a function.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: Recommended Practices
chunks.text:
1. **Explicit type hints**: Provide clear Python type hints for all arguments and the return value. This helps `create_python_function()` infer the function interface and helps agents understand expected inputs and outputs
2. **Use explicit named parameters**: Prefer clearly named, explicitly typed parameters so the tool schema is easy to understand and use
3. **Supported data types**: Ensure input and output types are compatible with Databricks and Spark SQL type systems. Refer to the supported types guidance in the Databricks documentation ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/create-custom-tool) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/generative-ai/agent-framework/create-custom-tool) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/create-custom-tool)) and [Spark SQL data types documentation](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-datatypes.html)
4. **Write clear docstrings**: Use a structured docstring format, such as [Google-style formatting](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html#383-functions-and-methods), to describe what the function does, each argument, and the return value
 - Make descriptions precise and meaningful so agents can better determine when to use the tool
5. **Import external libraries inside the function when needed**: For functions that depend on external libraries, importing them inside the function body is the safest pattern and aligns with Databricks examples for Python UC tools and UDF-style execution

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: C2. Python Tool: Extract Airbnb Listing Information
chunks.text:
We'll create a Python function that demonstrates capabilities beyond SQL's reach - making HTTP requests to external APIs and parsing HTML content. This function will:

1. Fetch HTML content from an Airbnb posting using the listing ID
2. Extract and parse key information including description, number of reviews, and rating
3. Return formatted text that can be easily consumed by an AI agent

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: C3. Test Python Function at Notebook Level
chunks.text: Before registering the function to Unity Catalog, it's important to test it at the notebook level to ensure it works as expected. This allows you to catch any errors early and validate the output format.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: C4. Register Python Tool Using `DatabricksFunctionClient()`
chunks.text:
Now that we've validated our function works correctly, we can register it to Unity Catalog using the `DatabricksFunctionClient`. 

We use `client.create_python_function()` and pass the following parameters:

- **`func`**: The Python function object we just created (`airbnb_posting_info`)
- **`catalog`**: The catalog name, which we stored earlier as `catalog_name`
- **`schema`**: The schema name, which we stored earlier as `schema_name`
- **`replace`**: Set to `True` to overwrite the stored Python function if it already exists

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: C5. Test Python Tool Using `DatabricksFunctionClient()`
chunks.text: Let's test the Python-based function using the `execute_function()` API to ensure it works correctly when called through Unity Catalog. Note that you will receive the same response as when we performed the query for the function defined within the current Python interpreter session.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: D. Discover and Test Tools via Model Context Protocol (MCP)
chunks.text:
Now that both SQL and Python tools are registered in Unity Catalog, let's see how an agent would actually **discover** and **call** them. Databricks provides managed MCP servers that expose UC functions as tools following the open [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) standard.

 
 
 
 Note 
 MCP is the recommended way to connect UC functions to agents. Rather than hard-coding function names, agents discover available tools dynamically through the MCP server. The MCP server acts as the bridge between your UC functions and any agent framework. 
 This means you register once in Unity Catalog and your tools are available to any agent, any framework, with full governance.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: D1. Initialize the MCP Client
chunks.text:
`DatabricksMCPClient` connects to whatever MCP server URL you give it, including Databricks-managed MCP servers like `/api/2.0/mcp/functions/{catalog}/{schema}`. 

1. Import `WorkspaceClient` from the Databricks Python SDK and create an authenticated client for the workspace.
2. Import the MCP client class `DatabricksMCPClient` and build the URL for the managed MCP server that exposes all Unity Catalog functions in the given catalog and schema.
3. Import `nest_asyncio` and call `nest_asyncio.apply()`, which patches the notebook’s running event loop so you can safely call code that uses asyncio under the hood.

4. Create a `DatabricksMCPClient` instance pointed at the managed MCP server URL.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: D2. Discover Available Tools
chunks.text:
Let's list all the tools the MCP server exposes. Notice that both our SQL function (`avg_neigh_price`) and Python function (`airbnb_posting_info`) are discoverable. An agent would use these descriptions to decide which tool to call.

 
 
 
 Note 
 When you call list_tools() each method call sends a standard HTTP POST request to the server URL with a JSON-RPC 2.0 payload.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: D3. Call a Tool via MCP
chunks.text: We can also execute a tool through the MCP protocol, just as an agent would. Let's call `avg_neigh_price` to verify it works end-to-end through MCP. Select the tool by name rather than by its position in the list, because the list order isn't guaranteed.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: E. Test Your Tools with a Model
chunks.text:
An agent's model decides which tool to call, and what arguments to pass, by reading each tool's name, description, and parameters. In this section, you send a question to a model, first without tools and then with both of your tools, and see what it decides to do.

 
 Note 
 
We won't dive into this code much. The Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks demo, later in the course, covers connecting to a model and building agents in detail. For now, focus on the output. The code calls a model service , agent-training-model , that the classroom setup created in your catalog and schema. A model service is our way of connecting to a model endpoint. We'll cover the details later in the course.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: E1. Connect to a Model Using an SDK
chunks.text: Run the next cell to connect to the model service and define `ask_model`. It sends a question to the model, offers it the UC functions you name as tools, and prints either the model's answer or the tool calls it wants to make. It doesn't run the tools: running them and passing the results back to the model is the job of an agent.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: E2. Ask Without Tools
chunks.text: This question needs both data analysis and external information. With no tools, the model can only answer from what it already knows. Expect a general answer, or a description of the information it would need.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: E3. Ask With Both Tools
chunks.text: Now offer the model both tools. Notice that it chooses to call `avg_neigh_price` for the neighborhood average and `airbnb_posting_info` for the listing, and that it fills in each argument, such as `neighborhood_name` and `id`, from the question. It knows how because of the names, type hints, and descriptions you gave each function. A model's choices can vary slightly from run to run.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: F. Managed MCPs
chunks.text:
In addition to custom MCPs like the ones shown above, we can connect to out-of-the-box MCPs using the Databricks SDK. To see what OOB MCPs are available: 
1. Navigate to **Unity Gateway** using the menu to the left
2. Select **MCPs** to see the list of available MCP servers

We will test the **Genie One** MCP.

3. Select **genie_one_mcp** under **MCPs**
4. Click on **Overview** and view the **Get started** information. Here you will see different ways to call the MCP services from your agentic applications. 

All account users have `EXECUTE` permissions on the `system.ai` schema per this notebook's lab configuration.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: F1. Genie One MCP
chunks.text:
We'll ask a simple question: explain Lakebase to a new Databricks user. This will be accomplished in a series of steps:
1. Setup client connection
2. Ask a question
 - Genie answers are asynchronous, so we will need to handle that with care
3. Poll until Genie has a complete answer
4. Get the full query result

1. Connect to the client like before, but this time with a different server URL (one that points to **Genie One** instead of our custom tools). Notice in this case, we'll need to get the Workspace ID to construct the correct managed URL for Genie One. 

2. Define question you wish to ask using the client we just created and its `call_tool` method. 

3. At this point:
 - **Unity Gateway** has received the HTTP POST and has resolved the URL to connect to the Genie One MCP server. 
 - It has also authenticated you to check that you have `EXECUTE` permission on `system.ai`. 
 - The JSON-RPC request has been forwarded to the server. Let's now poll for the results. To do this, we need to extract the `conversation_id` and `response_id` from the ask result.

Now begin polling (we will do 30 polls with 3 seconds between each). 

 
 
 
 Why await acall_tool() instead of call_tool() ? 
 Notebook cells on Serverless execute inside a running asyncio event loop. The sync call_tool() is a convenience wrapper around the async acall_tool() — internally it creates an asyncio.TaskGroup and calls loop.run_until_complete() to bridge from sync to async. When that bridge runs inside an already-running event loop, the TaskGroup 's exception propagation can conflict with the outer loop's task management, raising an ExceptionGroup that escapes normal try/except handling. 
 The fix is to stay fully async: use await acall_tool() and await asyncio.sleep() so the code cooperates with the event loop rather than nesting inside it. Databricks Serverless supports top-level await in cells, making this straightforward.

chunks.lecture: 02 Demo - Building Agent Tools on Databricks
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
You've now learned how to create a comprehensive AI agent toolkit by combining both SQL and Python functions in Unity Catalog and exposing them via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Throughout this demonstration, you've gained hands-on experience with:

- **Building both SQL and Python UC functions** for AI agents using multiple registration approaches
- **Understanding the strengths of each approach** - SQL for data analysis and Python for external integrations and complex logic
- **Discovering and calling tools via MCP** - using the Databricks-managed MCP server to dynamically discover UC functions and invoke them programmatically, just as an agent framework would
- **Connecting to Databricks managed MCPs** like Genie One to query data with natural language, demonstrating the breadth of the MCP ecosystem beyond custom tools
- **Testing functions individually and collectively** through multiple methods including direct execution, `DatabricksFunctionClient()`, MCP, a model, and Genie One
- **Creating comprehensive agent toolkits** that can handle diverse user queries requiring both data analysis and external information
- **Seeing how a model selects tools** by offering it your SQL and Python tools and watching which ones it calls, and with what arguments

By combining Unity Catalog's governance framework with MCP's open standard for tool discovery, SQL's analytical capabilities, and Python's computational flexibility, you're now equipped to build secure, scalable AI agent solutions that can intelligently interact with both your internal data and external systems. This comprehensive approach enables you to create production-ready agent tools that leverage the best of both worlds while maintaining enterprise governance and security standards.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
In this lab, you will take a Unity Catalog function that works correctly but is poorly documented, see how it confuses an agent, and fix it. An agent decides when to call a tool, and what to pass it, based only on the tool's name, docstring, and parameter descriptions, so documentation is the interface between an agent and its tools. You will rewrite the function's documentation, re-register it to Unity Catalog, and verify the improvement through MCP and by testing it with a model.

Each step has a **TODO** with ` ` placeholders. The instructions above each TODO tell you what to fill in, and you can reveal the answer if you get stuck.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:
1. Identify documentation problems that keep an agent from using a UC function correctly
2. Rewrite a Python function with descriptive parameter names, type hints, and a structured docstring
3. Re-register an updated Python function to Unity Catalog with `DatabricksFunctionClient`
4. Discover and call a UC function through a Managed MCP server
5. Compare the arguments a model passes to a tool before and after improving the tool's documentation

chunks.text:
.scn3{font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,sans-serif;color:#0b2026;width:100%;max-width:100%;box-sizing:border-box;margin:0;padding:8px}.scn3 .scen{background:#FFFFFF;color:#0b2026;padding:26px 30px;border-radius:12px;box-sizing:border-box;overflow:hidden;box-shadow:0 2px 16px rgba(27,49,57,0.10),0 1px 4px rgba(27,49,57,0.06);border:1px solid rgba(27,49,57,0.08)}.scn3 .kicker{font-size:14px;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:1.2px;color:#5A6F77;margin-bottom:10px;font-weight:700;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px}.scn3 .body{font-size:15px;line-height:1.7;color:#0b2026}.scn3 .body p{margin:0 0 14px}.scn3 .body p:last-child{margin:0}.scn3 .tools{background:#F9F7F4;border:1px solid rgba(27,49,57,0.10);border-radius:8px;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Consolas,monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:1.9}.scn3 .fn{color:#0B8F5F}.scn3 .arg{color:#5A6F77}.scn3 .dsc{color:#5A6F77;opacity:.8}.scn3 code{background:rgba(27,49,57,0.07);padding:2px 6px;border-radius:4px;font-size:14px;font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Consolas,monospace;color:#0b2026}.scn3 .eq{background:rgba(0,169,114,.10);border-left:4px solid #00A972;padding:10px 14px;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;margin:10px 0 14px;font-size:14px;font-style:italic;line-height:1.6;color:#0b2026}.scn3 .eq-q{background:#FFF6F4;border-left:4px solid #FF5F46;padding:10px 14px;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;margin:10px 0 14px;font-size:14px;line-height:1.6;color:#0b2026} 
 Scenario 
 
 Your team recently registered a Unity Catalog function called est_listing_value to help an agent estimate the annual revenue of an Airbnb listing. The logic is correct — but when you give it to a model as a tool, the model consistently misuses it: passing values to the wrong parameters, inventing values the tool can't use, and returning a confident but wrong answer. 

 est_listing_value (p1, p2, p3) — "Calculates value." 

 The problem isn't the code — it's the documentation. The function has meaningless parameter names ( p1 , p2 , p3 ), a two-word description, and a docstring that is out of date: it says p1 is the price, but the code uses p1 as the number of bedrooms. An agent decides when to call a tool, what to pass it, and how to interpret the result based entirely on its name, docstring, and parameter descriptions. When those are unclear, the agent guesses. When they are wrong, the agent confidently follows them. 

 A user sends a perfectly reasonable request

```python
client = DatabricksFunctionClient()
```

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: B. Examine a Poorly Documented Agent Tool
chunks.text:
As part of the classroom setup, a Python function called `est_listing_value` has been registered to Unity Catalog. This function is intended to estimate the annual revenue of an Airbnb listing based on its characteristics, but its documentation is **vague and out of date**.

Let's look at the function as it currently exists.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: B1. Review the Bad Function

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: B2. See How a Model Uses the Tool
chunks.text:
Give the poorly documented tool to a model and see what it does with a realistic request. Run the next cell to connect to the model and define `ask_model`, the same helper as in the *Building Agent Tools on Databricks* demo, with one change: when you offer tools, it requires the model to call one, so you always see the arguments it chooses. It sends a question to the model, offers it the tools you name, and prints the tool calls the model wants to make without running them.

 
 Note 
 
We won't dive into this code much. The Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks demo, later in the course, covers connecting to a model and building agents in detail. For now, focus on the output. The code calls a model service , agent-training-model , that the classroom setup created in your catalog and schema. A model service is our way of connecting to a model endpoint. We'll cover the details later in the course.
 
 

Now ask the question from the scenario. Look closely at the arguments. The model reads `p1: price`, `p2: count`, and `p3: market`, so it will likely pass the $250 price as `p1`, which the code treats as the bedroom count, and a city such as `"San Francisco"` as `p3`. Nothing would fail if the tool ran: a call like that returns about $9,798 a year, when the right answer is about $88,148. The model can't tell, because it trusts the documentation. The exact call can vary from run to run.

 
 Expected output 
 The model wants to call:
 - est_listing_value({'p1': 250, 'p2': 2, 'p3': 'San Francisco'}) 
 
The values are in the wrong parameters. The $250 price went into p1 , which the code uses as the bedroom count, and a city went into p3 , where the code expects a room type. If this call ran, the tool would return $9,798.42 , a believable but wrong estimate. Your exact output can vary, for example 250.0 instead of 250 , or a different value for p3 , but expect the price in p1 and something other than a room type in p3 .

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: C. Fix the Function Description
chunks.text:
The function logic is correct -- the problem is entirely in the documentation. An agent reads the function name, docstring, and parameter descriptions to decide:
1. **When** to call the function
2. **What** values to pass for each parameter
3. **How** to interpret the result

Without clear documentation, the agent is guessing.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: C1. Rewrite the Function with Proper Documentation
chunks.text:
**TODO:** Redefine the function with:
- Descriptive, typed parameters: rename `p1`, `p2`, and `p3` to `num_bedrooms`, `nightly_price_usd`, and `room_type`, and give each a type hint. The function body already uses these names, and the test and MCP call below pass them by name.
- A clear docstring explaining the function's purpose and when to use it, and that matches what the code actually does
- Detailed parameter descriptions with types, units, and examples
- A clear return value description

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
def est_listing_value(
 nightly_price_usd: float,
 num_bedrooms: float,
 room_type: str
) -> str:
 """
 Estimate the annual revenue for a San Francisco Airbnb listing based on
 its nightly price, number of bedrooms, and room type. Assumes 70%
 occupancy year-round.

 Use this tool when a user asks how much a listing could earn per year.

 Args:
 nightly_price_usd: The nightly price of the listing in US dollars (e.g. 250.0).
 num_bedrooms: The number of bedrooms in the listing (e.g. 1, 2, 3). A
 studio should be passed as 1. Each additional bedroom beyond
 the first increases the estimate by 15%.
 room_type: The Airbnb room type. Must be exactly one of:
 "Entire home/apt", "Private room", or "Shared room".

 Returns:
 A string describing the estimated annual revenue in USD.
 """
 base_value = nightly_price_usd * 365 * 0.7 # assume 70% occupancy
 bedroom_factor = 1 + (num_bedrooms - 1) * 0.15
 if room_type.lower() == 'entire home/apt':
 multiplier = 1.2
 elif room_type.lower() == 'private room':
 multiplier = 0.8
 else:
 multiplier = 0.5
 estimated = base_value * bedroom_factor * multiplier
 return f"Estimated annual revenue: ${estimated:,.2f}"
```

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: C2. Test the Improved Function Locally
chunks.text: Before re-registering, verify the function works correctly at the notebook level.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: C3. Re-register the Function to Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
**TODO:** Use `DatabricksFunctionClient` to re-register the improved function with `replace=True`.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy

```python
 func=est_listing_value,

)
```

chunks.heading: D. Verify the Improved Tool via MCP
chunks.text: In the demo, you saw how MCP allows agents to discover and call UC functions. Let's use MCP to verify that our re-registered function has the improved description and works correctly.

chunks.heading: D1. Discover the Tool
chunks.text:

```python
for tool in tools:
```

chunks.heading: D2. Call the Tool via MCP
chunks.text:
**TODO:** Execute `est_listing_value` through MCP to verify it works end-to-end.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
result = mcp_client.call_tool(f"{catalog_name}__{schema_name}__est_listing_value", 
{
 "nightly_price_usd": 250.0,
```

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: E. Validate the Improved Tool with a Model
chunks.text:
Ask the model the same question as in B2. `ask_model` reads the tool's definition from the MCP server each time, so it now sees your improved names, type hints, and docstring.

 
 Expected output 
 The model wants to call:
 - est_listing_value({'nightly_price_usd': 250, 'num_bedrooms': 2, 'room_type': 'Entire home/apt'}) 
 
Each value is now in the right parameter. If your docstring lists the allowed room types, as the answer does, room_type is one of them. If this call ran, the tool would return $88,147.50 , the correct estimate. Numbers may appear as 250.0 and 2.0 .
 
 

Compare the arguments with B2. The model now passes `nightly_price_usd`, `num_bedrooms`, and `room_type`, with values taken from the question, and uses a `room_type` from the list your docstring allows. The improved documentation gives the model the context it needs to use the tool correctly.

chunks.lecture: 03 Lab - Assessing and Fixing Agent Tools
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this lab you learned that **documentation is the interface** between an agent and its tools. The same function logic can be useless or powerful depending on how well it's documented. You also verified your tools work through MCP -- the same protocol that agents use in production to discover and call tools.

Here's what changed between B2 and E for the same question:

| | Bad tool (B2) | Fixed tool (E) |
|---|---|---|
| **Call the model makes** | `est_listing_value(p1=250, p2=2, p3="San Francisco")` | `est_listing_value(nightly_price_usd=250, num_bedrooms=2, room_type="Entire home/apt")` |
| **What the tool would return** | $9,798.42 (wrong) | $88,147.50 (correct) |
| **Why** | The out-of-date docstring sent each value to the wrong parameter | The names, types, and docstring match what the code does |

Key takeaways:
- Poor parameter names and docstrings make tools unusable by agents
- Out-of-date documentation is worse than none: the agent follows it confidently and gets a believable wrong answer
- Good documentation includes: clear names, detailed descriptions with examples, and business context
- MCP provides a standard way for agents to discover and call UC functions
- Always test tools via MCP, and with a model, before integrating them with agent code

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Now that you know how to create and govern agent tools, this lecture surveys the most popular frameworks for building agents on Databricks. The discussion will be facilitated with a focus on the **OpenAI Agents SDK**. We cover its orchestration patterns, rapid tool prototyping across frameworks, MCP integration, and multi-agent concepts before briefly comparing other supported frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, DSPy). This lecture closes with how MLflow provides observability across single-agent and multi-agent flows.

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
1. Identify the orchestration patterns supported by the OpenAI Agents SDK (handoffs, agents-as-tools, sequential, parallel, feedback loops)
2. Prototype agent tools with `@function_tool` (OpenAI Agents SDK), `@tool` (LangChain), and plain functions (DSPy) before registering them to Unity Catalog
3. Explain how `McpServer` connects agents to Unity Catalog functions via MCP
4. Understand multi-agent concepts: supervisor agents, handoffs, and worker specialization
5. Compare other supported frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, DSPy) and when you might choose them
6. Explain how MLflow tracing captures agent execution as hierarchical spans

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: A. OpenAI Agent Orchestration Patterns
chunks.text: [The OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/) supports multiple patterns for coordinating agents. These fall into two categories: **LLM-driven** (the model decides what happens next) and **code-driven** (your code controls the flow deterministically).

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. LLM-Driven Orchestration

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: A2. Code-Driven Orchestration

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: B. Rapid Prototyping with Framework Tool Decorators

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. From Prototype to Governed Tool
chunks.text:
A prototyped tool exists only in your notebook session. Once it works, the recommended path is the same in every framework: register the logic as a **Unity Catalog function** so it is governed and reusable, then let agents reach it through a **Managed MCP server**.

 
 1. Prototype Decorator or plain function. Local to the notebook. 
 → 
 2. Register to Unity Catalog Governed, permissioned, and reusable across agents. 
 → 
 3. Expose through MCP Discoverable at runtime by any MCP-aware framework. 
 

Each framework connects to the governed tool in its own way:

| Framework | Prototype a tool | Use the governed UC tool |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | `@function_tool` | `McpServer` from `databricks_openai.agents`, passed as `mcp_servers=[...]` (see section C) |
| **LangChain** | `@tool` | Discover tools with `DatabricksMCPClient` and wrap each one as a LangChain `StructuredTool` |
| **DSPy** | A plain typed function, optionally wrapped in `dspy.Tool` | Convert MCP tools with `dspy.Tool.from_mcp_tool(...)`, or wrap a call to the UC function in a plain function |

 
 Note 
 
Tool definition is not where DSPy stands out. Its strength is optimizing the prompts and modules around your tools, which section E covers. For tools, think of DSPy as the lightest option: no decorator, just a well-documented function.

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: C. Databricks MCP Tools with `databricks_openai.agents.McpServer`

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: D. Multi-Agent Concepts

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: E. Other Supported Frameworks

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: F. MLflow Integration
chunks.text:
Want to know more about how MLflow integrates with the OpenAI Agent SDK on Databricks? Ask Genie Code. Click on the genie icon and begin querying. For example, click the Copy button below and paste into Genie Code .
 

 
 What does set_trace_processors([]) from the OpenAI Agents SDK do? Why is it needed with MLflow? 
 Copy

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: F1. Traditional ML vs Agents
chunks.text:
For robust operations with GenAI applications and agents, you often need deeper insight into **server-side behavior**, including **latency/cost metrics** and **API logging**, beyond what is typically required for traditional ML batch workloads.

| | Traditional ML | Agents |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape** | Single call | Multi-step, often looped |
| **Visible by default** | Input, output | Input, final output |
| **Unit of observation** | The call | A **span** per step |
| **Needed to debug** | Features, latency | Per-step I/O, tokens, tool args |
| **MLflow captures** | Request / response | Full **trace** (tree of spans) |

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: Agents need more insight
chunks.text:
- Agents perform multiple intermediate steps (for example: retrieval, tool use, LLM calls), and you need to see each step, its inputs/outputs, and per-step latency/token usage to debug and improve quality.
- **MLflow Tracing** captures these as **traces** and **spans** automatically for supported libraries (such as the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, and other GenAI frameworks) and provides a UI and APIs to analyze them across development and production.
- In a **tracing system** such as OpenTelemetry and MLflow, a single operation is represented as a **span**. It records when the operation started and ended, along with the metadata, inputs, and outputs for that unit of work.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
 MLflow spans are designed to be compatible with the
 OpenTelemetry trace specification , so additional information (such as token counts) is stored as key-value attributes on the span, rather than as new top-level fields.

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: F2. Hierarchical Span Structure
chunks.text:
MLflow organizes trace data using a hierarchical span structure that mirrors agent execution, starting with a single root span that represents the overall request or workflow, with nested child spans for each sub-step.

- **Parent spans**: High-level operations like "process user request"
- **Child spans**: Detailed steps like "call retrieval tool" or "generate response"
- **Span relationships**: Clear parent-child relationships that show execution flow, which should mimic your application's execution plan.
- **Span types**: Categorization of spans (`TOOL`, `CHAT_MODEL`, `RETRIEVER`) for better organization

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: F3. Registering MLflow Traces with Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
You can point an experiment at a catalog and schema, and every trace your app emits lands as a governed managed UC table with ready-to-query views. 

 
 
 .mlt{background:#ffffff;max-width:1600px;margin:0 auto;padding:24px 20px 40px;}
 .mlt svg{display:block;width:100%;height:auto;}
 .mlt svg text{font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Arial,sans-serif;fill:#0b2026;}
 .mlt .h {font-weight:800;}
 .mlt .b {font-weight:700;}
 .mlt .m {fill:#618794;font-weight:500;}
 .mlt .mono,.mlt .mono text{white-space:pre;font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;font-variant-ligatures:none;font-feature-settings:"liga" 0,"calt" 0;}
 .mlt .pfx {fill:#FF5F46;}
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 1 · YOUR GENAI APP 
 Any LLM framework 
 one-line autologging 
 
 
 OpenAI

 LangChain

 LlamaIndex

 DSPy

 @mlflow.trace

 2 -->
 
 
 
 2 · MLFLOW TRACING 
 Each trace captures 
 
 Inputs & outputs

 Token usage

 BIND TO UNITY CATALOG

 experiment_name="…", 
 trace_location=UnityCatalog( 
 catalog_name= "prod" ,

 Needs a SQL warehouse: 
 MLFLOW_TRACING_SQL_WAREHOUSE_ID 
 3 -->
 
 
 
 
 3 · Unity Catalog

 One row per span: the call tree with 
 timing, inputs and outputs 
 
 
 
 
 oai_sa _otel_logs 
 OpenTelemetry log records emitted 
 while the app runs

 Assessments, feedback and tags 
 attached to traces

 recorded alongside traces 
 
 views -->
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 2 SQL views over the tables

 One row per trace: spans, metadata 
 and assessments together 
 
 FULL DETAIL

 Tags, metadata and assessments only, 
 no span payloads 
 
 FAST FILTERING 
 
 
 
 
 
 Govern : grants · lineage · audit 
 
 Query : Databricks SQL 
 
 Read : mlflow.search_traces()

chunks.lecture: 04 Lecture - Building Agents with Popular Frameworks on Databricks
chunks.heading: G. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this lecture, you learned the building blocks for agent development on Databricks:

- **Orchestration patterns**: handoffs, agents-as-tools, sequential, parallel, and feedback loops
- **Rapid prototyping**: `@function_tool`, `@tool`, and plain DSPy functions let you try a tool before registering it to Unity Catalog
- **MCP integration**: `McpServer` connects agents to governed UC functions at runtime
- **Multi-agent concepts**: supervisor routing, worker specialization, and MCP-scoped tools
- **Other frameworks**: LangChain, LangGraph, and DSPy as alternative authoring options
- **MLflow tracing**: hierarchical spans that capture every step of agent execution

chunks.heading: REQUIRED - SELECT A COMPUTE ENVIRONMENT
chunks.text:
Select Compute 
 Before starting this notebook, select the required compute environment listed below.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. Import Libraries
chunks.text:
To get started with the OpenAI SDK, we have a few things that need to be setup:
1. Configure the OpenAI Agents SDK to use Databricks model routing **using Unity Gateway Model Services** using `AsyncDatabricksOpenAI(use_ai_gateway=True)`.
1. Import MCP components needed to connect to agent tools that have already been registered to UC.
1. Initialize the Databricks `WorkspaceClient`.
1. Set the default trace processor to MLflow.

Additional documentation and reading:
- [`set_default_openai_client`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/#agents.set_default_openai_client)
- [`set_default_openai_api`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/#agents.set_default_openai_api)
- [`set_trace_processors`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/docs/tracing.md)

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. Define the `classify_price_tier` Tool
chunks.text:
The `classify_price_tier` tool classifies an Airbnb listing's nightly price into one of four market tiers based on the SF pricing distribution:

| Tier | Price Range | Percentile Band |
|---|---|---|
| **Budget** | Under $100 | Bottom 25% |
| **Mid-Range** | $100 -- $174 | 25--50% |
| **Premium** | $175 -- $299 | 50--75% |
| **Luxury** | $300+ | Top 25% |

The `@function_tool` decorator registers this function as a tool that the agent can invoke. The SDK extracts the function signature and docstring to generate the tool schema that the LLM uses to decide when and how to call the tool.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
An example production workflow is: prototype with @function_tool , then register to Unity Catalog, then access via a Managed MCP server. This demo follows the first two steps of that progression. In Section C, we explicitly re-register the function to Unity Catalog for governance.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2. Create the Agent
chunks.text:
With the tool defined, we create a single agent that uses 
- `classify_price_tier` to answer questions about SF Airbnb pricing
- `instructions` parameter shapes the agent's behavior and tells it when to use the tool
- A Unity Catalog model service, referenced by its fully qualified name `{catalog_name}.{schema_name}.agent-training-model`

This is accomplished with the `Agent` class. You can read more about `Agent` [here](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/src/agents/agent.py).

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2.1 Inspect and Load the Agent Configuration
chunks.text:
We will load the agent configuration file. This is a recommended practice since any updates to the agents' system prompts, name, etc. live outside this notebook. These variables will be stored in the dictionary `agents`:
- `agents["X"]['name']`: The agent's name
- `agents["X"]['llm_endpoint']`: The name of the Unity Catalog **model service** the agent calls (`agent-training-model`). The next cell combines it with your catalog and schema into the service's fully qualified name.
- `agents["X"]['system_prompt']`: The agent's system prompt

Navigate to the folder **agent_config** and inspect the agent contents for **data_analyst_agent.yaml**

 
 Why a model service? 
 
In this course, agents call a model service registered in your catalog and schema instead of calling a foundation model endpoint such as databricks-gpt-5-2 directly. The classroom setup created the service agent-training-model , which routes requests through Unity Gateway to databricks-gpt-5-2 . Because the service is a Unity Catalog object, access to it is governed with Unity Catalog permissions, and because agents reference the service rather than the model, the model behind it can change without changing agent code.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: B3. Test the Agent
chunks.text:
We send three progressively complex queries to validate that the agent correctly invokes the tool and interprets the results. Each call uses `await Runner.run()`, which is the execution interface. It executes the full agent loop: the LLM decides whether to call a tool, executes it if needed, and generates a final response.

1. The next cell will run a straightforward pricing question that requires a single tool call.

2. The next cell will run a direct tier classification at the high end of the price spectrum.

3. The next cell will run multiple prices in a single request, testing whether the agent calls the tool multiple times.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: C1. Register `classify_price_tier` as a Python UC Function
chunks.text:
The inline `@function_tool` is local to this notebook session. To make the tool governed, discoverable, and reusable across agents and workspaces, we register it to Unity Catalog as a Python function using `DatabricksFunctionClient`.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
The function registered below is a plain Python function (no @function_tool decorator). The DatabricksFunctionClient inspects the function signature and docstring to create the UC function metadata. The logic is identical to the tool we prototyped above.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: C2. Verify Registered Functions
chunks.text:
Confirm that the function is visible in the Unity Catalog schema, then call it directly to verify it returns the expected output.
1. Navigate to the **Catalog Explorer** on the left side menu and search for `classify_price_uc`
1. Run the next cell to test the output from calling the function from UC

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: C3. Access the UC Function via a Managed MCP Server
chunks.text:
Databricks provides **Managed MCP servers** that automatically expose Unity Catalog functions as tools. Any agent can discover and call these functions through the MCP protocol without custom integration code.

The MCP server endpoint for UC functions follows this pattern:
`https://workspace/api/2.0/mcp/functions/catalog/schema`

With the OpenAI Agents SDK, you use `McpServer` from `databricks_openai.agents` to connect as shown in the next cell.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
The McpServer class from databricks_openai.agents is an async context manager designed for the Databricks Apps runtime. In a notebook, we use DatabricksMCPClient from databricks_mcp to interact with the same MCP endpoint.
See: Managed MCP servers ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: C4. Call the UC Function Through MCP
chunks.text: Now we call the registered UC function through the MCP protocol, just as an agent would. The default tool name is of the form `catalogName__schemaName__toolName` as demonstrated in the next cell.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: D1. Enable Autologging
chunks.text:
MLflow autologging for the OpenAI integration automatically captures execution traces for every agent run by patching the OpenAI SDK so that every call to various methods automatically generates MLflow traces. Each trace records the full sequence of LLM calls, tool invocations, inputs, outputs, and latencies without requiring any code changes to the agent itself.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
Autologging captures: LLM call spans (model, prompt, completion tokens), tool call spans (function name, arguments, return value), and the overall agent run span with total latency. All traces are stored in the MLflow experiment associated with this notebook.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: D2. Registering Traces to Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
At this point, our traces haven't been logged. This means we have no insight into things like token usage, execution time per tool call, etc. 

Next, we'll show how to register traces in Unity Catalog. Databricks recommends this pattern for new and production workloads. 

1. Instantiate the `UnityCatalog` class from `mlflow` and call it `uc`.

2. Create and set the experiment location using `mlflow.set_experiment()`. In the code below, we will use `dbutils`, which is a Databricks utility library that allows users to do things like get the current notebook path within the workspace.

3. Navigate to Unity Catalog and see that we now have multiple tables and views with the prefix we set earlier, `oai_sa` ("OpenAI Single Agent"). These tables are empty since we haven't made any calls with our agent. Let's stress test the agent with and without MCP tools.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: D3. Tracing without MCP
chunks.text:
With autologging enabled, the next agent run will produce a full execution trace, which we will inspect in a moment. The trace captures the LLM reasoning step, the tool call to `classify_price_tier`, and the final response generation.

Navigate to the `oai_sa_otel_spans` table and click on the **Sample Data** tab. In the **name** column you will see `data_analyst_mcp_execution` and `AsyncDatabricksCompletions` This course does not go into details on spans and OTel concepts, but you can read more here ([AWS](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/trace-unity-catalog) | [Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/databricks/mlflow3/genai/tracing/trace-unity-catalog) | [GCP](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/trace-unity-catalog)).

 
 
 
 Why Two Traces? 
 
You may notice that a single agent query produces two separate traces in MLflow. This is expected behavior with mlflow.openai.autolog() . Because autologging patches at the OpenAI client level , each individual API call becomes its own top-level trace. A single Runner.run() call typically makes two underlying LLM calls:
 
 
 First LLM call : The model receives the user query, reasons about it, and decides to invoke the classify_price_tier tool. 
 Second LLM call : After the tool returns its result, the model generates the final natural-language response. 
 
 
Without a parent span grouping them, each call appears as a separate trace. The next section solves this by wrapping the full agent run in @mlflow.trace() , which concatenates all spans into one unified trace .

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: D4. Tracing with MCP
chunks.text:
In a Databricks App deployment, the `McpServer` from `databricks_openai.agents` is used as an async context manager with the `Agent()` class.

 
 @function_tool Local only 
 → 
 UC Function Governed + reusable 
 → 
 MCP Server Agent-accessible + standardized 
 → 
 Agent Ready for testing 
 

This is the recommended progression: start with `@function_tool` for rapid prototyping, register to UC for governance, then expose through MCP for production agent access.

1. Run the next cell to expose only `classify_price_uc` to the agent. 

2. **Redefine our agent** from before, but this time we pass `mcp_servers=[mcp_server]` instead of `tools`. The agent now discovers its tools at runtime from the UC function MCP server rather than from inline `@function_tool` definitions.

 
 
Why do we need @mlflow.trace, async def, and async?
 
 
 
 @mlflow.trace(...) : Without this, the MCP connection, LLM call, and tool call each produce separate traces. Wrapping them in a single decorated function concatenates all spans into one unified trace. 
 async def : Runner.run() is async (it makes HTTP calls to the model endpoint), and McpServer is an async context manager. Both require await , which means the enclosing function must be async def . 
 async with mcp_server: : Opens the HTTP connection to the Databricks Managed MCP server before the agent runs, and closes it after. The agent calls tools/list and tools/call over this connection during execution.

chunks.lecture: 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: D5. View MLflow Traces
chunks.text: Finally, now that we have some traces logged with MLflow, we can view the traces in either the **Experiments** UI or directly from the unified trace table stored in the schema `agent_training` with the table prefix `oai_sa`.

2. Search for the experiment **oai-sa-sdk-training**. There you will see traces under the **Traces** tab. Click any trace to see a detailed breakdown of tools used and model calls.

2. Click on the **_otel_spans** table and click on **Sample Data** and ask a question in the provided query box like _Which trace took the longest to run?_ This will automatically generate a sql query (you might be asked to grant auto-run, click accept). The answer will be returned to you.
3. Run the next cell to see logged traces here in the notebook. Notice the same information is captured in the column `spans`.

chunks.heading: E. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. Configured the OpenAI Agents SDK to call a Unity Catalog model service through Unity Gateway

4. Registered `classify_price_tier` as a Python UC function for governance and connected it to the agent via MCP
5. Enabled MLflow autologging and inspected execution traces capturing LLM calls, tool invocations, and response generation

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
In this lab, you will apply what you learned in the *Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks* demo to build a multi-agent system yourself. You will configure the SDK, connect two worker agents to Unity Catalog functions through Managed MCP servers, create a supervisor that routes requests with handoffs, refine the supervisor's routing instructions in its YAML config, and trace the full orchestration with MLflow.

Each step has a **TODO** with ` ` placeholders. The instructions above each TODO tell you what to fill in, and you can reveal the answer if you get stuck.

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1. **Configure the OpenAI Agents SDK** to route requests through Databricks model services
2. **Connect worker agents to Unity Catalog functions** using Managed MCP servers, with `DatabricksMCPClient` for discovery and `McpServer` for agent integration
3. **Build a supervisor agent** that delegates user requests to worker agents with `handoffs`
4. **Validate and refine routing** by testing queries and editing the supervisor's YAML instructions
5. **Capture multi-agent execution** with MLflow autologging
6. **Combine spans into a single trace** with `@mlflow.trace` and `mlflow.start_span`

chunks.text:
Before building agents, verify that the UC functions are registered and discoverable. This lab uses two ways to work with the Databricks-managed MCP server:
1. `DatabricksMCPClient`: a synchronous API for direct MCP tool calls (good for notebooks)
1. `McpServer`: an asynchronous context manager that connects MCP servers to OpenAI Agents SDK agents (useful for applications)

chunks.heading: B2. Build MCP-Backed Agents
chunks.text:
Each agent will have its own configuration file. Additionally, each agent will have its own `McpServer` scoped to a single UC function. This ensures each agent can only access the tool it needs:
1. `classify_price_tier` → **Data Analyst agent**
1. `neighborhood_summary` → **Business Analyst agent**

chunks.heading: B2.1 Load the Agent Configuration
chunks.text:
We will load the agent configuration file. This is a recommended practice since any updates to the agents' system prompts, name, etc. live outside this notebook. These variables will be stored in the dictionary `agents`:
- `agents["X"]['name']`: The agent's name
- `agents["X"]['llm_endpoint']`: The name of the Unity Catalog **model service** the agent calls (`agent-training-model`). In the next step you combine it with your catalog and schema into the service's fully qualified name.
- `agents["X"]['system_prompt']`: The agent's system prompt

Running the following cell will store config variables for the data analyst, business data analyst, and the supervisor agent that will be used later.
 - Navigate to the folder **agent_config** and inspect the agent contents for each: **business_data_analyst_agent.yaml**, **data_analyst_agent.yaml**, and **supervisor_agent.yaml**

It routes requests through Unity Gateway to `databricks-gpt-5-2`. Agents reference the service, not the model, by its fully qualified name, `catalog.schema.service`, just as in notebook 05. The YAML configs store only the service name in `llm_endpoint`.

chunks.heading: C1. Build the Supervisor
chunks.text:
The supervisor agent analyzes each user request and delegates to the appropriate worker using the **handoff** mechanism from the [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents). When the supervisor hands off to a worker, that worker takes over the conversation and responds directly to the user.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
The handoffs parameter tells the supervisor which agents it can delegate to. The supervisor's instructions guide its routing decisions. The LLM reads each worker's name and instructions to decide which one is best suited for the request.
See: Orchestration and handoffs 
 
 
 
 

**TODO:** Create the supervisor and give it both worker agents as handoffs. The supervisor has no tools of its own: its only job is to pick a worker.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
supervisor = Agent(
 name=agents["sa"]["name"],
 instructions=agents["sa"]["system_prompt"],
 model=model_fqn,
 handoffs=[data_analyst_agent, business_analyst_agent],
)

print(f"Created supervisor with handoffs to: {[a.name for a in supervisor.handoffs]}")
```

chunks.heading: C2. How the Supervisor Routes Requests

chunks.heading: D1. Data Question
chunks.text:
This question is about price classification. The supervisor should route it to the Data Analyst agent, which will call `classify_price_tier` via MCP. You can verify this in MLflow interface as a part of running the next cell. 

We are connecting to the Databricks managed MCP server via`McpServer`, which is an async context manager, hence we need to be mindful of using `async` and `await`. Similarly, `Runner.run()` is also async.

**TODO:** Fill in:
- both MCP servers in the `async with` statement, since they must stay open while the agents run
- the `Runner` method that runs the supervisor (the same one you used in notebook 05)
- the `result` attributes for the agent that produced the final answer and for the final response text

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer

```python
data_query = "Is $200/night a good deal for an Airbnb in SF?"

async def test_data_query():
 async with da_mcp_server, ba_mcp_server:
 result = await Runner.run(supervisor, data_query)
 return result

result = asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(test_data_query())
print(f"User: {data_query}")
print(f"Handled by: {result.last_agent.name}")
print(f"Response: {result.final_output}")
```

chunks.heading: D3. Mixed Routing Test
chunks.text:
Run multiple queries and show how the supervisor routes each one to the appropriate worker agent. Notice that in the output there are multiple traces. In the next section, we will see how to concatenate them into 1 trace and perform proper logging as a series of events so we have a more comprehensive picture of the flow from input to output via the supervisor agent.

**TODO:** For each query, fill in the agent you expect the supervisor to hand off to, using `agents["da"]["name"]` or `agents["ba"]["name"]`. The last query combines a price with a neighborhood, so think about which tool can actually answer it: `classify_price_tier` only knows citywide price tiers, while `neighborhood_summary` knows each neighborhood's average price.

Routing is an LLM decision, so a `MISMATCH` can appear on any run. You will tighten the routing rules in the next step.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
import pandas as pd

test_queries = [
 ("Is $150/night a good deal in SF?", agents["da"]["name"]),
 ("What is the average price in Mission?", agents["ba"]["name"]),
 ("Would $350/night be considered luxury?", agents["da"]["name"]),
 ("Is the average price in Mission higher or lower than in Noe Valley?", agents["ba"]["name"]),

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: Needs the Mission's average price, which only neighborhood_summary provides
chunks.text:
("Is $250/night expensive for the Mission?", agents["ba"]["name"]),
]

async def test_mixed_routing():
 async with da_mcp_server, ba_mcp_server:
 results = []
 for query, expected in test_queries:
 result = await Runner.run(supervisor, query)
 actual = result.last_agent.name
 status = "PASS" if actual == expected else "MISMATCH"
 results.append({
 "Query": query,
 "Expected Agent": expected,
 "Actual Agent": actual,
 "Status": status,
 })
 return results

results = asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(test_mixed_routing())
display(pd.DataFrame(results))
```

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: E. Enable MLflow Tracing
chunks.text: Now that we have built and validated our multi-agent system, we enable autologging with MLflow to capture execution traces. This section will have fractured traces showing each handoff and tool call as a separate trace. We will see later how we can bring these together in 1 trace. For now, let's focus on the individual outputs to see how a multi-agent system appears as multiple traces.

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: E1. Enable Autologging
chunks.text:
We enable MLflow tracing so the next agent runs produce full execution traces.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
In the MLflow Experiment UI, multi-agent traces show nested spans: the supervisor's LLM call appears at the top level, followed by the handoff event, and then the worker's LLM and tool calls as child spans. This makes it easy to debug routing decisions and tool selection.

```python
mlflow.openai.autolog()

print("MLflow OpenAI autologging enabled.")
print(f"Traces will appear in experiment: {mlflow_experiment_path}")
```

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: E2. Run with Tracing
chunks.text: Run the supervisor again with tracing enabled. The trace will capture the full handoff flow from supervisor to worker. The `transfer_to_Data_Analyst` and `transfer_to_Business_Analyst` tools do not exist in your code. The SDK generates them automatically from `handoffs=[data_analyst_agent, business_analyst_agent]` using the pattern `transfer_to_{agent.name}`.

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: F. Distributed Tracing
chunks.text:
Notice the output from the previous section may produce multiple separate trace outputs. MLflow supports distributed tracing to stitch spans from different calls into a single unified trace.

The key idea: wrap the entire multi-agent flow in a parent `@mlflow.trace` span. All child spans (from autologging, tool calls, and handoffs) automatically nest under it, producing one clean trace tree instead of scattered fragments.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
For cross-service distributed tracing (e.g., an agent calling another agent over HTTP), MLflow provides get_tracing_context_headers_for_http_request() and set_tracing_context_from_http_request_headers() to propagate trace context via W3C TraceContext headers. Both services must log to the same MLflow tracking server and experiment. On Databricks, the trace destination must be set to Unity Catalog.
See: MLflow Distributed Tracing docs

chunks.lecture: 06 Lab - Multi-Agent Orchestration with The OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks
chunks.heading: F1. Build Traced Agent Wrappers
chunks.text:
To make handoffs visible in the trace, we wrap each agent's execution in its own `@mlflow.trace` span. The supervisor routes the question, then we call the selected worker inside a labeled span. This produces a trace tree like:

```
supervisor_orchestration
 +-- route_decision (supervisor LLM call)
 +-- data_analyst_execution OR business_analyst_execution
 +-- AsyncDatabricksCompletions (worker LLM + tool calls)
```

1. Create a trace wrapper for the agents defined above. Here we are setting the `span_type` to `AGENT` and defining the names of the agents as they will appear in the trace. Again, we are connecting to the Databricks managed MCP server via`McpServer`, which is an async context manager, hence we need to be mindful of using `async` and `await` as mentioned in section **D**.

**TODO:** Fill in:
- the span type for each wrapper (the same span type you used for the agent wrapper in notebook 05, section D4)
- the MCP server each worker needs open while it runs
- the agent each wrapper runs

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
@mlflow.trace(span_type="AGENT", name="data_analyst_execution")
async def run_data_analyst(question: str) -> str:
 async with da_mcp_server:
 result = await Runner.run(data_analyst_agent, question)
 return result.final_output

@mlflow.trace(span_type="AGENT", name="business_analyst_execution")
async def run_business_analyst(question: str) -> str:
 async with ba_mcp_server:
 result = await Runner.run(business_analyst_agent, question)
 return result.final_output
```

 
 

2. Define the router and the parent trace. The router is a plain agent with **no handoffs**. It reuses the supervisor's instructions, so instead of handing off it replies with the name of the worker that should handle the request, and we read that reply as the route. The parent `@mlflow.trace` span, `supervisor_orchestration`, is provided.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: In this demo, you will build a single Data Analyst agent using LangChain on Databricks. You will define a custom tool with LangChain's `@tool` decorator, register it to Unity Catalog, discover it via a Managed MCP server, and connect it to a LangChain agent with MLflow tracing.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this demo, you will be able to:
1. Define custom tools using LangChain's `@tool` decorator
2. Build and test a LangChain agent with `create_agent`
3. Register tools to Unity Catalog for governance
4. Discover UC tools via Managed MCP servers
5. Rebuild the agent with MCP-sourced tools
6. Enable MLflow autologging and inspect execution traces

 
 
 
 Note 
 
This notebook mirrors notebook 05 Demo - Introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK on Databricks , using LangChain instead of the OpenAI Agents SDK.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: A1. Import Libraries
chunks.text:
We import the core components needed for this demo:
- `ChatDatabricks` for connecting to Databricks model serving endpoints
- `@tool` decorator for defining agent tools
- `create_agent` from `langchain.agents` for building the agent

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. Define the `classify_price_tier` Tool
chunks.text:
The `classify_price_tier` tool classifies an Airbnb listing's nightly price into one of four market tiers based on the SF pricing distribution:

| Tier | Price Range | Percentile Band |
|---|---|---|
| **Budget** | Under $100 | Bottom 25% |
| **Mid-Range** | $100 -- $174 | 25--50% |
| **Premium** | $175 -- $299 | 50--75% |
| **Luxury** | $300+ | Top 25% |

LangChain's `@tool` decorator registers this function as a tool that the agent can invoke. The SDK extracts the function signature and docstring to generate the tool schema that the LLM uses to decide when and how to call the tool.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
An example production workflow is: prototype with @tool , then register to Unity Catalog, then access via a Managed MCP server. This demo follows that full progression. In Section C, we register the function to Unity Catalog. In Section D, we connect via MCP.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: B2. Create the Agent
chunks.text:
With the tool defined, we create an agent using LangChain's `create_agent`. This takes three inputs:
1. **LLM**: `ChatDatabricks` connects to a Databricks model serving endpoint
2. **Tools**: The list of tools the agent can call
3. **System prompt**: Instructions that shape the agent's behavior, passed as `system_prompt`

The agent runs a ReAct loop: the LLM reasons about which tool to call, executes it, observes the result, and generates a final response. `create_agent` replaces LangGraph's `create_react_agent`, which is deprecated as of LangGraph 1.0, and still runs on LangGraph under the hood.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: B3. Test the Agent
chunks.text:
We send three progressively complex queries to validate that the agent correctly invokes the tool and interprets the results.

1. A straightforward pricing question that requires a single tool call.

2. A direct tier classification at the high end of the price spectrum.

3. Multiple prices in a single request, testing whether the agent calls the tool multiple times.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: C1. Register `classify_price_tier` as a Python UC Function
chunks.text:
The inline `@tool` is local to this notebook session. To make the tool governed, discoverable, and reusable across agents and workspaces, we register it to Unity Catalog as a Python function using `DatabricksFunctionClient`.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
The function registered below is a plain Python function (no @tool decorator). The DatabricksFunctionClient inspects the function signature and docstring to create the UC function metadata. The logic is identical to the tool we prototyped above.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: C2. Verify Registered Functions
chunks.text:
Confirm that the function is visible in the Unity Catalog schema, then call it directly to verify it returns the expected output.
1. Navigate to the **Catalog Explorer** on the left side menu and search for `classify_price_tier_uc`
1. Run the next cell to test the output from calling the function from UC

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: D1. Connect to the Managed MCP Server
chunks.text:
Databricks provides **Managed MCP servers** that automatically expose Unity Catalog functions as tools. Any agent can discover and call these functions through the MCP protocol without custom integration code.

The MCP server endpoint for UC functions follows this pattern:
`https://workspace/api/2.0/mcp/functions/catalog/schema`

 
 
 
 Note 
 
We use DatabricksMCPClient from databricks_mcp to interact with the MCP endpoint in a notebook context.
See: Managed MCP servers ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: D2. Call the UC Function Through MCP
chunks.text: Now we call the registered UC function through the MCP protocol, just as an agent would. The default tool name is of the form `catalogName__schemaName__toolName`.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: D3. Load MCP Tools into LangChain

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: E1. Enable Autologging and UC Registration
chunks.text:
MLflow autologging for LangChain automatically captures execution traces for every agent run. Each trace records the full sequence of LLM calls, tool invocations, inputs, outputs, and latencies without requiring any code changes to the agent itself.

 
 
 
 Note 
 
When using LangChain, use mlflow.langchain.autolog() . Autologging captures: LLM call spans (model, prompt, completion tokens), tool call spans (function name, arguments, return value), and the overall agent run span with total latency.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: E2. Build the MCP-Powered Agent
chunks.text: We rebuild the agent using the same LLM and system prompt, but now the tools come from MCP rather than inline `@tool` definitions. The `create_agent` call is identical.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: E3. Test the MCP-Powered Agent
chunks.text: With autologging enabled, each agent run produces a full execution trace. The trace captures the LLM reasoning step, the tool call to `classify_price_tier_uc` (now routed through MCP), and the final response generation.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: E5. View MLflow Traces
chunks.text: Finally, now that we have some traces logged with MLflow, we can view the traces in either the **Experiments** UI or directly from the unified trace table stored in the schema `agent_training` with the table prefix `lc_sa`.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: Experiment UI
chunks.text:
1. Navigate to **Experiments** in the left sidebar, right click, and select **Open Link in New Tab**. 
2. Search for the experiment **langchain-sdk-training**. There you will see traces under the **Traces** tab. Click any trace to see a detailed breakdown of tools used and model calls via **ChatDatabricks**.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: MLflow Unified Tables from Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
1. Navigate to the **Catalog Explorer** and search for **lc_sa**. This surfaces 6 default tables that have been created. 
 - 4 tables: **lc_sa_otel_logs**, **lc_sa_otel_spans**, **lc_sa_otel_annotations**, and **lc_sa_otel_annotations**
 - 2 views: **lc_sa_trace_unified**, and **lc_sa_trace_metadata**
2. Click on the **_otel_spans** table and click on **Sample Data** and ask a question in the provided query box like _Which trace took the longest to run?_ This will automatically generate a SQL query (you might be asked to grant auto-run, click accept). The answer will be returned to you.
3. Run the next cell to see logged traces here in the notebook. Notice the same information is captured in the column `spans`.

chunks.lecture: 07 Demo - Introduction to LangChain on Databricks
chunks.heading: F. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. Defined a `classify_price_tier` tool using LangChain's `@tool` decorator to classify Airbnb prices into market tiers
2. Built a single Data Analyst agent with LangChain's `create_agent` and tested it with progressively complex pricing queries
3. Registered `classify_price_tier` as a Python UC function for governance
4. Discovered the UC function through a Managed MCP server and wrapped it as a LangChain `StructuredTool`
5. Rebuilt the agent with MCP-sourced tools and enabled MLflow tracing with `mlflow.langchain.autolog()`

The same `@tool` to UC to MCP progression works across frameworks -- whether you use LangChain (this demo) or the OpenAI Agents SDK (notebook 05).

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
In this lab, you will build a tool-calling agent with **DSPy**, a framework where you declare *what* a language model should do with **signatures** and let **modules** decide *how* to prompt it. You will connect DSPy to a Databricks model, prototype one tool as a plain Python function, wrap a Unity Catalog function as a second tool, and combine them in a `dspy.ReAct` agent that you trace with MLflow. This notebook acts as a primer for the DSPy framework and is by no means comprehensive. 

Each step has a **TODO** with ` ` placeholders. The instructions above each TODO tell you what to fill in, and you can reveal the answer if you get stuck.

1. Configure DSPy to use a Databricks model serving endpoint
2. Define DSPy signatures, in shorthand and as classes
3. Prototype agent tools as plain Python functions, and wrap a Unity Catalog function as a DSPy tool
4. Build a `dspy.ReAct` agent that reasons and calls tools
5. Inspect an agent's trajectory and its MLflow trace
