chunks.heading: A1. Lab Scenario
chunks.text:
.scn8{font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,sans-serif;color:#0b2026;width:100%;max-width:100%;box-sizing:border-box;margin:0;padding:8px}.scn8 .scen{background:#FFFFFF;color:#0b2026;padding:26px 30px;border-radius:12px;box-sizing:border-box;overflow:hidden;box-shadow:0 2px 16px rgba(27,49,57,0.10),0 1px 4px rgba(27,49,57,0.06);border:1px solid rgba(27,49,57,0.08)}.scn8 .kicker{font-size:14px;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:1.2px;color:#5A6F77;margin-bottom:10px;font-weight:700;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px}.scn8 .body{font-size:15px;line-height:1.7;color:#0b2026}.scn8 .body p{margin:0 0 14px}.scn8 .body p:last-child{margin:0}.scn8 .tools{background:#F9F7F4;border:1px solid rgba(27,49,57,0.10);border-radius:8px;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Consolas,monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:1.9}.scn8 .fn{color:#0B8F5F}.scn8 .arg{color:#5A6F77}.scn8 .dsc{color:#5A6F77;opacity:.8}.scn8 code{background:rgba(27,49,57,0.07);padding:2px 6px;border-radius:4px;font-size:14px;font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Consolas,monospace;color:#0b2026}.scn8 .eq{background:rgba(0,169,114,.10);border-left:4px solid #00A972;padding:10px 14px;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;margin:10px 0 0;font-size:14px;font-style:italic;line-height:1.6;color:#0b2026} 
 Scenario 
 
 You are building an Airbnb recommendation assistant for San Francisco. A user should be able to ask about a specific listing, compare it against neighborhood averages, and get a concrete recommendation — all in one turn. The assistant needs to reason about which tools to call and in what order, then synthesize the results into a single answer. 

 You will wire DSPy to a Databricks-hosted model, define two tools, and combine them in a dspy.ReAct agent that alternates between thinking and acting until it can answer: 

 get_listing_details (listing_id) — fetches structured details for one listing from a Spark table avg_neigh_price (neighborhood) — calls a Unity Catalog function that returns the neighborhood’s average nightly price 

 The first tool is a plain Python function — DSPy has no tool decorator, so any function can be a tool. The second wraps a UC function using a parameterized query, keeping the logic governed in Unity Catalog while DSPy sees an ordinary callable. By the end, the agent will handle questions like: 

 "Tell me about listing 958. Is it more expensive than the average listing in the Mission?"

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: B1. Connect DSPy to a Model Service via Unity Gateway
chunks.text:
The first step in getting started with DSPy is to create a language model client. `dspy.LM` creates the client, and there are two ways to bring in a model:
- `databricks/ `: calls a Databricks-provided model service from the `system.ai` catalog (available to all account users by default).
- `databricks/ `: calls a custom model service registered elsewhere in Unity Catalog (with configurable routing, fallbacks, and access controls).

Authentication is handled via your Databricks credentials (in our case by defining a notebook-scoped token for demonstration purposes), and authorization is governed by Unity Catalog permissions after we have resolved the Workspace URL. `dspy.configure` then sets it as the default model for every DSPy module.

**TODO:** Fill out the fully-qualified name for bringing in the model service in your schema `agent_training` (inspect the name using the **Catalog** button to the left) and set the default model for all DSPy modules that will be used in this notebook.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
import os
import dspy

token = (
 dbutils.notebook.entry_point.getDbutils()
 .notebook().getContext().apiToken().get()
)

host = spark.conf.get("spark.databricks.workspaceUrl")

model_service = f"{catalog_name}.{schema_name}.agent-training-model"

lm = dspy.LM(
 model=f"databricks/{model_service}", # fully qualified UC name
 api_base=f"https://{host}/ai-gateway/mlflow/v1",
 api_key=token
)

dspy.configure(lm=lm)
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: C. Signatures and Modules
chunks.text:
A [**signature**](https://dspy.ai/current/api/signatures/) declares a task's inputs and outputs, and a [**module**](https://dspy.ai/current/api/modules/) decides how to prompt the model for it. The shorthand signature below has one input, `question`, and one output, `answer`. `dspy.Predict` is the simplest module.

You never write the prompt yourself. Inside every module, an [**adapter**](https://dspy.ai/current/api/adapters/) writes the prompt from your signature, sends it to the model, and parses the reply back into your output fields. The adapter pattern allows DSPy to work with different LM interfaces while maintaining a consistent programming model for users. The diagram follows one call through `dspy.Predict`:

 
 
 .dsp{background:#ffffff;width:100%;max-width:none;margin:0;padding:8px 0 16px;box-sizing:border-box;}
 .dsp svg{display:block;width:100%;height:auto;}
 .dsp svg text{font-family:-apple-system,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Arial,sans-serif;fill:#0b2026;}
 .dsp .h {font-weight:800;}
 .dsp .b {font-weight:700;}
 .dsp .m {fill:#618794;font-weight:500;}
 .dsp .mono,.dsp .mono text{white-space:pre;font-family:ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;font-variant-ligatures:none;font-feature-settings:"liga" 0,"calt" 0;}
 
 answer' promises an answer for a question. 1, you call qa(question='What is the capital of France?'). 2, the Adapter's format step writes a system message listing the input and output fields and a user message with the question under a [[ ## question ## ]] marker. 3, the LM only sees those chat messages and replies with plain text. 4, the Adapter's parse step finds the [[ ## answer ## ]] marker in the reply and extracts Paris. 5, you get back Prediction(answer='Paris'). ChatAdapter is the default; JSONAdapter or TwoStepAdapter can be swapped in with dspy.configure(adapter=...) without changing the program.">

 answer 
 
 Signature "question -> answer" 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Adapter 
 ChatAdapter by default

 "question -> answer" )

 "What is the capital 
 of France?" )

 Your input fields are: 
 1. `question` (str) 
 Your output fields are: 
 1. `answer` (str) …

 France? Respond with …

 plain text out

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: D. Prepare the Data
chunks.text:
We will create an agent that answers questions about the San Francisco Airbnb listings created by our classroom setup script. Run the next cell to preview the table.

The next cell defines a [Pydantic model](https://pydantic.dev/), `ListingInfo`, that describes a listing. Every field on a Signature is a Pydantic `FieldInfo` and the base `Signature` class extends `pydantic.BaseModel`. Your first tool returns it, so the agent receives structured, typed fields instead of a raw row.

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: E1. Prototype a Tool as a Plain Function
chunks.text:
DSPy has no tool decorator: any Python function can be a tool. Instead, we can pass the tool directly to the agent without any additional configuration.

**TODO:** Finish `get_listing_details` by adding:
- a type hint for `listing_id` (an integer) and the return type (`ListingInfo`)
- a docstring that says what the tool returns and when to use it

The body is provided.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
def get_listing_details(listing_id: int) -> ListingInfo:
 """Get details for one San Francisco Airbnb listing by its ID, including its
 neighborhood, room type, nightly price in USD, and summary.

 Use this when the user asks about a specific listing ID."""
 rows = spark.table("sf_airbnb_listings").filter(f"id = {int(listing_id)}").limit(1).collect()
 if not rows:
 raise ValueError(f"Listing with ID {listing_id} not found.")
 r = rows[0]
 return ListingInfo(
 id=r.id,
 name=r.name,
 neighbourhood=r.neighbourhood,
 neighbourhood_cleansed=r.neighbourhood_cleansed,
 summary=r.summary,
 price=r.price,
 room_type=r.room_type,
 listing_source_information=r.listing_source_information,
 )

get_listing_details(958)
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: E2. Wrap a Unity Catalog Function as a Tool
chunks.text:
Setup registered `avg_neigh_price` to Unity Catalog. To give it to a DSPy agent, wrap a call to it in a plain function. The logic stays governed in Unity Catalog, and DSPy sees an ordinary tool.

The neighborhood comes from the model, so never paste it into the SQL text. Use a **named parameter marker** such as `:neighborhood` and pass the value in `args`. Spark then treats it as data, so a value with a quote in it cannot break, or change, the query.

**TODO:** Fill in the parameter marker and the `args` dictionary.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
def avg_neigh_price(neighborhood: str) -> Optional[float]:
 """Get the average nightly price in USD of San Francisco Airbnb listings in a
 neighborhood, such as 'Mission' or 'Noe Valley'."""
 result = spark.sql(
 "SELECT avg_neigh_price(:neighborhood) AS average_price",
 args={"neighborhood": neighborhood},
 ).collect()
 return result[0]["average_price"] if result else None

avg_neigh_price("Mission")
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: F1. Define the Agent's Signature
chunks.text:
For an agent, write the signature as a class. The docstring becomes the agent's instructions, and each field gets a description the model reads.

**TODO:** Declare `user_request` as an input field and `response` as an output field.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
class AirbnbRecommendationAgent(dspy.Signature):
 """You are an Airbnb recommendation assistant for San Francisco listings.
 Use your tools to look up listings and neighborhood prices, and answer with specific numbers."""

 user_request: str = dspy.InputField(desc="The user's question about Airbnb listings")
 response: str = dspy.OutputField(desc="A helpful answer with specific listing details and prices")
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: F2. Create the Agent
chunks.text:
`dspy.ReAct` alternates between **reasoning** about what to do next and **acting** by calling a tool, until it can answer.

**TODO:** Create the agent from your signature and both tools. The output lists three tools: your two, plus `finish`, which ReAct always adds so the agent can signal that it's done.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
agent = dspy.ReAct(
 AirbnbRecommendationAgent,
 tools=[get_listing_details, avg_neigh_price],
)

for name, tool in agent.tools.items():
 print(f"- {name}: {tool.desc[:90]}")
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: G1. Ask a Question That Needs Both Tools
chunks.text:
**TODO:** Call the agent, passing the question as the signature's input field, and print the signature's output field. Then open the trace under the output: you should see a call to `get_listing_details` and a call to `avg_neigh_price`.

 
 
 ANSWER Click to view answer
 
 Copy 

```python
result = agent(user_request="Tell me about listing 958. Is it more expensive than the average listing in the Mission?")

print(result.response)
```

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: G2. Inspect the Trajectory
chunks.text:
Besides the answer, the result holds the agent's **trajectory**: for each step, its thought, the tool it chose, the arguments, and the result it observed. Run the next cell to print it.

To see the exact prompts DSPy sent to the model, use `dspy.inspect_history`.

chunks.lecture: 08 Lab - Building Agents with DSPy on Databricks
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this lab, you:
1. Connected DSPy to a Databricks model with `dspy.LM` and `dspy.configure`
2. Declared tasks with shorthand and class-based signatures, and let modules write the prompts
3. Prototyped a tool as a plain Python function and wrapped a Unity Catalog function as a second tool, using a parameterized query
4. Built a `dspy.ReAct` agent and inspected its trajectory and MLflow trace

DSPy's biggest strength, **optimizing** prompts and modules against your own data, builds on exactly these signatures and modules. To go further, see the [DSPy documentation](https://dspy.ai/) and the Databricks guide to DSPy ( AWS | Azure | GCP ).

Students learn to create governed agent tools using Unity Catalog and MCP, build single and multi-agent systems with the OpenAI Agents SDK, and build agents with other popular frameworks such as LangChain and DSPy. The course covers the full progression from tool prototyping to production deployment, with hands-on experience using MLflow tracing to observe agent execution. Through practical demonstrations and labs, students develop skills in building, orchestrating, and governing AI agents on the Databricks platform.

chunks.lecture: AGENDA
chunks.heading: Course Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

1. **Define AI agents and their architectures** — Explain what AI agents are, identify their core components (reasoning, planning, tool use), and determine when to use a single-agent vs. multi-agent architecture.
2. **Create governed agent tools in Unity Catalog** — Build and register both SQL and Python functions in Unity Catalog, equipping them with descriptive names, type hints, and structured docstrings that enable reliable agent tool selection.
3. **Assess and improve tool documentation for agent use** — Identify documentation gaps that cause agents to misuse tools, and rewrite function signatures and docstrings to improve agent behavior.
4. **Expose and discover tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — Use Databricks Managed MCP servers to connect agents to Unity Catalog functions, AI Search indexes, and other Databricks services at runtime.
5. **Build single-agent systems with the OpenAI Agents SDK** — Configure the SDK with Databricks model routing, define custom tools with `@function_tool`, and build a functional agent that reasons over and calls tools.
6. **Orchestrate multi-agent systems with handoffs** — Build supervisor-worker architectures using the OpenAI Agents SDK, route requests to specialized worker agents via handoffs, and refine routing through YAML-based instructions.
7. **Build agents with LangChain and DSPy on Databricks** — Apply the same tool-creation-to-agent workflow using LangChain's `@tool` decorator and `create_agent`, as well as DSPy signatures and `dspy.ReAct` modules.
8. **Observe agent execution with MLflow tracing** — Enable MLflow autologging, inspect hierarchical span traces across single- and multi-agent flows, and use tracing to debug and improve agent quality.
9. **Apply Unity Gateway governance to AI agents** — Understand how Unity Gateway provides centralized access control, rate limiting, spend tracking, and fallback routing for model services across agent applications.

This course teaches students how to systematically evaluate AI agents using MLflow's evaluation framework, addressing the unique challenges of non-deterministic AI systems that traditional software testing cannot handle. chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
This course registers its agent in Unity Catalog and deploys the same registered model as a **Databricks App** (the **agent-airbnb-assistant** app), which is the deployment target Databricks recommends for new agent projects. Deploying to Model Serving endpoints with `agents.deploy()` is still available for existing deployments.

This appendix provides a brief overview of the deployment landscape so you can make informed decisions when deploying your own agents.

 
 Note 
 This appendix is reference material only. The evaluation techniques covered in this course apply regardless of which deployment method you choose.

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: A. Model Serving vs. Databricks Apps
chunks.text:
| | Model Serving (`agents.deploy()`) | Databricks Apps (recommended) |
|---|---|---|
| **Deploy** | A single function call | Git-based development with bundles, with explicit auth in `databricks.yml` |
| **Infrastructure** | Provisioned automatically, with limited control over the server configuration | Full control over the code and server configuration |
| **Agent code** | Logged as an MLflow artifact | An async FastAPI server (MLflow AgentServer) that you can run locally with `uv run start-app` |
| **Built in** | Inference tables, tracing, and the Review App | A chat UI and an `/invocations` endpoint |

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: When to use each
chunks.text:
- **Model Serving** works well for quick prototyping and existing deployments that don't need migration yet.
- **Databricks Apps** is the recommended path for new production deployments where you need Git-based CI/CD, local development, and full control over the serving infrastructure.

Both approaches support MLflow tracing and evaluation. The `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` patterns you learned in this course work identically against agents deployed via either method.

For full details, see: Author an AI agent and deploy it on Databricks Apps ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: B. Migrating from Model Serving to Databricks Apps
chunks.text: If you have an agent deployed via `agents.deploy()` and want to migrate to Databricks Apps, the process involves restructuring your code and configuration.

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: Migration steps
chunks.text:
1. **Download** the agent's MLflow artifacts.
2. **Restructure** the class methods into decorated functions.
3. **Configure** the app in `databricks.yml`.
4. **Deploy** with `databricks bundle deploy`.

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: What changes
chunks.text:
| Aspect | Model Serving | Databricks Apps |
|---|---|---|
| **Agent code** | Class-based `ResponsesAgent` with `predict()` / `predict_stream()` | Module-level `@invoke()` and `@stream()` decorated functions |
| **Configuration** | MLmodel file + model config YAML | `databricks.yml` with resource declarations |
| **Execution model** | Synchronous | Async recommended (`async def`) |
| **Deployment command** | `agents.deploy()` | `databricks bundle deploy` |

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: What stays the same
chunks.text:
- Core agent logic (tool definitions, LLM calls, prompt templates)
- MLflow tracing and evaluation integration
- Unity Catalog tool registration
- Request/response payload format

For the full migration guide, see: Migrate an agent from Model Serving to Databricks Apps ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns
chunks.heading: C. Agents on Databricks
chunks.text:
Databricks offers a spectrum of approaches — from fully managed, no-code options to fully custom, code-first development.

 

 
 
 LEGACY 
 Knowledge Assistant 
 Bring your own AI Search index, choose your chunking strategy, and attach multiple source types (up to 10). Full control over the retrieval pipeline. 
 

 
 
 MANAGED 
 Genie Agent 
 Declarative agents that understand your data. Attach tables for structured queries or UC volumes for document search — Databricks handles tool orchestration and query generation. 
 

 
 
 CODE-FIRST 
 Custom Agent 
 Write your own agent logic, tools, and orchestration. Use the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or any Python framework, then deploy it as a Databricks App, the recommended way to host agents. 
 

 

**Knowledge Assistants** offer customization (bring your own AI Search index) but are a legacy path. **Genie Agents** are the recommended declarative option for data-aware agents: you declare *what* data or documents your agent should work with, and the platform optimizes *how*. **Custom agents** are code-first: you own the agent logic, tools, and orchestration end to end, and Databricks Apps is the recommended way to host them.

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: MLflow provides research-validated built-in judges for common evaluation criteria like correctness, relevance, safety, and retrieval quality. This lecture introduces the spectrum of available judge types and takes a deep dive into built-in judges: the fastest way to start evaluating your agents.

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Describe the spectrum of evaluation judge types available in MLflow
- Identify appropriate built-in judges for common evaluation criteria
- Understand which judges require ground truth and which do not
- Apply built-in judges using `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: A1. Evaluation Judge Spectrum
chunks.text:
LLM JUDGES 
 
 
 
 OUT OF THE BOX 
 Built-in judges 
 Research-validated judges such as Correctness and Safety for common criteria. Use them for a quick quality baseline. 
 
 
 
 NATURAL LANGUAGE 
 Guideline judges 
 Pass/fail rules you write in plain language with Guidelines . Use them for tone, policy, and style requirements. 
 
 
 
 FULLY CUSTOM 
 Custom LLM judges 
 Your own instructions and output type (scores, categories, or booleans) with make_judge() . Use them for domain-specific quality. 
 
 
 OTHER SCORERS 
 
 
 
 DETERMINISTIC 
 Code-based scorers 
 Python checks decorated with @scorer , with no LLM call. Use them for exact match, format validation, and latency. 
 
 
 
 EXTERNAL 
 Third-party scorers 
 Metrics from open-source evaluation frameworks. Use them to reuse metrics your team already trusts.

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B1. Research-Validated Judges
chunks.text: MLflow provides research-validated judges for common evaluation tasks. These judges have been developed through extensive research, validated against human expert judgment, and optimized for specific evaluation criteria.

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B2. Common Built-in Judges
chunks.text:
| Judge | What it checks | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| `Correctness` | The response is factually correct against the ground truth | `expectations` |
| `Safety` | The response is free of harmful, offensive, or unsafe content | Nothing extra |
| `RelevanceToQuery` | The response directly addresses the user's query | Nothing extra |
| `RetrievalGroundedness` | The response is grounded in the retrieved context, not hallucinated | Traces with `RETRIEVER` spans |
| `RetrievalSufficiency` | The retrieved context has enough information for the ground-truth answer | `expectations` and `RETRIEVER` spans |
| `RetrievalRelevance` | The retrieved documents are relevant to the query | Traces with `RETRIEVER` spans |

 
 Full list of built-in judges 
 MLflow provides additional built-in judges including Guidelines , ExpectationsGuidelines , and multi-turn scorers ( ConversationCompleteness , UserFrustration , etc.). See the complete reference: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 2.1 Lecture - Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B3. Example Usage Pattern

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: In this demo, we'll use MLflow's built-in `Correctness` and `Safety` judges to evaluate the Airbnb agent. You'll create judge instances, load evaluation datasets, run `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`, and inspect the results.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this demo, you will be able to:
1. Configure built-in judges for correctness and safety assessment
2. Execute evaluations using `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` with multiple scorers
3. Interpret evaluation results using MLflow's UI and result dataframes

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: REQUIRED - SELECT A COMPUTE ENVIRONMENT
chunks.text:
Select Compute 
 Before starting this notebook, select the required compute environment listed below. 
 
 Serverless Compute, Version 6 : How to select an environment version ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) 
 
 NOTE: This notebook was developed and tested using Serverless V6 . Other compute options may work but are not guaranteed to behave the same or support all features demonstrated.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B. Correctness Evaluation
chunks.text:
The `Correctness` judge assesses whether the agent's response is factually correct by comparing it against ground truth defined as `expected_facts` or `expected_response`.

We'll specify the judge's model using the `model` parameter with the format `databricks:/ . . `. The judges in this course use **Unity Gateway model services** that workspace setup created as a shared resource: `correctness_eval_endpoint` points to `dbacademy.agent_eval.judge-model`, so every judge call goes through Unity Gateway, where permissions, rate limits, and usage tracking apply.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B1. Load Evaluation Dataset
chunks.text: The correctness evaluation dataset is stored in the UC volume. Each entry contains `inputs` (the query) and `expectations` with `expected_facts` that the response should contain.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B2. Run Correctness Evaluation
chunks.text:
`mlflow.genai.evaluate()` takes three key parameters:
- **data**: The evaluation dataset
- **predict_fn**: A function that calls the agent for each input
- **scorers**: The list of judges to apply

After running the cell, click **View evaluation results in MLflow** to inspect the traces and feedback.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: B3. Inspect Results
chunks.text: The `EvaluationResult` object contains `metrics` (aggregated scores) and `result_df` (per-row details with values and rationales). Click on any row to view the full MLflow trace.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: C. Safety Evaluation
chunks.text: The `Safety` judge checks whether content is free from harmful, offensive, or toxic material. Unlike Correctness, it does not require ground truth: it evaluates the agent's response directly.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: C1. Load Safety Evaluation Dataset
chunks.text: Unlike the correctness dataset, the safety dataset does not require `expected_facts` or ground truth. The judge evaluates the response in isolation, checking for harmful, offensive, or toxic content regardless of factual accuracy.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: C2. Run Safety Evaluation
chunks.text: The same `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` pattern applies here. Since `Safety` doesn't need ground truth, the dataset only needs `inputs`: making it easy to generate adversarial test cases that probe the agent's guardrails.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: C3. Inspect Results
chunks.text: Safety scores are binary: `yes` (safe) or `no` (unsafe). The rationale explains which safety category was flagged (if any). Look for cases where the agent might have been tricked into producing harmful content despite its system prompt.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: D. Evaluating Multiple Scorers at Once
chunks.text:
You can pass multiple scorers in a single `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` call. All metrics are logged to the same evaluation run, which means:
- A single set of traces is generated (reducing LLM calls to the agent)
- All judge scores appear side-by-side in the results dataframe
- The MLflow UI displays a unified view for comparing across dimensions

This is the recommended pattern for production evaluation pipelines where you want to assess multiple quality dimensions simultaneously.

chunks.lecture: 2.2 Demo - Using MLflow Built-In Judges
chunks.heading: E. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. Configured built-in `Correctness` and `Safety` judges with a Unity Gateway model service as the judge model
2. Loaded evaluation datasets from a UC volume and ran evaluations with `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`
3. Inspected per-row results including scores, rationales, and traces
4. Combined multiple scorers in a single evaluation run

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: While built-in judges cover common criteria, many evaluation needs are specific to your business: tone, compliance, formatting, or domain-specific rules. Guideline judges let you express these requirements in natural language, making evaluation accessible to domain experts without code changes.

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Distinguish between global and per-row guideline judges
- Implement the `Guidelines` class for uniform evaluation criteria
- Apply the `ExpectationsGuidelines` class for scenario-specific evaluations
- Write effective natural language guidelines

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: A1. Global vs. Per-Row Guidelines
chunks.text:
| | Global guidelines | Per-row guidelines |
|---|---|---|
| **Scorer** | `Guidelines()` | `ExpectationsGuidelines()` |
| **Rules** | The same rules for every row | Different rules for each example |
| **Use for** | Tone, style, formatting, and compliance | Scenario-specific criteria |

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: A2. Implementation Patterns

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: B1. Why Guideline Judges
chunks.text:
- **Accessible to experts**: domain experts can write rules without coding.
- **Fast to iterate**: change a rule without changing code.
- **Interpretable**: the rules document what you expect.
- **Flexible**: rules can capture complex, context-dependent requirements.

chunks.lecture: 2.3 Lecture - Guideline Judges
chunks.heading: B2. Writing Effective Guidelines
chunks.text:
Key rule: Refer to inputs as "the request" and outputs as "the response" 
 The LLM judge automatically extracts request/response data from your trace. When writing guidelines, always frame them in terms of "the request" (inputs) and "the response" (outputs). 
 

**Recommended phrasing patterns:**
- "The response must …" (required behavior)
- "The response must not …" (prohibited behavior)
- "The response may optionally …" (suggested but not required)

**Additional tips:**
- Be specific and concrete ("The response must cite the source document" vs. "The response should be credible")
- Write guidelines that can be objectively verified
- Focus on observable attributes in the response
- Leave as little ambiguity as possible
- Test guidelines on multiple examples to ensure they work as intended

Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.heading: D. Per-Row Guidelines with ExpectationsGuidelines
chunks.text:
`ExpectationsGuidelines` applies different guidelines to each row using the `expectations` field in the dataset. This is useful when different interactions require different evaluation criteria.

 
 
 
 ExpectationsGuidelines requires an outputs field. 
 They can be passed directly in the dataset or as a trace containing them. We will pass them directly.

chunks.text: Unlike global `Guidelines`, `ExpectationsGuidelines` reads the `expectations` field from each row in the dataset. Each row can specify its own list of guidelines, enabling scenario-specific evaluation without separate evaluation runs.

chunks.lecture: 2.4 Demo - Guideline Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D2. Inspect Per-Row Results
chunks.text: Each row is scored against its own `expectations` guidelines. Rows meeting their specific criteria pass; those that don't will show which guideline was violated.

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: When built-in and guideline judges don't cover your specific evaluation needs, MLflow supports fully custom evaluation logic: both code-based scorers for deterministic checks and custom LLM judges for sophisticated assessments. This lecture also covers `Feedback` objects, which provide the structured rationales that make evaluation results interpretable and actionable.

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Create code-based scorers using the `@scorer` decorator
- Understand when and how to implement custom LLM judges with `make_judge()`
- Work with `Feedback` objects and understand the role of rationales
- Choose the right judge type for your evaluation requirements

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: A1. Deterministic Evaluation with `@scorer`

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: B1. When to Use Custom LLM Judges
chunks.text:
Custom LLM judges are for evaluation criteria not covered by built-in or guideline judges:

- **Domain-specific criteria** unique to your application
- **Nuanced assessments** beyond what built-in judges capture
- **Proprietary standards**, such as regulations and compliance rules
- **Multi-signal logic** that combines several data sources

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: B2. Building Custom LLM Judges with `make_judge()`

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: C1. Structured Feedback
chunks.text:
All MLflow judges return structured `Feedback` objects: not just scalar scores. This makes evaluation results interpretable and actionable.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 1 · WHAT THE JUDGE READS 
 
 
 
 inputs 
 "Count the number of Private room 
 listings in Nob Hill." 
 
 
 
 outputs 
 "There are no Private room listings in 
 Nob Hill." 
 
 
 
 expectations 
 "expected_facts": [..., "Count is 0"] 
 
 
 
 trace 
 every span, when the judge needs it 
 2 · THE JUDGE 
 3 · THE FEEDBACK IT RETURNS 
 
 
 MAKE_JUDGE 
 response_completeness 
 instructions 
 
 Evaluate if the response is coherent... 
 Question: {{inputs}} 
 Response: {{outputs}} 
 feedback_value_type 
 Literal["complete", "partial", 
 "incomplete"] 
 model 
 databricks:/dbacademy.agent_eval. 
 custom-judge-model 
 UNITY GATEWAY MODEL SERVICE 
 
 
 FEEDBACK 
 name 
 response_completeness 
 value 
 complete 
 rationale 
 The response answers the question 
 in one clear, consistent 
 statement. 
 source 
 LLM_JUDGE 
 custom-judge-model 
 
 Attached to the trace as an assessment. Read it 
 in the MLflow UI or with search_traces(). 
 
 
 
 

 For @scorer , source is auto-populated as CODE . For make_judge() , auto-populated as LLM_JUDGE . Set manually only when calling your own LLM inside a @scorer .

chunks.lecture: 2.5 Lecture - Custom Judges and Feedback
chunks.heading: C2. Why Rationales Matter
chunks.text:
Rationales explain *why* a judge reached its decision. Use them for:

- **Debugging**: see why a response failed, not just that it failed.
- **Judge validation**: check that the judge's reasoning is sound.
- **Pattern finding**: themes that repeat across rationales point to systematic issues.
- **Communication**: explain results to stakeholders.

 
 Using rationales effectively 
 
 
 Read rationales for all failures to identify patterns 
 Spot-check rationales for passes to ensure judge is reasoning correctly 
 Extract common rationale phrases to categorize failure types 
 Share representative rationales when discussing evaluation with teams

chunks.heading: B. Load Evaluation Dataset
chunks.text: The `custom_eval.json` dataset contains queries without expectations. We'll use it to evaluate the agent's response completeness.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: C. Standard Custom Judge - Response Completeness
chunks.text:
We'll use `make_judge()` to create a judge that evaluates whether responses are complete. The `instructions` parameter uses the `coherent_instructions` loaded from the agent eval config, which references `{{inputs}}` and `{{outputs}}` template variables.

The `feedback_value_type` is set to a `Literal` type so the judge returns one of `"complete"`, `"partial"`, or `"incomplete"`.

 
 Why metrics will be empty 
 Because the feedback type is a Literal (categorical), MLflow cannot compute a numeric mean — so metrics will be {} . Boolean feedback types (like in section D) do produce a mean metric.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D. Trace-Based Custom Judge - Tool Usage
chunks.text:
Trace-based judges analyze the full execution trace using `{{trace}}` in the instructions. This judge validates whether the agent used tools correctly.

 
 How trace-based judges work 
 When instructions contain {{trace}} , the judge receives the full trace object and uses tool calling to inspect span data (inputs, outputs, tool calls, timing). The model parameter is optional.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D1. Generate Traces
chunks.text: To evaluate tool usage, we first need traces. The helper function below queries the agent and wraps each call in an MLflow span with session metadata, then we search for those traces.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D2. Evaluate a Single Trace
chunks.text:
Search for the traces we just generated using the session ID, then evaluate the first one individually.

The judge returns a `Feedback` object with a boolean `value` (pass/fail) and a `rationale` explaining its reasoning.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D3. Batch Trace Evaluation
chunks.text: Evaluate all session traces at once using `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: D4. Inspect Batch Results
chunks.text: Review the aggregated metrics and per-trace results from the batch evaluation. Because `feedback_value_type=bool`, MLflow can compute a mean — `1.0` means all traces passed.

chunks.lecture: 2.6 Demo - Custom Judges with MLflow
chunks.heading: E. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. Created a standard custom judge with `make_judge()` using `Literal` feedback types
2. Built a trace-based judge that analyzes agent tool usage via `{{trace}}`
3. Generated traces with session metadata and evaluated them individually and in batch

Did your agent pass your expectations? If not, try updating the system prompt in `Includes/artifacts/configs/nyc_taxi_agent_config.yaml` so that the agent aligns with your evaluation expectations. Iterate until all evaluations **Pass**.

For example, the default system prompt is

```

```

Which isn't very descriptive if, for example, we pass the question _What is the average fare for trips from zip code 10001 to 10002?_ and expect the following in our output
- Pickup zip code is 10001,
- Dropoff zip code is 10002,
- Response includes average fare information,
- Response includes 'Are there any additional questions I can help with?'

then we might update our system prompt with _You are an expert in answering questions regarding NYC Taxi data. You will always respond with "Are there any additional questions I can help with?"_ (see screenshot below).

chunks.text:
In this lab, you have successfully implemented a comprehensive evaluation framework for AI agents using MLflow's built-in and guideline judges. You learned how to:

- Configure and execute multiple types of judges for different evaluation needs
- Create properly structured evaluation datasets for various judge types
- Analyze evaluation results using MLflow's tracing and result analysis capabilities
- Apply best practices for evaluation configuration and model management

These evaluation techniques provide the foundation for ensuring your AI agents meet quality standards and perform reliably in production environments. The combination of objective built-in judges and flexible guideline judges enables comprehensive quality assessment that can adapt to your specific business requirements.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Traditional software testing approaches are fundamentally insufficient for AI agents due to their non-deterministic nature, emergent behaviors, and context-dependent responses. This lecture explores why conventional testing fails with AI agents and introduces the unique challenges that require specialized evaluation frameworks.

We'll examine how AI agents break traditional testing paradigms, understand the complexity of multi-step reasoning evaluation, and learn why evaluation must be treated as a continuous process rather than a one-time validation step.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Explain why traditional software testing approaches are insufficient for AI agents
- Identify the key challenges unique to evaluating AI agents (non-determinism, emergent behavior, context dependency)
- Understand why evaluation must be treated as a continuous process
- Recognize the importance of proper evaluation dataset design
- Describe the operational setup requirements for systematic agent evaluation

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: A1. The Deterministic Testing Paradigm
chunks.text: Traditional software testing relies on deterministic inputs and expected outputs. You write unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests that verify your code produces the exact same result every time given the same input.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: A2. How AI Agents Break the Paradigm
chunks.text:
AI agents fundamentally break the deterministic testing paradigm:

| | Traditional software | AI agents |
|---|---|---|
| **Output** | The same input gives the same output | The same input can give different outputs because of temperature and sampling |
| **Behavior** | Every decision path is programmed | The agent makes tool and reasoning decisions no one wrote |
| **Context** | Fixed inputs | Responses depend on retrieval, conversation history, and external data |
| **Verification** | Assert an exact string or number | Judge whether the response is good |
| **Edge cases** | Enumerated and tested up front | Open-ended and hard to anticipate |

 
 Example: Why exact matching fails 
 
An agent answering "What's the weather in San Francisco?" might respond:
 
 "It's currently 65°F and sunny in San Francisco." 
 "San Francisco weather: 65 degrees, clear skies." 
 "The temperature in SF is 65°F with no clouds." 
 
All three are correct, helpful, and appropriate. Yet none match exactly. Traditional assert output == "expected_response" would fail on all three.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: B1. Multi-Dimensional Complexity
chunks.text:
Evaluating AI agents introduces unique complexities beyond traditional software: 
 Multi-step reasoning : Agents may invoke multiple tools, retrieve various documents, and build complex reasoning chains. Evaluation must assess not just the final answer but the quality of intermediate steps. 
 Tool calling accuracy : Did the agent select the right tools? Did it pass appropriate parameters? Did it correctly interpret tool results? 
 Retrieval quality : For RAG-based agents, evaluation must verify that retrieved documents contain relevant information and that the agent correctly synthesizes information from multiple sources.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: B2. Safety and Real-World Variability
chunks.text:
Safety and alignment : Agents must avoid harmful outputs, respect user boundaries, and decline inappropriate requests. These qualities require sophisticated evaluation beyond simple pass/fail tests. 
 Real-world variability : Production agents encounter diverse user queries, unexpected phrasings, and edge cases that are difficult to anticipate during development. 
 These challenges demand a more sophisticated evaluation framework specifically designed for the probabilistic, contextual nature of AI agents.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: C1. The Continuous Evaluation Cycle
chunks.text:
STAGE 01 
 Development 
 Rapid iteration with frequent 
 evaluation 
 
 
 STAGE 02 
 Pre-deployment 
 Comprehensive validation 
 against a quality bar 
 
 
 
 STAGE 03 
 Production 
 Continuous monitoring of live 
 interactions 
 
 
 
 STAGE 04 
 Dataset evolution 
 New failure cases join the 
 evaluation dataset 
 
 
 
 Feedback drives the next iteration 
 
 

Unlike traditional software where comprehensive test suites provide stable quality signals, AI agent evaluation is an ongoing process:

**Development phase**: Rapid iteration requires frequent evaluation to validate that changes improve quality without introducing regressions.

**Pre-deployment validation**: Comprehensive evaluation across diverse test cases ensures agents meet quality bars before production release.

**Production monitoring**: Continuous evaluation of live interactions identifies quality degradation, emerging failure patterns, and opportunities for improvement.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: C2. Why Continuous Evaluation Matters
chunks.text:
This continuous evaluation cycle means your evaluation infrastructure must be scalable, automated, and integrated into your development workflow. The evaluation framework must support:

- **Rapid feedback loops** during development
- **Comprehensive validation** before deployment
- **Ongoing monitoring** in production
- **Dataset evolution** as usage patterns change

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: D1. Why Preparation Matters
chunks.text:
Before using any evaluation framework, it's important to make evaluation both purposeful and reproducible. AI agents are non-deterministic and context-dependent, so traditional assertion-style tests fall short. Instead, effective evaluation requires defining quality dimensions, assembling representative datasets, and enabling tracing so judges can assess not just answers, but how those answers were produced.

By clarifying goals, curating datasets, and selecting appropriate judges up front, you create a feedback loop where metrics reflect real user needs and failures are diagnosable through traces and rationales: not just pass/fail scores.

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: D2. Designing Your Evaluation Dataset
chunks.text:
1 · INPUTS 
 Required 
 What the agent receives. predict_fn passes these keys to 
 the agent as keyword arguments. 
 
 
 2 · EXPECTATIONS 
 Optional 
 Ground truth for judges such as Correctness: expected 
 facts, an expected response, or per-row guidelines. 
 
 
 OUTPUTS 
 Optional, not in this record 
 A pre-generated response. Include it to score answers 
 without calling the agent again. 
 ONE RECORD FROM correctness_eval.json 
 { 
 "inputs" : { 
 1 
 "input": [{"role": "user", 
 "content": "Count the number of Private 
 room listings in Nob Hill."}] 
 }, 
 "expectations" : { 
 2 
 "expected_facts": [ 
 "Neighborhood is Nob Hill", 
 "Room type is Private room", 
 "Count is 0"] 
 } 
 } 
 
 

Your evaluation dataset defines what you test and how trustworthy your signals will be. At minimum, it should include inputs (queries) and, where appropriate, expected answers, per-row guidelines, and metadata that reflects retrieval and tool usage.

**Key principles:**

- **Representativeness:** Include common, high-impact user queries so offline results generalize to production
- **Edge cases:** Add ambiguous, out-of-scope, and adversarial prompts to surface failure modes early
- **Diversity:** Vary length, complexity, domain, and user expertise to expose blind spots in reasoning and retrieval
- **Ground truth and/or guidelines:** Use expected answers or fact sets for objective questions; use natural-language guidelines where style, policy, or completeness matter
- **Storage and versioning:** MLflow evaluation datasets are stored in Unity Catalog, which provides built-in versioning, lineage, sharing, and governance

chunks.lecture: 1.1 Lecture - The Challenge of Evaluating AI Agents
chunks.heading: D3. Operational Setup Requirements
chunks.text:
Establish consistent scaffolding so results are comparable and auditable:

- **Track** with MLflow experiments and runs: use stable experiment names, tag runs with the agent and dataset versions, and compare metrics in the UI.
- **Govern** with Unity Catalog: control access to datasets and traces, version them, follow their lineage, and register agents for end-to-end traceability.
- **Learn** from production: log traces from the deployed agent to an MLflow experiment and collect user feedback to mine new evaluation examples.

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: In this demo, we'll load the course's tool-calling agent, which is registered to Unity Catalog, and verify it works by generating MLflow traces. This agent will be used throughout the remaining demos and labs for evaluation exercises. The same registered agent is also deployed as a **Databricks App**, which you'll use in the **Developer and SME Feedback with MLflow** lab.

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this demo, you will be able to:
1. Load a Unity Catalog-registered agent by name and alias
2. Generate traces by interacting with the agent
3. Locate the registered agent in Unity Catalog and its traces in your MLflow experiment

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: REQUIRED - SELECT A COMPUTE ENVIRONMENT
chunks.text:
Select Compute 
 Before starting this notebook, select the required compute environment listed below. 
 
 Serverless Compute, Version 6 : How to select an environment version ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) 
 
 NOTE: This notebook was developed and tested using Serverless V6 . Other compute options may work but are not guaranteed to behave the same or support all features demonstrated.

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: B. Load the Agent
chunks.text:
Workspace setup registered a tool-calling agent to Unity Catalog as `dbacademy.agent_eval.airbnb`. It's a shared model: every learner loads the same version. We'll load it using `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()` with the model's UC path and `@champion` alias.

 
 
 
 About This Agent 
 This is a simple tool-calling agent backed by SQL UDFs registered to Unity Catalog. It calls its model through a Unity Gateway model service ( dbacademy.agent_eval.agent-model ) and runs its tools through the Databricks managed MCP server. The agent itself is not the focus - it exists so we can practice evaluation techniques.

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: C. Query the Agent and Inspect Traces
chunks.text:
Let's send some questions to the agent using its `predict()` method. Each call automatically generates an **MLflow trace**: a structured record of the agent's full execution flow, including:

- **Spans** for each step (LLM call, tool invocation, retrieval)
- **Input/output payloads** at every span
- **Latency** for each operation

Traces are the foundation for evaluation. They let us verify *what* the agent did, not just what it returned.

The helper below formats our question into the **ChatCompletionRequest** schema the agent expects: a list of message objects with `role` and `content` fields, matching the OpenAI-compatible message format used by MLflow's pyfunc serving interface.

This first question is a **metadata query**: the agent can answer it directly from its system prompt without invoking any tools. Notice that the resulting trace will show only an LLM span with no tool-call spans.

The next question will trigger both `avg_neigh_price` and `cnt_by_room_type` tool calls. Inspect the trace output to see the tool invocations.

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: D. View the Agent and Its Traces
chunks.text:
Navigate to **Catalog Explorer**, open the **dbacademy** catalog and the **agent_eval** schema, and find the registered model **airbnb** with the alias **@champion**. Workspace setup registers a new version each time it runs, and the **@champion** alias always points to the version that the demos and the app use.

Your traces are in your own MLflow experiment. Navigate to **Experiments**, open **airbnb_experiment**, and click **Traces** to see the two requests we just sent.

**What to look for:**
- **Span hierarchy** - expand a trace to see nested spans (LLM → tool calls → tool responses)
- **Inputs & outputs** - click any span to inspect the exact payload sent and received
- **Latency breakdown** - identify which step (LLM reasoning vs. tool execution) took the most time
- **Contrast the two traces** - the first has no tool spans; the second shows two parallel tool invocations

chunks.lecture: 1.2 Demo - Agent Setup
chunks.heading: E. Conclusion
chunks.text:
In this demo, you:

1. Loaded a Unity Catalog-registered agent using `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model()`
2. Queried the agent and observed MLflow traces capturing tool calls
3. Located the registered agent in Unity Catalog and its traces in your MLflow experiment

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
MLflow provides a comprehensive evaluation framework specifically designed for generative AI applications, offering automated judges, tracing capabilities, and systematic assessment tools. This lecture explores MLflow's architecture, core components, and how they work together to enable rigorous agent evaluation.

We'll examine the three fundamental components of MLflow evaluation, understand the `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` function, and explore how tracing provides the foundation for sophisticated evaluation capabilities.

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Describe MLflow's evaluation framework architecture and key components
- Understand the role of evaluation datasets, scorers, and predict functions
- Explain how the `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` function orchestrates evaluation
- Understand the role of tracing in agent evaluation and debugging
- Recognize how production monitoring and Unity Gateway extend evaluation to a deployed agent

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: A1. MLflow for Agent Evaluation
chunks.text:
During development, an **evaluation harness** helps you quickly execute your application for every record in your evaluation set and then run each output through your LLM judges and metric computations. In this module, we focus on the evaluation-specific capabilities that are purpose-built for assessing AI agents using Databricks AI Agent Evaluation.

The five MLflow capabilities you will use most for agent evaluation are **tracing**, **scorers and judges**, **`mlflow.genai.evaluate()`**, **evaluation experiments** for comparing runs, and **production monitoring**.

 
 OpenTelemetry Compatible 
 MLflow traces are fully compatible with OpenTelemetry specs, enabling export to external observability platforms (Datadog, Grafana, Splunk, etc.) via MLflow-only, OTel-only, or dual export modes. 
 Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: B1. Three Fundamental Components
chunks.text:
MLflow's evaluation architecture centers on three components that flow into `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`:

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 EVALUATION DATASET 
 What to test 
 inputs, expectations, outputs 
 
 
 SCORERS 
 How to grade 
 built-in, guideline, custom, code 
 
 
 PREDICT FUNCTION 
 How to call the agent 
 optional for pre-generated outputs 
 
 
 ORCHESTRATES 
 mlflow.genai.evaluate() 
 Calls the agent for each row, traces every 
 call, runs each scorer, and logs the run 
 to MLflow. 
 
 
 RETURNS 
 EvaluationResult 
 A run_id and aggregated metrics such as 
 correctness/mean. Per-row assessments 
 live on each row's trace. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Evaluation Dataset 
 
Your evaluation dataset defines what you're testing. Each record in an evaluation dataset represents a single test case with the following structure:
 
 inputs (required): The test input data that will be passed to your model or application 
 outputs (optional): The actual outputs generated by your model, typically used for post-hoc evaluation 
 expectations (optional): The expected outputs or quality criteria that define correct behavior (e.g., expected facts, expected responses, or per-row guidelines) 
 source (optional): Provenance information about how this record was created 
 tags (optional): Metadata specific to this individual record for organization and filtering 
 
Datasets are typically stored as JSON files or Pandas DataFrames for easy manipulation and versioning.
 
 

 
 Scorers (Judges) 
 
Scorers evaluate your agent's outputs against defined criteria. Choose the right type depending on how much customization and control you need:
 
 Built-in judges - Research-validated LLM-based assessments for common quality dimensions (Correctness, Safety, RelevanceToQuery, RetrievalGroundedness, etc.). This category also includes Guidelines and ExpectationsGuidelines judges that check whether responses pass or fail custom natural-language rules. 
 Custom LLM judges - Fully customized LLM judges with detailed evaluation criteria and feedback optimization. Capable of returning numerical scores, categories, or boolean values. 
 Code-based scorers - Programmatic and deterministic scorers for exact matching, format validation, and performance metrics. 
 Third-party scorers - Specialized metrics from open-source evaluation frameworks. 
 
Start with built-in judges for quick evaluation. As your needs evolve, build custom LLM judges for domain-specific criteria and create custom code-based scorers for determinis

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: C1. Central Orchestration Point
chunks.text:
The `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` function provides an **evaluation harness**: a structured way to feed in test data, run your app, and automatically score the results.

 
 How it works 
 
Instead of manually running your app and checking outputs one by one, MLflow Evaluation connects offline testing with production monitoring: the same evaluation logic you use in development can also run in production.

 
import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.scorers import Correctness

results = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
 data=eval_dataset, # EvaluationDataset, DataFrame, list[dict], etc.
 scorers=[Correctness()], # Built-in and/or custom scorers
 predict_fn=my_app, # Optional: direct evaluation

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: C2. Key Parameters
chunks.text:
mlflow.genai.evaluate() 
 results = mlflow.genai. evaluate ( 
 data=eval_dataset, 
 predict_fn= lambda input: agent.predict({ "input" : input}), 
 scorers=[ 
 Correctness(model= "databricks:/dbacademy.agent_eval.judge-model" ), 
 Safety(model= "databricks:/dbacademy.agent_eval.judge-model" ), 
 completeness_judge, # make_judge(...) 
 ], 
 ) 
 
 results.run_id, results.metrics 
 
 
 DATA 
 What to test 
 Rows of inputs, plus optional 
 outputs and expectations: a list 
 of dicts, a DataFrame, or an 
 evaluation dataset in Unity 
 Catalog. 
 
 
 PREDICT_FN 
 How to call the agent 
 Called once per row with the 
 row's inputs. Leave it out to 
 score outputs that are already in 
 the data. 
 
 
 SCORERS 
 How to grade 
 Built-in, guideline, custom, and 
 code scorers. Each judge's model 
 is a Unity Gateway model service. 
 
 
 RESULTS 
 What you get back 
 An EvaluationResult with a run_id 
 and aggregated metrics. Per-row 
 assessments live on each row's 
 trace. 
 
 

 
 predict_fn requirements 
 When provided, predict_fn must accept keys from the inputs dictionary as keyword arguments, return a JSON-serializable dictionary, be instrumented with MLflow Tracing, and emit exactly one trace per call. 
 

Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: C3. Evaluation Workflow
chunks.text:
When you call `mlflow.genai.evaluate()`, it runs these steps:

1. **Load the data** and validate its structure.
2. **Generate outputs** by calling `predict_fn` for each row. This step is skipped when the data already has outputs.
3. **Create traces**: each call is traced automatically.
4. **Run the scorers** on every row.
5. **Aggregate and log** the metrics and results to MLflow.

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: C4. Return Value and Results Access
chunks.text:
EVALUATION RUN 
 airbnb_experiment 
 run_id 3f9c2e… 
 
 
 correctness/mean 
 0.80 
 
 
 safety/mean 
 1.00 
 
 
 tone/mean 
 0.60 
 results.metrics 
 
 INPUT 
 CORRECTNESS 
 SAFETY 
 TONE 
 How many Entire home/apt listings are in the Mission? 
 YES 
 YES 
 YES 
 
 Count the number of Private room listings in Nob Hill. 
 YES 
 YES 
 NO 
 
 
 What is the average listing price in Haight Ashbury? 
 NO 
 YES 
 YES 
 
 What's the average price in Middle Earth? 
 YES 
 YES 
 YES 
 
 How many Shared room listings are in Middle Earth? 
 YES 
 YES 
 NO 
 
 
 
 
 CORRECTNESS RATIONALE 
 Average price in Haight Ashbury 
 The response gives an average of 92.40, but 
 the expected facts say the average price is 
 87.71. 
 
 PER-ROW RESULTS LIVE ON THE TRACES 
 traces = mlflow.search_traces(run_id=results.run_id, return_type= "list" ) 
 
 

The function returns an `EvaluationResult` object with `run_id`, `metrics` (aggregated dictionary), `artifacts`, and `tables` (per-example DataFrames). Per-example traces and feedback are accessed separately.

 
 Evaluation run structure 
 
Each evaluation run contains:
 
 Traces - One trace for each input in your evaluation dataset 
 Feedback - Quality assessments from scorers attached to each trace 
 Metrics - Aggregate statistics (average score, pass rate, etc.) 
 Metadata - Information about the evaluation configuration 
 
The EvaluationResult object provides run_id and metrics (aggregated dictionary).
 
 

 
 Accessing per-example results 
 
In MLflow 3, per-example results are accessed via traces:
 
eval_traces = mlflow.search_traces(run_id=results.run_id, return_type="list")

for trace in eval_traces:
 assessments = trace.info.assessments
 for assessment in assessments:
 print(f"Scorer: {assessment.name}, Value: {assessment.value}")
 
Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: D1. Comprehensive Observability
chunks.text:
MLflow Tracing provides comprehensive observability into agent execution, capturing every step of your agent's reasoning process. Tracing is enabled when using `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` with properly instrumented predict functions.

Each trace records the model calls (prompts, responses, and parameters), tool invocations (inputs and return values), retrieval operations (documents and metadata), the duration of every operation, and the parent-child hierarchy that ties them together.

Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: D2. Span Types in Traces
chunks.text:
MLflow organizes traces into spans with specific types. Here is one trace from a tool-calling agent like the course's Airbnb agent, with the tool span selected:

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 EXAMPLE TRACE · TOOL-CALLING AGENT 
 What is the average listing price in Haight Ashbury? 
 SPAN 
 TYPE 
 TIMELINE 
 
 0 s 
 
 1 s 
 
 2 s 
 
 3 s 
 airbnb_assistant 
 AGENT 
 
 3.20 s 
 
 predict_stream 
 AGENT 
 
 3.12 s 
 
 chat.completions 
 CHAT_MODEL 
 
 1.30 s 
 
 
 avg_neigh_price 
 TOOL 
 
 0.46 s 
 
 chat.completions 
 CHAT_MODEL 
 
 1.18 s 
 Spans nest like a call tree. Select one to see its inputs, outputs, and timing. 
 
 
 SELECTED SPAN 
 avg_neigh_price 
 TOOL 
 INPUTS 
 
 {"neighborhood_name": "Haight Ashbury" } 
 OUTPUTS 
 
 87.71 -- average listing price 
 ATTRIBUTES

 0.46 s 
 status 
 OK 
 via 
 managed MCP server 
 
 Judges read these spans to grade tool choice, 
 not just the final answer. 
 
 

The span types you will see most often in agent evaluation:

| Span type | What it records |
|---|---|
| `AGENT` | The agent's own reasoning and orchestration steps |
| `CHAT_MODEL` | Requests to a chat model and its responses |
| `TOOL` | Tool and function calls, with their inputs and results |
| `RETRIEVER` | Fetches from AI Search or another retriever |
| `CHAIN` | A sequence of operations run in order |

 
 Full list of span types 
 MLflow supports additional span types including LLM , EMBEDDING , GUARDRAIL , PARSER , RERANKER , EVALUATOR , MEMORY , TASK , WORKFLOW , and UNKNOWN . See the complete reference: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: D3. Why Tracing Matters for Evaluation
chunks.text:
Certain evaluation judges, like `RetrievalSufficiency`, require traces to function. They analyze what was retrieved (not just the final response) to assess whether the retrieval system provided adequate information. Without traces, these sophisticated evaluations would be impossible.

Tracing also enables debugging by allowing you to inspect exactly what happened during a failed evaluation, identifying whether issues stem from retrieval quality, tool selection, or LLM reasoning.

Docs: ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 1.3 Lecture - MLflow's Evaluation Framework
chunks.heading: E. Production Monitoring and Unity Gateway
chunks.text:
Evaluation doesn't stop at deployment. The same MLflow pieces you use offline also cover a deployed agent:

- **Traces from production**: the deployed agent logs a trace for every request to an MLflow experiment. In this course, the Airbnb assistant app on Databricks Apps logs to its own experiment, and the feedback users give in the app is saved on those traces.
- **Production monitoring**: register the same scorers you use offline so they run automatically on a sample of production traces, with `.register()` and `.start()`.
- **Unity Gateway**: every model call from the agent and from the judges goes through a Unity Gateway model service, so permissions, rate limits, and usage tracking apply to both.

Failures and edge cases you find in production become new rows in your evaluation dataset. The **Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies** lecture walks through that loop.

Production Monitoring ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

 

 

 

 

 
 Want to learn more about MLflow's evaluation capabilities? Ask Genie Code. Click on the genie icon and begin querying. For example, click the Copy button below and paste into Genie Code .

chunks.lecture: 3.1 Lecture - Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Effective agent evaluation requires both offline validation using curated datasets and online monitoring of production performance. This lecture explores the complementary roles of offline and online evaluation, their respective strengths and limitations, and how to create feedback loops between them.

We'll examine when to use each approach, understand their implementation patterns, and learn how to build evaluation systems that evolve with real-world usage while maintaining rigorous quality standards.

chunks.lecture: 3.1 Lecture - Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:
- Identify when to use offline versus online evaluation strategies
- Understand the strengths and limitations of each approach
- Describe how offline and online evaluation complement each other
- Explain how to create feedback loops between production and evaluation
- Recognize best practices for comprehensive evaluation strategies

chunks.lecture: 3.1 Lecture - Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies
chunks.heading: A1. Two Complementary Approaches
chunks.text:
OFFLINE · BEFORE DEPLOYMENT 
 Curated datasets 
 
 
 1 
 Curate a dataset of use cases and edge cases 
 
 
 2 
 Run the agent on every row 
 
 
 3 
 Score each response with judges 
 
 
 4 
 Gate the release on the results 
 Controlled and reproducible 
 
 
 ONLINE · IN PRODUCTION 
 Real user traffic 
 
 
 1 
 Trace every production request 
 
 
 2 
 Score a sample of traces automatically 
 
 
 3 
 Collect user feedback on answers 
 
 
 4 
 Monitor quality and alert on drops 
 Real-world and continuous 
 Ship the version that passed 
 
 
 Feedback loop 
 Failures become new test cases 
 
 
 

Agent evaluation requires both controlled validation and real-world monitoring. Offline and online evaluation serve different but complementary purposes in ensuring agent quality throughout the development and deployment lifecycle.

chunks.lecture: 3.1 Lecture - Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies
chunks.heading: B1. Offline Evaluation Workflow
chunks.text:
Offline evaluation tests your agent using curated datasets before deployment. Controlled, reproducible, and gated.

1. **Curate a dataset** of common use cases and edge cases.
2. **Define expectations**: optional ground truth or guidelines.
3. **Run the agent** to generate responses.
4. **Apply scorers**: run several judges over every response.
5. **Analyze and iterate**: compare results across runs.

 
 Strengths and limitations 
 
 
 
 Strengths 
 Rigorous validation before users encounter the agent A/B testing different configurations Baseline metrics for production 
 
 
 Limitations 
 May not fully represent real user behavior Static datasets become stale Cannot capture scale/diversity issues 
 
 
 
 

Evaluation Datasets ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 3.1 Lecture - Offline vs. Online Evaluation Strategies
chunks.heading: C1. Online Evaluation Workflow
chunks.text:
Online evaluation analyzes agent performance using real user interactions: capturing actual usage patterns, unexpected inputs, and diverse user populations.

1. **Deploy with tracing**, so every production request is traced. In this course, the Airbnb assistant app logs a trace for each request to its MLflow experiment.
2. **Capture traces** in an MLflow experiment.
3. **Score automatically** by registering scorers and starting them with `.register()` and `.start()`.
4. **Alert and collect feedback** to monitor quality.
5. **Augment the dataset** with production examples.

 
 Supported scorer types: 
 Built-in judges, make_judge() , Guidelines , and @scorer decorated functions all support production monitoring via .register() + .start() . Only direct Scorer subclasses and third-party scorers are excluded. 
 

 
 Production monitoring capabilities 
 
 
 Auto scoring : LLM judges run on production traces 
 Sampling : configurable sample rates

chunks.heading: E1. Governance for Evaluation
chunks.text:
Unity Catalog provides the governance layer for your evaluation workflow: traceability, access control, and lineage tracking across agents, datasets, and traces.

- **Agent registration**: dependencies, access controls, and aliases such as `@champion`
- **Dataset storage**: versioned, governed evaluation datasets

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
This lab provides hands-on experience with MLflow's human feedback capabilities, focusing on collecting and managing assessments from different reviewer personas. You'll learn to implement feedback workflows that support development iteration, domain expert evaluation, and end-user input collection. The lab covers MLflow Assessments, which allow you to attach structured feedback, scores, and ground truth to traces and spans for quality evaluation and improvement.

Human feedback is critical for improving AI applications, as it provides qualitative insights that complement automated metrics. This lab demonstrates how to systematically collect, organize, and analyze feedback from multiple stakeholder types to drive continuous improvement of your AI systems.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:
- Implement developer feedback workflows using MLflow Assessments
- Collect SME (Subject Matter Expert) feedback through the chat UI of an agent deployed as a Databricks App
- Distinguish between feedback and expectation assessment types
- Navigate MLflow's tracing interface to add and review assessments
- Review SME feedback programmatically in a Databricks Notebook

chunks.text:
The workspace setup deployed the agent you've been evaluating as a **Databricks App** named **agent-airbnb-assistant**. The app has no agent code of its own: it loads `dbacademy.agent_eval.airbnb@champion` from Unity Catalog, the same registered model you load in your notebooks. That's what makes SME feedback from the app useful: the experts review the exact agent version that you evaluate in code.

The app logs every chat as an MLflow trace in its own experiment, `/Shared/agent-eval-app`. Its chat UI asks whether each answer was correct, and saves your answer and comment on that trace as a **human feedback** assessment named `user_feedback`, with your email as its source.  Databricks recommends deploying agents as Databricks Apps . This course registers the agent in Unity Catalog, evaluates it in notebooks, and deploys the same registered model as an app. See the Appendix - Agent Deployment Patterns for the deployment options.
