chunks.heading: Traces stored in Unity Catalog can pass outputs as JSON text

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B4. Verify Sessions and Run the Job

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B5. Verify Your Scorers Are Running
chunks.text:
Confirm all five scorers were deployed correctly and are active. In production, this is the same audit step you would run to verify what is evaluating your traces and at what rates.

**TODO**: Use `list_scorers()` to enumerate all registered scorers. You should see 5 active scorers.

 
 
 ANSWER B5. Verify Scorers
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import list_scorers
 
scorers = list_scorers()
print(f"Found {len(scorers)} registered scorers:\n")
for s in scorers:
 status = "ACTIVE" if s.sample_rate > 0 else "STOPPED"
 print(f" {s.name}: rate={s.sample_rate} [{status}]")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: C. Sampling Strategy
chunks.text:
Scenario 
 Your scorers have been running and the quality signals are stabilizing. Now you need to tune the sampling rates to balance cost and coverage for production.

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: C1. Update a Sampling Rate
chunks.text:
After running the judges for a while, you notice the completeness scorer's results have stabilized: the pass rate hasn't changed in the last several evaluation cycles. Continuing to evaluate 50% of traces is wasting LLM calls. You can reduce the rate to 5% to save costs while still catching regressions. This is the typical production lifecycle: start high for fast feedback, dial back once the signal is stable.

 
 
 Return value pattern 
 .update() changes the scorer's configuration on the server but returns a new Python object reflecting the change. Always reassign: scorer = scorer.update(...) 
 
 

 
 
 ANSWER C1. Update and Verify
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import get_scorer, list_scorers, ScorerSamplingConfig

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Fetch and update
chunks.text:
original = get_scorer(name="conversation_completeness")
print(f"Original rate: {original.sample_rate}")
 
updated = original.update(
 sampling_config=ScorerSamplingConfig(sample_rate=0.05)
)
print(f"Updated rate: {updated.sample_rate}")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Full audit
chunks.text:
print("\nAll scorers:")
for s in list_scorers():
 status = "ACTIVE" if s.sample_rate > 0 else "STOPPED"
 print(f" {s.name}: rate={s.sample_rate} [{status}]")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: D. Stop and Clean Up Scorers
chunks.text: When you are done with the scorers, stop them to pause evaluation, then delete the ones you no longer need.

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: D1. Stop Deployed Scorers
chunks.text:
You have confirmed the scorers work and tuned a sampling rate. Now stop all five scorers. In production, you would stop a scorer when you want to pause evaluation temporarily without losing the scorer's registration. The background job stops running once all scorers have `sample_rate = 0`.

**TODO**: Stop all five scorers: `completeness`, `frustration`, `safety`, `length_scorer` (from B3), and the `professional` judge (use `get_scorer(name="professional")` since it was created via the UI). Note that `.stop()` returns a new Python object. Always reassign (e.g., `safety = safety.stop()`) so your local variable reflects the updated state.

 
 
 ANSWER D1. Stop Deployed Scorers
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import get_scorer

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Programmatic scorers (B1)
chunks.text:
completeness = completeness.stop()
print(f"Sample rate for completeness: {completeness.sample_rate}")
frustration = frustration.stop()
print(f"Sample rate for frustration: {frustration.sample_rate}")
safety = safety.stop()
print(f"Sample rate for safety: {safety.sample_rate}")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Custom scorer (B3)
chunks.text:
length_scorer = length_scorer.stop()
print(f"Sample rate for response_length: {length_scorer.sample_rate}")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: UI-created scorer (B2): fetch it with get_scorer, since there is no local variable
chunks.text:
professional = get_scorer(name="professional")
professional = professional.stop()
print(f"Sample rate for professional: {professional.sample_rate}")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: D2. Delete Scorers
chunks.text:
In a shared workspace, abandoned scorers continue consuming resources. The background job keeps running, making LLM calls on every evaluation cycle. Deleting scorers you no longer need is important for cost management. Unlike `.stop()` (which pauses but keeps the scorer registered), `delete_scorer()` permanently removes it. Historical assessments already written to traces are preserved.

**TODO**: List all scorers, delete each one using `delete_scorer(name=...)`, and verify the list is empty.

 
 
 ANSWER D2. Delete Scorers
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import list_scorers, delete_scorer
 
scorers = list_scorers()
print(f"Deleting {len(scorers)} scorers:\n")
 
for s in scorers:
 print(f" Deleting: {s.name}...", end=" ")
 delete_scorer(name=s.name)
 print("done")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Verify
chunks.text:
remaining = list_scorers()
print(f"\nRemaining scorers: {len(remaining)}")

chunks.lecture: 6 - Lab - Online Evaluation with Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
1. **Multi-turn judges** evaluate entire conversations using the `mlflow.trace.session` metadata to group traces into sessions
2. **Custom scorers** use the `@scorer` decorator with all imports inline and support `aggregations` for numeric metrics
3. **Sampling rates** should be tuned by scorer type: 100% for safety, 5% for expensive LLM judges once stable, 30-50% during active development
4. **Return value pattern**: `.update()` and `.stop()` change the server state but return new Python objects -- always reassign so your local variable reflects the change
5. **`list_scorers()`** lets you audit what is running and at what rates
6. **UC-backed trace monitoring** requires setting the SQL warehouse ID on the experiment **before** registering any scorers — the monitoring job reads this from the `mlflow.monitoring.sqlWarehouseId` experiment tag, not from environment variables
7. **Permissions for UC traces**: explicit `MODIFY` and `SELECT` on trace tables (`ALL_PRIVILEGES` is not sufficient), `CAN USE` on the SQL warehouse, and `CAN EDIT` on the experiment

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
This lab focuses on production monitoring, backfill, and querying traces stored in Unity Catalog.

In this lab, you manage a production travel agent. The setup script creates an MLflow experiment that stores its traces in Unity Catalog, logs multi-turn conversation traces to it, and deploys a `ConversationCompleteness` judge. Your job is to inspect the existing setup, run the monitoring job, add a new scorer via backfill, query the traces and their assessments with SQL, and clean up when done.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
1. Inspect an MLflow experiment with deployed judges and run the trace metrics computation job
2. Backfill a new scorer on historical traces using `BackfillScorerConfig`
3. Query traces and assessments stored in Unity Catalog with SQL
4. Stop and delete scorers using management APIs

 
 
 Jobs Created in This Lab 
 As you work through this lab, two types of Lakeflow jobs will be created. You can find them in Jobs & Pipelines : 
 
 [experiment_id] Trace Metrics Computation Job : created by the setup when it deploys the ConversationCompleteness judge via .start() . Runs scorers on incoming traces. 
 [experiment_id] Metric Backfill Computation Job : created when you call backfill_scorers() . Retroactively evaluates historical traces.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: REQUIRED - SELECT A COMPUTE ENVIRONMENT
chunks.text:
Select Compute 
 Before starting this notebook, select the required compute environment listed below. 
 
 Serverless Compute, Version 6 : How to select an environment version ( AWS | Azure | GCP ) 
 SQL Warehouse : The setup uses shared_warehouse to write and read the traces stored in Unity Catalog. You need CAN USE on it. 
 
 NOTE: This notebook was developed and tested using Serverless V6 . Other compute options may work but are not guaranteed to behave the same or support all features demonstrated.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B. Metric Backfill
chunks.text:
Scenario 
 The setup script created an MLflow experiment with multi-turn conversation traces and deployed a ConversationCompleteness judge. Your first task is to verify the setup, run the monitoring job, and inspect the results. Then you will add a new Safety scorer and backfill it on the historical traces. 
 

 
 
 
 Experimental 
 The ConversationCompleteness judge in this lab uses multi-turn evaluation, which is Experimental. Its API and behavior might change in future releases.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B1. Inspect the Experiment and Run the Deployed Job

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B2. Backfill a New Safety Scorer
chunks.text:
Now that you have seen the completeness results, you want to add a **Safety** scorer to check all historical traces for harmful content. Since Safety is a single-turn scorer, you can use `backfill_scorers` with a `BackfillScorerConfig` to retroactively evaluate the existing traces at a custom sample rate.

 
 
 Why backfill instead of just .start()? 
 .start() only evaluates new incoming traces . The 9 traces from the setup already exist. To evaluate them, you need backfill_scorers() which retroactively applies the scorer to historical traces. 
 
 

Running `backfill_scorers()` will create a **[experiment_id] Metric Backfill Computation Job** in Jobs & Pipelines. After running the TODO cell below, navigate to the job in the Jobs UI to inspect the output. You should see the traces being fetched and the Safety scorer evaluating them.

**TODO:** Register and start a `Safety` scorer at `sample_rate=1.0` (safety checks run on every trace), then backfill it on the historical traces using `BackfillScorerConfig` with `sample_rate=1.0`.

 
 
 ANSWER B2. Backfill a New Safety Scorer
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import Safety, ScorerSamplingConfig
from databricks.agents.scorers import backfill_scorers, BackfillScorerConfig

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Register and start the Safety scorer
chunks.text:
safety = Safety(model=judge_model).register(name="safety_check")
safety = safety.start(sampling_config=ScorerSamplingConfig(sample_rate=1.0))

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Backfill every historical trace
chunks.text:
job_id = backfill_scorers(
 scorers=[BackfillScorerConfig(scorer=safety, sample_rate=1.0)]
)
print(f"Backfill job ID: {job_id}") 
 

 
 

 
 
 DEEP DIVE What does backfill_scorers() actually do?
 
 

 backfill_scorers retroactively applies scorers to historical traces that already exist in the experiment. Per the docs: "You can retroactively apply new or updated scorers to historical traces." 

 Step by step: 
 
 Resolves the active experiment . Uses the currently active MLflow experiment, or an explicit experiment_id= parameter 
 Looks up scorers . Accepts name strings (uses registered sample rates) or BackfillScorerConfig objects (custom rates per scorer) 
 Creates a backfill job . Returns a job_id (string) for status tracking 
 

 
 Scheduled job (.start()) Backfill (backfill_scorers()) 
 
 Evaluates new incoming traces on a recurring schedule Evaluates historical traces retroactively, once 
 Ongoing One-shot 
 

 Important constraints: 
 
 Scorers must already be registered and started in the experiment 
 Without start_time or end_time , the backfill covers only the last seven days. Pass an explicit start_time to evaluate older traces 
 

 Source: Backfill historical traces with scorers ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: B3. Verify Assessments on Traces
chunks.text: Run the cell below to search for recent traces and confirm that the Safety backfill assessments have been attached. The backfill runs as a separate job and takes a few minutes. If the `assessments` column is still empty, wait for the **Metric Backfill Computation Job** run to finish in Jobs & Pipelines, then rerun the cell.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: C. Traces in Unity Catalog
chunks.text:
Scenario 
 The data engineering team wants to build AI/BI dashboards over agent traces and their assessments. This experiment already stores its traces in Unity Catalog, so the data is in governed Delta tables in your schema. There is nothing to copy or sync.

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: C1. Explore the Trace Tables

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: C2. Query Assessments with SQL
chunks.text:
Because the assessments are stored with the traces, one SQL query shows every judge's result for every session. Run it after the jobs from section B finish, so the results are there to query. This is the kind of query an AI/BI dashboard would run.

**TODO:** Query `{catalog_name}.{schema_name}.backfill_traces_trace_metadata` and list each session's user, assessment name, and value. Expand the `assessments` array with `LATERAL VIEW explode(...)` and skip assessments whose scorer returned an error.

 
 
 ANSWER C2. Query Assessments with SQL
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 display(spark.sql(f"""
 SELECT trace_metadata:['mlflow.trace.session']::STRING AS session_id,
 trace_metadata:['mlflow.trace.user']::STRING AS user_id,
 a.assessment_name,
 a.feedback.value AS value
 FROM {catalog_name}.{schema_name}.backfill_traces_trace_metadata
 LATERAL VIEW explode(assessments) t AS a
 WHERE a.feedback.error IS NULL
 ORDER BY user_id, a.assessment_name
"""))

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: D. Cleanup: Stop and Delete All Scorers
chunks.text:
Stop all scorers, then delete them. Use `list_scorers()` to enumerate, `.stop()` to pause, and `delete_scorer()` to remove permanently. Stopping first is optional, since `delete_scorer()` also removes a running scorer, but it shows both lifecycle steps. Historical assessments remain on their traces even after deletion.

 
 
 ANSWER D. Cleanup
 
 

 
 
 
 
 Python 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 from mlflow.genai.scorers import list_scorers, delete_scorer
 
scorers = list_scorers()
print(f"Stopping and deleting {len(scorers)} scorers:\n")
 
for s in scorers:
 print(f" {s.name}...", end=" ")
 stopped = s.stop()
 delete_scorer(name=stopped.name)
 print(f"stopped (rate={stopped.sample_rate}) and deleted")

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Verify
chunks.text:
remaining = list_scorers()
print(f"\nRemaining scorers: {len(remaining)}")

chunks.lecture: 7 - Lab - Backfilling and Querying Multi-Turn Conversations
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
1. **Metric backfill** (`databricks.agents.scorers.backfill_scorers`) retroactively evaluates historical traces with per-scorer sample rate and time range controls
2. **Two backfill modes**: pass scorer name strings (uses registered rates) or `BackfillScorerConfig` objects (custom rates)
3. **Traces in Unity Catalog** (`trace_location=UnityCatalog(...)`) are governed Delta tables from the start: query traces and assessments with SQL, manage access with Unity Catalog grants, and skip the older trace archive job
4. **Management APIs** (`list_scorers`, `get_scorer`, `delete_scorer`) let you audit, update, and clean up scorers in production
5. **Cleanup matters**: always stop and delete scorers when done to avoid unnecessary evaluation costs

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
The **Agent Bricks CLI** (`databricks-agentbricks`) is a command-line tool for building and deploying custom agents in code. It scaffolds a project from a framework template, runs it locally, and deploys it to the Databricks agent runtime. Along the way, it handles model access, memory, sessions, tools, and tracing so you can focus on your agent's logic.

This appendix introduces the core concepts and commands so you know what the CLI does and when you might reach for it.

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: Learning Objectives
chunks.text:
By the end of this appendix you will be able to:
- Describe what the Agent Bricks CLI manages for you and what you still write
- Explain the `init`, `dev`, and `deploy` lifecycle
- Explain the role of `agent.toml` as the declarative source of truth for agent resources
- Compare the CLI with deploying an agent as a Databricks App with Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs)

 
 Note 
 The Agent Bricks CLI is in Beta , so its commands and behavior may change. Treat this appendix as reference material and check the docs for the latest details.

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: A. What the CLI Does for You
chunks.text:
When you build an agent with the Agent Bricks CLI, the work splits into two parts. You write the application logic, and the CLI wires that logic up to Databricks-managed resources.

 
 
 
 YOU WRITE 
 Application logic 
 
 Model choice 
 Prompts 
 Custom Python tools 
 
 
 + 
 
 
 CLI MANAGES 
 Databricks resources 
 
 Model access 
 Managed memory and sessions 
 Managed tools (MCP, UC functions, sandbox) 
 MLflow tracing 
 Deployment and permissions 
 
 
 

| Capability | What the CLI handles |
|---|---|
| **Model access** | Provisions access to a Databricks-served model, so you don't manage credentials or endpoints. |
| **Managed memory** | Long-term memories the agent can write and search, partitioned by actor. Persists facts and preferences across sessions. |
| **Managed sessions** | Conversation transcripts held in managed session stores, partitioned by actor. Sessions can be forked into independent copies. |
| **Tools** | Databricks-managed tools declared in `agent.toml`: a downscoped Unity Catalog sandbox, a Databricks-managed MCP service, or a Unity Catalog function. |
| **Tracing** | MLflow tracing is on by default and sends each run's traces to a per-project MLflow experiment. |
| **Deployment** | Deploys to the Databricks agent runtime and grants the agent's service principal access to its bound stores. |

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: B. The Three-Command Lifecycle
chunks.text:
Three commands take an agent from an empty directory to production.

 
 
 
 1. SCAFFOLD 
 agentbricks init 
 Creates the project from a framework template and writes agent.toml . 
 
 → 
 
 
 2. RUN LOCALLY 
 agentbricks dev 
 Runs the agent on port 8000 with the same runtime and environment as Databricks. 
 
 → 
 
 
 3. DEPLOY 
 agentbricks deploy 
 Provisions the resources in agent.toml and rolls out to the agent runtime.

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: What it looks like
chunks.text:
**Prerequisites:** the Databricks CLI on your path, and Python 3.10 or above with pip.

The CLI ships two framework templates: `langgraph` for LangGraph and `openai` for the OpenAI Agents SDK. The examples below use LangGraph, matching the docs.

 
 
 
 
 Terminal 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 # Install the Agent Bricks CLI
pip install databricks-agentbricks

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: Authenticate with OAuth and set the profile as the CLI's default
chunks.text:
databricks auth login --host https://<your-workspace-url> --profile <profile>
agentbricks login --profile <profile>

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: 1. Scaffold a project (templates: langgraph or openai)
chunks.text:
agentbricks init --framework langgraph my-agent
cd my-agent

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: 3. Deploy to the Databricks agent runtime
chunks.text:
agentbricks deploy my-agent 
 

When the deployment finishes, the CLI returns the URL of the live agent. The deployed agent is named `agent-bricks-<name>`.

For the step-by-step walkthrough, see: Agent Bricks quickstart ( AWS | Azure | GCP )

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: C. agent.toml: The Source of Truth
chunks.text:
`agent.toml` declares every Databricks-managed resource your agent depends on. CLI commands write to it, and `agentbricks deploy` reads it to provision and wire everything up. The file, not hand-written setup code, is what deploys.

 
 
 WRITE 
 agentbricks init agentbricks tools add agentbricks memory bind agentbricks sessions bind agentbricks tracing bind 
 
 → 
 
 agent.toml 
 declares resources 
 
 → 
 
 DEPLOY 
 agentbricks deploy 
 
 Creates stores 
 Binds tools 
 Grants access 
 Rolls out agent

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: A generated agent.toml
chunks.text:
This is the file that `agentbricks init` generates for a LangGraph agent named `my-agent`:

 
 
 
 TOML 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 schema_version = 1
 
[agent]
framework = "langgraph"
server = "agentbricks"
 
[memory_store]
name = "my-agent-memory"
 
[session_store]
name = "my-agent-session"
 
[tracing]
experiment_name = "/Shared/agentbricks_traces/my-agent"

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: Updating it with CLI commands
chunks.text:
You can add tools and bind stores at any point, not only at `init`. You can also edit `agent.toml` directly.

 
 
 
 
 Terminal 
 
 
 
 
 Copy 
 
 
 # Bind managed session and memory stores (created if they don't exist)
agentbricks sessions bind my-agent-session
agentbricks memory bind my-agent-memory

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: Add a built-in MCP service as a tool
chunks.text:
agentbricks tools list --kind mcp
agentbricks tools add mcp system.ai.web_search

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: View traces from local and deployed runs
chunks.text:
agentbricks tracing list 
 

By default, a tool runs with the permissions of the user who sent the request. Add `--auth app` to run it as the agent's service principal instead.

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: D. Bringing an Existing Agent
chunks.text:
If you already built an agent with LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK, the `--existing` flag helps you move it to the Agent Bricks CLI. The CLI doesn't rewrite your code. Instead, it prepares migration instructions for a coding agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, to follow.

| Step | Command or action | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Prepare** | `agentbricks init --framework langgraph --existing .` | Writes an `agent-bricks-migrate/` directory with instructions, a prompt, and a reference project. Doesn't change your code or create workspace resources. |
| **2. Convert** | Paste the prompt into your coding agent | The coding agent converts the project to use `agent.toml` and a `DurableAgentServer` entrypoint. |
| **3. Check** | `agentbricks doctor .` | Inspects the project files without running code or contacting Databricks. A failed report means the conversion isn't finished. |
| **4. Ship** | `agentbricks dev`, then `agentbricks deploy` | Delete `agent-bricks-migrate/` and its skills first, then run and deploy as usual. |

Switching to a managed session store doesn't move existing conversation history, so decide how to handle earlier conversations before you migrate.

chunks.lecture: 8 - Lecture - Appendix_ Agent Bricks CLI
chunks.heading: E. Comparing the CLI with Apps and DABs
chunks.text:
A common way to deploy an agent is as a Databricks App with Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs). The Agent Bricks CLI is a code-first alternative that declares the agent's resources in `agent.toml` and provisions them on deploy.

| | Apps + DABs | Agent Bricks CLI |
|---|---|---|
| **Resource wiring** | Declared in `databricks.yml` | Declared in `agent.toml` |
| **Deploy** | `databricks bundle deploy`, then `databricks apps deploy` | `agentbricks deploy` |
| **MCP tools** | Connected in agent code with `McpServer` | `agentbricks tools add mcp <service>`, connected at runtime |
| **Tracing** | Added with autologging and `@mlflow.trace` | On by default, sent to a per-project MLflow experiment |

Because traces from a CLI-deployed agent land in a standard MLflow experiment, the same tracing, scorer, and online evaluation techniques apply.

chunks.lecture: AGENDA
chunks.heading: Deploying and Monitoring Agents on Databricks
chunks.text:
This course covers the end-to-end lifecycle for deploying and monitoring generative AI agents on Databricks. Participants will learn how to deploy agents as Databricks Apps using Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs), integrate tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), instrument agents with MLflow Tracing, and evaluate production quality using scorers, multi-turn judges, and online evaluation. Through hands-on demos and labs, participants will gain practical experience building, observing, and monitoring production-grade AI agents on the Databricks platform.

----

chunks.text:

- Familiarity with Unity Catalog
- Experience building agents using the OpenAI Agents SDK
- Basic knowledge of MLflow and Python
- Familiarity with GenAI agent concepts (LLM calls, tool invocation, retrieval)

chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
As developers increasingly use different tools for different stages and types of
work, multi-tool, multi-harness environments have become the default rather
than the exception.
 O P E R AT I O N A L I Z I N G A G E N T F L E E T S AT S C A L E                                         6

Agent quality depends on business-aware context
Once enterprises begin operationalizing agents, the next constraint is context. Agent quality depends
less on raw model power than on whether the agent actually understands the business: the data,
documents, entities, relationships and history it’s working over.

This is where many promising agents begin to fail. They miss the key clause in a contract, join the
wrong tables or choose the wrong tool, not because the model can’t reason, but because the business
context is fragmented.

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
According to Gartner, organizations deploy an average of 897 applications, scattering data, definitions
and institutional knowledge across hundreds of unintegrated silos. Semantics are hard-coded per
application, retrieval pipelines are rebuilt for each use case and memory is scattered across different
systems. In the claims example, one workflow draws from policy PDFs, another from CRM records
and another from adjuster notes in a separate system, so the same assistant gives different answers
depending on where it’s running.

Enterprises that move past this stop treating context as bespoke per-agent logic and start treating
it as a shared layer. They invest in a consistent ontology for data and documents, shared business
semantics and unified memory so agents can reason over the same source of truth across channels
and workflows.

When context becomes a durable asset instead of hidden plumbing, the question shifts from “How do
we make this one agent smarter?” to “How do we ensure every agent operates on the same business
understanding?”
 O P E R AT I O N A L I Z I N G A G E N T F L E E T S AT S C A L E                                         7

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
Governance as the control plane for agent fleets
As agents move deeper into business processes, governance is no longer limited to who can access a
model or table. It needs to extend to what agents can access, what tools they can invoke, what actions
they can take, how they’re monitored and how their costs are controlled. This is especially important
since most organizations don’t start from a clean slate. They govern data, models, agents and
enterprise tools through separate systems, which creates fragmented visibility, inconsistent policies
and duplicated governance work.

Runtime AI governance is often even weaker: static permissions, isolated guardrails and disconnected
monitoring tools provide limited control over agent behavior and rapidly growing AI spend. In insurance
claims, that means one team can see model logs, another can see data access records and a third
can estimate cost, but no one can answer the full question of what happened when an agent took an
action, what context it used and whether that behavior was policy-compliant.

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
According to Gartner, by 2027, 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous AI agents
because governance gaps are only discovered after incidents in production.

That’s why governance is becoming the control plane for enterprise AI. At fleet scale, organizations
can’t manage reliability, compliance and cost as separate processes. They need a unified way to
govern data, models, agents, tools, policies and runtime interactions together. Without that operating
layer, every new agent increases uncertainty. With it, every new agent becomes easier to understand,
control and improve.
 O P E R AT I O N A L I Z I N G A G E N T F L E E T S AT S C A L E                                                                            8

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
The Agentic Platform:
Choice, Context and
Control
                                                                    Enterprise teams that solve the four challenges do so by treating
                                                                    agents as part of a unified platform, not as one-off projects. The
                                                                    practical question for decision-makers becomes: what should that
                                                                    platform actually do and how should it be structured, so agents can be
                                                                    built, run and governed consistently on top of business data and tools?

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
Databricks approaches this with Agent Bricks agent platform for three
                                                                    linked priorities: choice in how agents are built, context in how they
                                                                    understand the business and control in how they are governed in
                                                                    production. Each priority maps directly back to the last-mile, shared-
                                                                    build-system, context and governance gaps described earlier.
 O P E R AT I O N A L I Z I N G A G E N T F L E E T S AT S C A L E                                                            9

Choice: Build and run agents without
rebuilding the stack
Agent Bricks lets teams build agents with the tools they already use,
including coding assistants, frameworks, SDKs and MCP servers.

Internal Databricks research shows that developers already use three
to five coding agent tools simultaneously, underscoring the need to
support a range of tools without rebuilding the underlying stack.

Agent Bricks is designed around that principle, so organizations spend

change underlying AI components as the market moves, instead of being
locked into early choices.

For leaders, the implication is straightforward: avoid architectures where
every new agent requires a new stack. The target state is an environment
where teams can swap models, harnesses or vendors based on evidence
and cost–quality tradeoffs, without touching downstream workflows.

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
Figure 4. The Databricks Platform Agentic Dev & Work and AI Control Plane
 O P E R AT I O N A L I Z I N G A G E N T F L E E T S AT S C A L E                                             12

Control: Centrally govern and optimize agents in production
Finally, a platform for agent fleets needs to act as a control plane. Agents, models, tools and external AI
services should be registered with shared permissions, policies, lineage and audits. When agents run,
they should do so in secure, isolated environments with down-scoped data access, and their activity
should be captured with standard traces, evaluations, telemetry and budgets.

With that layer in place, there is a single place to see what agents are doing and to adjust behavior
over time. Reliability, security and cost are managed as part of one control plane, so adding agents
increases visibility rather than uncertainty, and evaluation data can be reused to tune prompts, tools
and model choices across the portfolio instead of team by team.

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
Databricks’ Agent Bricks, combined with Unity Gateway, is structured to provide this kind of unified
view, but the underlying pattern is general: consolidate policies and monitoring where agents actually
execute, rather than around individual models or applications.

Unity Gateway provides the runtime control layer for these interactions. It provides organizations with
centralized visibility into how agents use models and tools, along with guardrails and contextual policies
to protect sensitive data and control agent actions. It also brings usage and cost into the same control
plane, with granular attribution, budgets, hard spend caps and smart routing to help teams manage and
optimize AI spend as agent fleets scale.

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
For leaders, the prescription is clear: treat governance as the operational backbone of agent fleets.
Choose or build a platform that offers both the flexibility to mix tools and harnesses and the discipline

Best Practices
for Evaluating
Agent Platforms
                                                                    As organizations move from prototypes to production, their requirements mulitply.
                                                                    The real question is not whether a platform can help build an agent, but whether it
                                                                    can support agents as durable parts of the business.

Three core actions to prioritize:

Choose a platform that absorbs the operational heavy lift

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
1       Start with the realities of production: deployment, isolation, tool safety, tracing,
                                                                               evaluation and cost controls. If teams still have to assemble that operating layer for
                                                                               every new agent, the platform is not doing enough.

Treat context as a core capability

2        Look for a unified context layer that combines structured and unstructured data from
                                                                               documents, external systems and business semantics. If every agent needs its own
                                                                               retrieval pipeline and hand-coded view of the business, quality will drift and scaling will
                                                                               get expensive.

Make unified governance non-negotiable

chunks.lecture: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale
chunks.heading: Operationalizing Agent Fleets at Scale (ebook)
chunks.text:
3        Insist on a single view of which agents exist, what they are doing, what they cost and
                                                                               how they are governed. If answering those questions means stitching together logs,
                                                                               policy engines and admin tools, governance is not truly unified.
